title: Investigate repeated lifecycle-boundary misses in fx agent trajectories
body:
## Scope

This is a narrowly scoped correctness investigation, not a confirmed product-wide fx bug. A held-out async lifecycle task produced the same failure signature under the baseline and two bounded remediation treatments. The evidence isolates a repeated agent trajectory, but not a good/bad fx revision or upstream product root cause.

No benchmark-private prompt, verifier, hidden assertion text, or reference solution is included here.

## Exact treatment identity

Pinned fx binary:

- reported version: `0.0.4`
- official release source commit: `d8db856b4c041f69aae436a98b1aa92649bac09c`
- Linux x86_64 binary SHA-256: `ce18caea9d04383b47e39fa9e0b36d135e5f87ea338ea0fa45ce61c1b54b2953`
- model route: `vercel-ai-gateway/zai/glm-5.2`
- effort: `high`
- permission mode: `auto`
- baseline argv shape: `fx ask --json --auto --no-save --no-color -- <prompt>`

Effective request identities:

- baseline/no-save tool-schema SHA-256: `c34ad4d1c1ce32f4d6c60bcded4111d1143eb595d0e67b891f2d7b1c1363f879`
- R1/no-save tool-schema SHA-256: `c34ad4d1c1ce32f4d6c60bcded4111d1143eb595d0e67b891f2d7b1c1363f879`
- R2/saved-ephemeral tool-schema SHA-256: `cd2725fdabb15c3b758e6b1c3eaeba7ac198972ca919c4d33b75377b83363e83`
- R1 and R2 used the same exact generic pre-existing engineering guidance; R2 removed `--no-save` and used a fresh ephemeral HOME
- saved mode added the `subagent` tool; both modes exposed the same twelve terminal actions

## Repeated observation

The generic scenario exercises bounded concurrent work, an interrupt while additional work is queued, and asynchronous cleanup for jobs that had already started.

| Treatment | Result |
|---|---|
| Baseline fx | Failed with the same signature in the original run and a fresh confirmation |
| R1: generic instruction parity, no-save | Failed first attempt; arm stopped |
| R2: generic instruction parity, saved-ephemeral | Failed first attempt; arm stopped |
| OMP control on the same task/model route/environment | Passed |

Failure signature in every fx case: two jobs started, then the parent exited after interruption with zero asynchronous cleanup completions from those started jobs. Independent model-free reruns of each generated patch reproduced the corresponding result.

The failed fx trajectories repeatedly generated implementations that propagated cancellation through a gather-like parent and then cancelled unfinished children again while cleanup was in progress. Their self-tests covered several cancellation cases but missed the combined queued-work + interrupt lifecycle boundary. This is trajectory evidence, not proof that the fx runtime itself causes the defect.

## Uncertainty and exclusions

- No good/bad fx revision has been isolated.
- The tested binary is the official v0.0.4 tag build; no floating-main or arbitrary-commit search was run.
- R1 did not validate a prompt-policy fix.
- R2 did not validate saved/ephemeral mode as a fix.
- Only the qualified GLM 5.2 route above was evaluated.
- Therefore this report does not claim general model inferiority, a product-wide cancellation bug, or a confirmed runtime/tooling cause.

## Requested investigation

1. Add a generic synthetic held-out eval for lifecycle boundaries: bounded work, interruption with queued work, and completion of asynchronous cleanup for started jobs. It should not copy this benchmark task or its private checks.
2. Investigate why repeated fx trajectories omit the combined boundary and re-cancel children already unwinding cleanup despite broader generic verification guidance.
3. Keep build identity available in diagnostics so treatment revisions are unambiguous. PR #231 adds the semantic version alongside the existing build revision in `fx status --json`: https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/pull/231

I can provide additional redacted aggregate request/accounting details if useful, without disclosing the private task material.

title: Auto-mode reviewer is not told which shell will interpret the command
body:
### Summary

In auto mode the classifier decides whether a command may run, and the evidence packet it decides from never names the interpreter that will run it. Shell-routed commands are exactly the ones that reach it, and they execute through the operator's login shell, where an alias or shell function can make an approved string do something else.

### What the reviewer is told

Captured from the real review path for a `git status` call:

```
action: command
command: git status
cwd: /tmp/workspace
background: false
backend: none
target_os: linux
sandbox_scope: restricted
action_evidence_incomplete: false
```

No environment, no shell, no path. The last line is the part that turns an omission into a misstatement: the packet asserts the action evidence is complete, so the model has no reason to withhold judgement over missing context.

### Why it matters

`requiresShellRoute` sends `.clean` and `.user` environments to approval as `dynamic_shell`, and in auto mode an approval-required command goes to `runAutomaticReview`. `capturedInvocation` then resolves `.user` as a login shell and, for bash, appends `-O expand_aliases`. Same command, two invocation shapes:

```
bash -c "git status"                       -> On branch main...
bash -l -O expand_aliases -c "git status"  -> PWNED-BY-ALIAS status
```

The second is the shape fx builds. Omitting the exec profile defaults to the user shell, so this is the ordinary path rather than a corner.

### Where it is dropped

The environment is resolved and in hand at both call sites. `runCommandContext` returns it inside the `CommandContext`, and `AdmissionFingerprint` records it so a granted approval cannot be replayed under a different environment. Only `CommandAction` and `SandboxWideningAction`, the two structs that reach the reviewer, leave it out.

### Scope

This is about reviews that happen. A separate question, which I am not raising here, is which commands reach the reviewer at all.

### Environment

Zig 0.16.0, Linux aarch64, reproduced on `195b73f`.

title: Tell the auto reviewer which shell will run the command
body:
Fixes #237.

`CommandAction` and `SandboxWideningAction` now carry the command environment, and `serializeEvidence` writes the tag plus, for the shell routes, the shell path. A shell-routed environment that cannot name its shell marks the action evidence incomplete, which already fails closed to `.invalid`, so an unnameable interpreter reaches a human instead of an automatic approval.

The field deliberately has no default. A caller has to state the environment rather than inherit a benign-looking one, and that is what surfaced every stale construction site instead of leaving them silently `legacy`. Both production sites take it from the `CommandContext` they were already copying every other field from. Execution and fingerprint matching are untouched.

### Verification

Three tests, each run against the mutation it exists to catch:

| Test | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| packet carries `environment: user` and the shell path | stub the environment writer | fails |
| a shell-routed command with no shell named cannot be auto-approved, even when the model answers allow | stub the environment writer | fails |
| the review request built for a user-profile command describes a user shell | hardcode the wired value to `legacy` | fails |

That third one is the reason it exists. The required field makes the wiring impossible to delete but not impossible to fill in wrongly, and before the test existed, hardcoding `legacy` passed the entire suite.

`zig build test` is 8410 passing against an 8407 baseline on `195b73f`, with an identical set of pre-existing failures. `zig fmt --check` clean.

### Scope

This hardens reviews that happen. It does not change which commands reach the reviewer, and the auto-approve fast path is out of scope here.

Two smaller gaps I did not close: the `.clean` environment and the widening branch have no dedicated tests, though both share the writer that the mutations above cover, and the alias behaviour was demonstrated with bash only, since zsh is not installed on this machine.

title: Support native Fish execution in the terminal tool
body:
Closes #118.

Fish login shells previously fell back to zsh or bash (#111, #121). Commands ran, but not in the user's shell: config.fish never loaded, fish functions and fish_add_path entries were missing, and an explicit fish executable was rejected with UnsupportedShell.

## What changed

- `shell_resolver` recognizes fish as a supported shell. `Invocation` now carries its resolved `ShellKind`, so downstream consumers stop guessing from basenames.
- PTY argv: `fish -l -i` for the user profile, `fish --no-config -i` for clean starts. `--no-config` requires fish 3.2 (March 2021) or newer.
- Captured runs: `fish --no-config -c` (clean) and `fish -l -c` (user). Fish loads functions without `-i`, and a forced interactive capture would leak greeting output, so the user capture drops `-i`.
- `buildBootstrap` takes a `ShellKind` and emits a fish dialect: `set -e fish_trace` guards tracing, `set fx_terminal_command (string collect < path)` preserves multi-line commands, and `eval` plus `$status` propagate the exit code. `buildSourceCommand` is unchanged; fish accepts `.` for `source`.
- Both `native_session` bootstrap call sites pass `invocation.kind`.
- The captured user-profile special case now switches on `invocation.kind` instead of the raw basename. This also fixes a latent edge where a fallback-to-bash invocation missed `-O expand_aliases`.

## Tests

- The three tests that locked in fish rejection now use nushell as the unsupported shell, preserving fallback coverage.
- New tests: fish argv (user and clean), fish captured invocations, fish-native profile resolution, and byte-exact fish bootstrap output for the commandless and command forms.
- `zig build test`: 8265/8266 pass, 1 pre-existing skip.

## Verification

On macOS arm64 with fish 4.7.1:

- Ran the exact generated fish bootstrap (asserted byte for byte in the unit test) through `fish --no-config -i -c ". 'path'"`. The command ran, exit code 7 propagated, a missing command file and a failed marker both returned 125, and multi-line commands survived `string collect`.
- Drove `./zig-out/bin/fx` end to end: `terminal start` with shell executable `/opt/homebrew/bin/fish` opened a session and fx read the fish prompt through the PTY. The same request fails with UnsupportedShell on the released v0.0.3.

## Known gaps

- No Bun E2E coverage yet. CI runners would need fish installed. Happy to add the suite if that works for you.
- Command generation is not told the session dialect, so agent-authored POSIX one-liners can still misfire inside fish sessions. That is the "make the active shell semantics clear to command generation" item from #118 and needs its own change.

Nushell, Elvish, and Xonsh remain out of scope per the issue.

title: Auto-approved commands are re-read by the operator's shell before they run
body:
### Summary

In auto mode, a command approved by the safe-command allowlist is then re-read by the operator's login shell, so the command that runs can differ from the command that was approved. No reviewer is involved, and the transcript still shows the original string.

### The invariant

`knownReversibleAutoCommand` states its own contract:

> Returns true only for a small parsed set of ordinary development commands whose effects are expected and recoverable in auto mode. Unknown syntax, dynamic shell expansion, publication, deletion, and wrappers remain on the normal review path.

Alias expansion is shell expansion, applied to the same string after that parse. So the effect that runs is not the effect that was parsed, and the exclusion the comment describes is what the execution layer then performs.

### The path

`resolveOrdinaryPermissionOutcome` consults `knownReversibleAutoCommand` in its auto branch and returns `shellPermissionOutcome(.auto_mode)` before `automaticReviewOutcome` is reached, so the reviewer is never called. `reversibleGit` accepts `git status` (`src/core/shell_command/command_effect.zig:130`). Execution resolves `.user` as a login shell and, for bash, appends `-O expand_aliases` (`capturedInvocation` in `src/core/terminal/shell_resolver.zig`), which is what lets the profile redefine the command.

### Reproduction

With `alias git='touch ALIAS_EXECUTED'` in the profile of an isolated HOME, auto mode, one `git status` tool call:

```
alias present: classifier requests 0, tool status success, exit 0, ALIAS_EXECUTED created
no alias:      classifier requests 0, exit 128 (git itself, outside a repository)
```

Trace from the same run: `approval_source=auto_mode decision=once` and `sandbox explicit command environment=user shell=/bin/bash`.

`ask` mode blocks it: the command never runs. The sandbox setting made no difference here, though its backend looks inert on Linux and I have not tested macOS seatbelt.

### What this is and is not

The aliases are the operator's own configuration, not remote input, so this is not remote code execution and I would not call it a vulnerability. What it is: an approval decision made about a different command than the one that runs, in the mode whose purpose is to skip human review. The consequence worth weighing is durability. Anything that writes one line into a shell profile, including an approved edit fx makes itself, turns every allowlisted command into unreviewed execution from then on, and nothing in the transcript shows it.

Existing fixtures miss it because the isolated HOME they build has no shell profile, so there is no alias to shadow anything.

### Environment

Zig 0.16.0, Linux aarch64, reproduced on `195b73f`.

Related but distinct: #237 is about reviews that happen not naming the interpreter. This is about commands that never reach a reviewer.

title: Treat Thai combining marks as zero-width cells
body:
## Problem

Typing Thai in the composer makes tone marks and above/below vowels disappear. Thai combining marks (U+0E31, U+0E34-U+0E3A, U+0E47-U+0E4E) were classified as width-1 cells, but terminals composite them onto the preceding cell without advancing the cursor. Every column computation (cursor math, incremental repaint addressing, soft-wrap, row clipping) therefore desyncs from the physical terminal: later glyphs get written into the wrong cells, and a wrap that splits a base character from its mark leaves the mark compositing onto the row-prefix space, where it is invisible.

## Fix

Add a `combining_ranges` table to `unicode_display_data.zig` covering the Thai block Mn/Me subset and consult it from `isCombining()` in `display_width.zig`. This single change propagates through the whole stack: width accounting, grapheme grouping in `text_boundaries.zig`, soft-wrap (no break between base and mark), the VT engine's combining-suffix path, cursor columns, and clipping budgets.

The table is named generically because it is intended to grow toward the full Mn/Me set script by script; this PR deliberately scopes to Thai to keep the blast radius reviewable (three Mn codepoints currently classified wide — U+302A-302D, U+3099-309A, U+16FE4 — are left for a follow-up).

## Commits

1. Add combining mark ranges for the Thai block (data)
2. Treat Thai combining marks as zero-width cells (policy + width tests)
3. Group Thai combining marks into single editing characters (boundary tests)

## Tests

Six new tests covering runeWidth, visibleWidth (e.g. กั้ง = 1 cell, น้ำ = 2 cells since SARA AM is spacing), displayUnitAt zero-width units, stacked-mark grouping (นุ้), SARA AM cluster splitting, and spacing-character non-absorption. All 42 existing width/boundary tests plus the fuzz invariants pass.

title: Terminal tool is unavailable when the uid has no passwd entry
body:
## Summary

The `terminal` tool is completely unavailable in any environment whose uid has no passwd entry, and it rejects POSIX `sh` even when an explicit shell path is provided. Containers launched with `docker run --user <uid>` — a standard hardening pattern — hit this immediately: every terminal action fails with `MissingLoginShell` and `shell_path: (unknown)`, leaving agents with no way to execute builds or tests while all file tools keep working.

## Mechanism

Verified at the v0.0.4 release commit (`d8db856`) and still present in v0.0.5 (`df7e624`), in `src/core/terminal/shell_resolver.zig`:

- `configuredLoginShellInto` resolves the login shell exclusively from the uid's passwd entry via `getpwuid_r`; the `SHELL` environment variable is never consulted anywhere in terminal resolution.
- `supportedLoginShell` returns `error.MissingLoginShell` when the passwd lookup yields nothing, which disables the tool for every profile (`user`, `clean`, and default).
- `shellKind` accepts only `bash` and `zsh`. An explicitly requested `/bin/sh` or `/bin/dash` fails with `error.UnsupportedShell`, so there is no user-side workaround inside the tool surface.

## Reproduction

```
docker run --rm --user 61000:61000 oven/bun@sha256:e10577f0db68676a7024391c6e5cb4b879ebd17188ab750cf10024a6d700e5c4 \
  sh -c 'getent passwd $(id -u) || echo NO_PASSWD_ENTRY; ls /bin/bash /bin/zsh'
```

The uid has no passwd entry, so any fx terminal action inside such a container fails with `MissingLoginShell`. The same image with a passwd-backed uid works, because the fallback `/bin/bash` exists.

## Observed impact

In the #233 investigation, both retained fx trajectories on the lifecycle task ran in such a container: 19/19 terminal invocations failed across all profiles and explicit shell paths, and the agent reported its patch was "reasoned through statically but unverified by execution." Headless agents in hardened CI/container environments lose all dynamic verification while appearing otherwise healthy.

## Suggested direction

1. When the passwd lookup fails, consult `SHELL`, then fall back to an existence-checked `/bin/bash` → `/bin/sh` chain for captured, non-interactive commands. Interactive sessions may keep the stricter login-shell contract.
2. Supporting POSIX `sh` for captured commands requires a bootstrap variant without `builtin eval --` (bash/zsh-only) and without `--login`/`--noprofile`-style flags.
3. Improve the diagnostic: name the actual cause ("no passwd entry for uid N; set a supported shell or run as a passwd-backed user") instead of `MissingLoginShell` with `shell_path: (unknown)`.

Related: #233 (investigation where this surfaced).


## Addendum: the error message blames the wrong thing

When shell resolution fails, the tool result rendered to the model is `terminal exec arguments are invalid: MissingLoginShell`. The arguments are not invalid — the environment has no resolvable shell — and in our retained transcripts this wording sent agents down long retry chains of alternate profiles and explicit shell paths instead of surfacing the environment problem. Whatever shape the fix takes, the failure should render as an environment/shell-availability error, not an argument-validation error.

title: glob_files misses untracked files in subdirectories when searching from the workspace root
body:
## What happens

In a git workspace, `glob_files` searching from the workspace root only sees tracked files plus untracked files sitting directly in the root. An untracked file one directory down is invisible. Searching the same file with `path` set to its directory finds it.

## Repro

In a git repo with at least one tracked file:

```
$ echo hi > src/untracked.txt        # not added
glob_files { "pattern": "**/*.txt", "path": "." }
[glob] 1 matches for **/*.txt
 - src/tracked.txt

glob_files { "pattern": "**/*.txt", "path": "src" }
[glob] 2 matches for **/*.txt
 - src/tracked.txt
 - src/untracked.txt
```

The same file is present or absent depending only on the search root. A tracked file at `src/` is found from the root, so the pattern itself is fine, and an untracked file at the root is found too.

## Why

`callWithWorkspaceOptions` sets `include_untracked` only for scoped search roots (`src/tools/filesystem/glob_files.zig:142`). At the root it stays false, so discovery runs `git ls-files -z --cached` (`src/core/workspace/workspace_files.zig:180`), which lists tracked files only. `mergeRootUntrackedCandidates` (`glob_files.zig:356`) exists to patch that gap, but it iterates the workspace root directory and keeps only `.file` and `.sym_link` entries, so it recovers untracked files at depth 1 and nothing deeper.

Scoped searches take the other branch: `force_fallback` is set alongside `include_untracked`, so they use the recursive walk and see everything.

## Impact

This is the write-then-search loop. A file the agent just created at `src/new.zig` does not show up in its own `**/*.zig` search from the workspace root until someone runs `git add`. The tool description promises to find file paths matching a glob pattern and says nothing about tracked-only results, and there is already a test asserting root globs include untracked files (`glob_files.zig:921`), so the depth limit looks unintended rather than deliberate.

Existing coverage misses it because the glob evals build their workspace with `createWorkDir`, which is not a git repo, so discovery falls back to the recursive walk and finds everything.

title: Reasoning effort is silently ignored for gateway models
body:
## Summary

The `effort` setting has no wire effect for gateway models. On the default gateway route (`/v3/ai/language-model`), fx sends only `headers`, `prompt`, `toolChoice`, and `tools` — no reasoning or thinking configuration, no `temperature`, and no `maxOutputTokens` — regardless of the configured effort. Only the OpenAI Codex provider maps effort into its requests, so for every gateway model the documented setting is silently ignored and reasoning-capable models run at whatever the provider default happens to be.

Verified against the v0.0.5 release commit (`df7e624`).

## Observed behavior

Captured against a loopback fake gateway (no credentials, `FX_GATEWAY_BASE_URL`/`FX_GATEWAY_CHAT_URL`/`FX_E2E_GATEWAY_MODELS_URL` overrides), model `zai/glm-5.2`, `~/.fx/settings.json` containing `"effort": "high"`:

- request body top-level keys: `headers`, `prompt`, `toolChoice`, `tools` — nothing else
- identical body shape with effort unset, so the setting produces no observable difference on this route

## Source

- `src/gateway/openai_codex.zig:87` maps `provider_options.reasoning` into `"reasoning":{"effort":…}` for the Codex provider
- the gateway request build in `src/gateway/client.zig` has no equivalent: no reasoning, sampling, or max-output mapping for `/v3/ai/language-model`

## Impact

- `effort` (settings key, a profile-owned documented option) is a silent no-op for the default provider
- thinking-capable gateway models (for example GLM 5.x) cannot have reasoning enabled, disabled, or budgeted from fx; behavior is pinned to upstream defaults with no user control
- users comparing effort levels on gateway models measure noise

For clarity: this did not cause #233 — the decisive rerun there passed 3/3 with no fx changes once the executor worked (see #233 for receipts). Filing separately because it is an independent contract gap.

## Suggested direction

1. Map effort into the gateway request via the AI SDK protocol's provider options for families that support it, mirroring the Codex mapping.
2. Where a model or family cannot express effort, surface that (documentation and/or a one-time notice) instead of silently accepting the setting.

Reproduction is deterministic with the env overrides above; happy to share the capture harness.


## Probe evidence (gateway route, exact fx headers)

Direct requests to `/v3/ai/language-model` with fx's headers (`ai-gateway-protocol-version: 0.0.1`, `ai-language-model-specification-version: 4`, model `zai/glm-5.2`) and a tiny prompt:

- baseline with no generation parameters: thinking is **on by default** — the stream contains `reasoning-start`/`reasoning-delta` and usage reports ~109 reasoning tokens, so the practical impact of this issue is missing *control*, not missing reasoning
- `providerOptions: { zai: { thinking: { type: "disabled" } } }` is **honored**: reasoning tokens drop to ~13 on the same prompt
- top-level `maxOutputTokens`, `temperature`, `reasoningEffort`, and `providerOptions.gateway.*` variants are all accepted with HTTP 200 (single samples; only the thinking-disabled case shows an unambiguous behavioral difference)

So a fix has at least one verified mapping point. The open product question is the effort-to-family semantics: OpenAI-family models can take fx's effort vocabulary directly (fx already maps it for the Codex provider, `minimal` → `low`), while binary-thinking families like Z.AI need a decision about which effort levels mean enabled versus disabled, and budget-based families (Anthropic, Google) need tier-to-budget choices. Happy to open a PR once a preferred shape exists; the conservative first slice would be plumbing `providerOptions` through the gateway request plus the unambiguous OpenAI-family mapping.

title: Find untracked files at any depth in root globs
body:
Fixes #275.

Root globs asked git for tracked files only and then tried to recover untracked ones by reading the workspace root directory, which caught files at depth 1 and nothing below. A file written to `src/` and not yet added was invisible to `glob_files **/*.zig` from the root, while the identical search with `path: "src"` found it, because scoped searches take the recursive-walk branch instead.

The fix sets `include_untracked` for root searches so discovery runs `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` and gets untracked files at any depth from git itself. The depth-1 readdir merge and its helpers go away with it.

Two behavior notes. Root globs no longer return gitignored files: the readdir merge used to surface them, but only when they sat directly in the workspace root, so the old behavior was inconsistent by depth rather than deliberate. And untracked files inside `node_modules`, `dist`, and the other ignored-name directories now reach root globs when they are not gitignored, which is what `grep_files` already does through its own untracked pass. Both are covered by tests so they stay decisions rather than accidents.

Coverage: two unit tests plus a parity test for the ignored-name case, and two e2e tests that drive the built binary through a fake gateway for both directions. Every one of them fails against the previous binary.

title: Respect the XDG base directories on Linux
body:
Resolves the fx profile through the three XDG base directory roots on Linux, appending `fx` to each.

Refs #110

| Root | Variable | Default | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| config | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | `~/.config/fx` | `settings.json`, `mcp.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `backups/` |
| state | `XDG_STATE_HOME` | `~/.local/state/fx` | `sessions/`, `logs/`, credentials, `terminal-host/` |
| data | `XDG_DATA_HOME` | `~/.local/share/fx` | `skills/`, `memories.json` |

An unset, empty, or relative value is ignored in favor of the default. Missing base components are created 0700, and one that already exists keeps its mode.

Two rules override that resolution:

* A legacy `~/.fx` holding a recognized entry collapses all three roots back onto it. Nothing is moved, copied, or deleted to migrate.
* Only Linux splits. macOS and every other target keep `~/.fx` whatever the environment exports.

The terminal host moves only its socket to `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and keeps its identity in the state root, so a runtime directory cleared at logout never takes the host with it. `fx doctor` reports the active layout and the three resolved roots.

Full CI for the exact head commit passes on all four platforms. The macOS arm64 PGSO candidate failed two p95 tail-latency comparisons while the corresponding p50 changes remained below the 10% threshold. It also failed on a tui-subagent-manager.test.ts case that passed after the bounded retry in Full CI for the same commit.

title: fx ask --json reports no token usage or spend
body:
## Summary

`fx ask --json` reports no token usage or spend information, and with `--no-save` there is no way to recover it afterwards: the result object contains only `output`, `exit_code`, `model`, `session_id`, `steps`, and `tool_calls` (plus `recovery`/`error` when relevant), while `fx usage` requires a saved session. Headless and CI consumers cannot account for tokens or cost at all, even though the gateway returns usage on every completion and fx already consumes it internally.

## Observed behavior

Run any headless prompt against a loopback fake gateway whose SSE `finish` carries `usage` (no credentials needed, `FX_GATEWAY_BASE_URL`/`FX_GATEWAY_CHAT_URL`/`FX_E2E_GATEWAY_MODELS_URL` overrides):

```
fx ask --json --auto --no-save --no-color -- "Create probe.txt containing probe."
```

The final JSON object contains no usage fields of any kind. The same is true for saved-session runs' `ask --json` output; only `fx usage` (saved sessions) exposes totals later.

## Impact

- Headless/CI callers cannot attribute tokens or spend to a run without a proxy in front of fx.
- `--no-save` runs are permanently unaccountable: the data is received, used for internal accounting, and dropped.
- Concretely, this blocked a paired benchmarking campaign from producing any fx cost-per-success figure while the competing harness's totals were measurable.

## Suggested direction

Include the turn's settled usage in the `ask --json` result, for example:

```
"usage":{"requests":3,"input_tokens":1200,"output_tokens":450}
```

with inputs summed per request (each request bills its full prompt), so the totals line up with what the gateway invoices. PR #280 proposes the first slice: main-agent completion token totals. Nested tool/provider usage and asynchronously reconciled spend remain part of this issue.

title: Report turn usage totals in ask --json output
body:
## Problem

`fx ask --json` drops completion token usage. With `--no-save`, that information cannot be recovered later.

## Change

- add a stable `usage` object to final JSON results: `requests`, `input_tokens`, and `output_tokens`
- sum every settled main-agent completion in the turn; input tokens remain full-prompt occupancy per request, matching provider billing
- count settled completions without token totals as one request with zero tokens
- preserve the existing saved-session behavior, which records the latest completion in session state
- carry settled totals through typed error results, including non-interactive permission failures
- render preflight and startup errors through the same result schema with zero usage

Scope is intentionally narrow: nested tool/provider usage and asynchronously reconciled spend are not represented by these fields. This PR exposes the completion usage already available on the main agent loop and leaves #279 open for those residuals.

title: Direct-subscription responses exhaust session usage reservations
body:
## Issue details

Saved sessions using the direct Codex subscription route leak one usage reservation per successful completion. After 64 completions, the next request fails locally with:

```text
System: request failed: UsageCapacityExceeded
```

This is not a ChatGPT subscription limit. The direct Codex response ID uses the `resp_*` namespace, while the session usage ledger accepts only Vercel AI Gateway `gen_*` generation IDs. Validation rejects the Codex ID, marks billing incomplete, and leaves the invocation reserved.

### Environment

- fx `0.0.5` (`df7e6245e199`)
- macOS arm64
- Provider: Codex subscription
- Model: `gpt-5.6-sol`
- `fx doctor`: authentication and startup checks pass

### Minimal reproduction

1. Sign in with `fx login codex`.
2. Run a saved request:

   ```sh
   FX_MODEL=gpt-5.6-sol fx ask --json --yolo "Reply with exactly OK."
   ```

3. Inspect the new session's `usage-v2.json`.

The request succeeds and returns `OK`, but its snapshot remains unsettled:

```json
{
  "billing": "incomplete",
  "next_sequence": 2,
  "settled_through_sequence": 0,
  "request_count": 0,
  "models": [],
  "pending": []
}
```

A reviewed trace contains:

```text
[session] usage generation checkpointed incomplete reason=InvalidGenerationId
[session] usage generation queued sequence=1 id=resp_[redacted]
```

Longer affected sessions reached `next_sequence: 65` and `next_sequence: 129` while `settled_through_sequence` remained `0`. Once 64 live reservations accumulate in one process, `GatewayObservation.begin` returns `UsageCapacityExceeded`. Restarting temporarily clears the in-memory reservations, but the leak resumes.

### Expected behavior

A successful direct-subscription completion should settle its usage reservation without requiring a Vercel AI Gateway generation ID. Invalid generation metadata must also never leave an active reservation behind.

### Existing fix

Draft PR #245 appears to address this exact failure by distinguishing direct Codex completions from Gateway generations and defensively settling rejected observations:

- https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/pull/245

Related retry issue #230 covers repeated transport failures, but not this deterministic `resp_*` identity mismatch and 64-reservation exhaustion.

## Trace

The relevant reviewed and redacted trace lines are included above. No credentials, full response IDs, prompts containing private data, or private paths are included.

## Sensitive information

- [x] I reviewed the information above and removed secrets and other sensitive data.

title: Forward Codex compute residency for Enterprise OAuth sessions
body:
## Problem

ChatGPT OAuth access tokens can include a namespaced `chatgpt_compute_residency` requirement. fx currently extracts `chatgpt_account_id` but does not forward the compute residency value to either direct ChatGPT Codex request path:

- `GET /backend-api/codex/models`
- `POST /backend-api/codex/responses`

A deterministic loopback reproduction with a token containing `chatgpt_compute_residency: "us"` captured both requests with `chatgpt-account-id` present and `x-openai-internal-codex-residency` absent. Region-constrained Enterprise and Edu workspaces can therefore receive geography or residency authorization failures even with valid subscription credentials.

This is inference routing metadata. `chatgpt_data_residency` describes storage at rest and should not override the compute claim. `no_constraint`, malformed, control-bearing, and oversized values should omit the header.

OpenCode implemented the same compute-residency behavior in [anomalyco/opencode#42432](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/42432).

## Expected outcome

- [ ] Extract bounded `chatgpt_compute_residency` from the namespaced OAuth access-token claim.
- [ ] Add `x-openai-internal-codex-residency` to direct Codex model-discovery and response requests.
- [ ] Omit the header for `no_constraint`, missing, malformed, unsafe, or oversized values.
- [ ] Keep ChatGPT credentials and residency metadata off Vercel AI Gateway requests.
- [ ] Cover claim semantics, both direct endpoints, and origin isolation deterministically.

title: Drop redundant saved notices for settings toggles
body:
## TL;DR

Setting toggles that already announce their new state printed a second, routine `saved to user settings (scope=user)` line right before the state line. This PR removes that redundancy so every toggle reports one line, matching the single-line pattern `/sound` already uses and asserts on in `tests/e2e/notifications.test.ts`.

Rebased onto `5ed3be1`. Net diff: 2 files, +10/−24.

## What changed

- **`src/core/app/app_commands.zig`** (core file)
  - `persistUserPreferences` gains an `announce_commit` param with the same semantics and doc comment as the existing `persistPreferenceTargets` in `session_commands.zig`.
  - The call site that also prints a state notice passes `false`: `/statusline`.
  - The `/sound` handler's inline attempt/report block was byte-for-byte equivalent to the generalized helper, so it collapses into one call.
  - `slash-menu-categories` keeps `true`: it has no state notice, so the saved line remains its only feedback.
- **`src/core/session/session_commands.zig`** (core file)
  - `selectEffortFromSettings` (settings-menu effort change) now announces state via the existing `applyEffort(effort, announce=true, persist=true)` path; persistence then drops its saved line through the pre-existing `!announce` wiring. `/history` is intentionally untouched.

No generated files, no mechanical-only files. Single commit, single concern.

## Behavior

- Success notices for `/statusline` and menu-driven effort changes go from two lines (or a bare "saved" line) to exactly one state line.
- Persistence failures still print, and commit warnings (shadowed sources, cleanup notes) are preserved by `reportUserSettingsCommit`'s existing non-benign check.
- Nothing else about ordering, tone, or persistence semantics changes.

## Risk

Low. The only suppressed output is the benign success line; every error/warning path still emits. Reviewer entry point: `applyStatuslineItem`, `handleNotificationsCommand`, and `persistUserPreferences` in `app_commands.zig`, plus `selectEffortFromSettings` in `session_commands.zig`.

## Test coverage

- `zig build test`: 8406 pass / 8 fail — identical failure set on the base commit `5ed3be1` (environment-specific session-picker, terminal-schema, and transcript-runtime failures, reproduced in a clean worktree of `origin/main`).
- `bun test config-persistence.test.ts notifications.test.ts`: 33 tests, 0 fail after rebase (covers statusline toggle persistence, sound notice assertions).
- Manual tmux verification against `zig-out/bin/fx`: `/statusline session` and `/statusline context` each emit exactly one line; `~/.fx/settings.json` persists correctly; stderr clean.

## Before / After

![before-after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/doanbactam/fx/pr-media/before-after.png)

Left: `main` prints a redundant `saved to user settings (scope=user)` line for every statusline toggle. Right: this PR prints one state line per toggle. Same commands, fresh HOME, both binaries built from their exact commits.

title: Send stable prompt cache keys for Codex sessions
body:
## Problem

Direct Codex `/responses` requests omit `prompt_cache_key`. Official Codex derives this field from the session identity and sends it with model requests: https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4f39251a010a8bd7d692d25fb33832ff06f1635a/codex-rs/core/src/client.rs#L485-L497

Without a stable key, requests in the same saved fx session cannot consistently share the intended prompt-cache partition across tool continuations and later turns.

## Reproduction

1. Point the direct Codex responses endpoint at a local recorder.
2. Run a saved `fx ask --json --auto` request that requires one tool continuation.
3. Inspect both request bodies.

Neither body contains `prompt_cache_key`.

## Expected behavior

- Use the existing saved fx session ID as `prompt_cache_key` on every direct Codex request in that session.
- Keep the key stable across tool continuations.
- Omit it when no saved session identity exists, including `--no-save`.
- Do not add cache TTL, retention, retry, telemetry, provider-state, or Gateway behavior.

title: Preserve Codex turn state within each user turn
body:
## Problem

Direct Codex responses can return `x-codex-turn-state`, an opaque routing value that the client must replay on later requests in the same user turn and clear before the next turn. Official Codex documents this as a per-turn contract and tests the reset boundary:

- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4f39251a010a8bd7d692d25fb33832ff06f1635a/codex-rs/core/src/client.rs#L284-L288
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4f39251a010a8bd7d692d25fb33832ff06f1635a/codex-rs/core/tests/suite/turn_state.rs#L24-L67

fx currently discards the response value, so direct Codex tool continuations never send it back.

## Reproduction

1. Point the direct Codex endpoint at a local server.
2. Return `x-codex-turn-state` with a tool-call response.
3. Capture the continuation request.

The continuation has no `x-codex-turn-state` header.

## Expected behavior

- Capture the first usable value from a successful response header or `response.metadata` event.
- Replay it byte-for-byte on later direct Codex requests in the same user turn.
- Ignore empty, whitespace-only, malformed, or oversized values without aborting the response.
- Reset before the next user turn.
- Never send or persist it through Gateway, model discovery, images, permission review, messages, provider state, recovery state, or session JSON.

title: Legacy Streamable HTTP MCP server can drive fx into a no-delay reconnect loop
body:
A legacy Streamable HTTP MCP server that closes a stream cleanly gets reconnected to with no delay at all, for as long as the session lives. Both the notification listener and the tool-call resume path are affected.

## Reproduction

Point fx at a legacy Streamable HTTP MCP server (any of 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26) that advertises `tools.listChanged`, and have its GET notification endpoint answer `200 text/event-stream` with a body that is already finished. Keep the session open.

Measured on `ea90c07` with a local fixture, fx binary built from that commit:

| case | requests | window |
|---|---|---|
| notification GET, stream closes immediately | 27482 | 5.0s |
| notification GET, server sends `retry: 1` then closes | 2164 | 3.0s |
| tool-call resume, server keeps closing a resumable stream | 16953 | 5.0s |
| notification GET, stream held open (control) | 1 | n/a |

The third case comes from a single `tools/call`, and it is bounded only by the operation deadline.

## Why the existing backoff does not catch it

`readNotificationStream` treats `EndOfStream` as a clean result and returns `retry_ms = 0` (`src/core/mcp/legacy_streamable_http.zig:608-617`). `notificationGetCore` guards its only wait, and with it the only cancellation and deadline check, behind `retry_ms > 0` (`:505-528`), so it reissues the GET immediately. Nothing errors, so the exponential backoff in `src/core/mcp/tool_subscription.zig:561-570` never runs, and the listener deadline is not a bound either: `listener_lifetime_ms` is `std.math.maxInt(u32)`, about 50 days (`tool_subscription.zig:18`).

`readSseWithResumption` (`legacy_streamable_http.zig:939-958`) has the same shape on the POST tool-call path.

The other two transports are not affected: both return an error on `EndOfStream` (`legacy_http_sse.zig:518`, `streamable_http.zig:941`), so the close reaches the outer backoff.

## Impact

A remote server, hostile or merely broken, decides fx's outbound request rate. It is not a hang, since cancellation still works and the session ends cleanly, but it burns CPU and hammers the server for the life of the session.

I have a fix and regression tests ready and will open a PR against this.

title: Wait between MCP legacy stream reconnects
body:
Fixes #301.

A legacy Streamable HTTP MCP server that closes a stream cleanly was reconnected to with no delay, for the life of the session. A clean close is not an error, so the exponential backoff in `tool_subscription.zig` never saw it, and the listener deadline is `maxInt(u32)`, so nothing else bounded it either. The same shape existed on the tool-call resume path in the same file.

Both loops now wait one second between reconnects when the server sent no `retry` hint, and check the control deadline every iteration rather than only when the server asked for a delay. A hint the server did send is used as given. SEP-1699 makes the retry field a MUST, so the one second is a default and never a floor over an explicit value.

Measured with the new fixtures, before and after:

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| listener, stream closes immediately | 14598 reconnects / 3s | <= 10 |
| tool-call resume, server keeps closing | 15838 / 5s | <= 10 |
| listener, stream held open (control) | 1 | 1 |

The other two transports already return an error on `EndOfStream` (`legacy_http_sse.zig:518`, `streamable_http.zig:941`), so their closes reach the outer backoff and they needed no change.

## Tests

Three fixture modes (`closed_listener`, `retry_hint_listener`, `resume_storm`) and four cases in `mcp-legacy-remote.test.ts`. Each assertion was checked against the unfixed binary first, so none of them is vacuously green:

- Reconnect spacing, not just a count in a window. A bare count passes under any delay, including one too small to matter; the spacing assertion fails at 0ms without the default.
- A lower bound alongside the upper one. Disabling the listener makes the test fail with `Received: 0`, which is what keeps the upper bound honest.
- The listener still delivers. From its second attempt the fixture sends `tools/list_changed` before closing, and the test asserts the tool list is refetched, so "stopped storming" cannot be confused with "stopped listening".
- The resume loop honors a short operation deadline between attempts, exiting in about two seconds with a cancellation sent upstream.
- An explicit `retry: 500`, the value the conformance suite uses, is honored rather than replaced. Observed spacing is 501ms across seven reconnects, and the assertion bounds it on both sides at the suite's own too-early and very-late thresholds.

The MCP conformance suite is 471 passed / 0 failed, with `sse-retry` on 2025-11-25 reporting `client-sse-retry-timing SUCCESS` and the GET landing 504ms after the stream close. The full `mcp-legacy-remote` suite is green at 41 tests. `mcp-http` and `mcp-stdio` match the pre-change baseline on the same commit, including their pre-existing failures.

## Trade-off worth naming

Against a server that sends no hint the wait is flat, so a well-behaved server that closes its stream cleanly waits up to a second before the listener reconnects. An escalating backoff would be gentler on a persistently broken server but adds state to a loop that currently has none, and one second is already three orders of magnitude below the behavior being fixed. A server that does send a hint sets its own pace, including a very short one, which is what the spec asks for.

The no-hint default is back to one second here. 500ms was picked while the value was a floor over the hint and had to clear the conformance window; now that the hint is honored the default only governs servers that sent nothing, so it is an independent choice. Happy to take 500ms instead if you prefer it.

title: Honor FX_EFFORT as a process-wide reasoning effort override
body:
## Summary

Adds an `FX_EFFORT` environment variable with the same contract `FX_MODEL` already has for the model:

- Wins over `~/.fx/settings.json` and over the preferences of a resumed session, for interactive sessions, `fx ask`, native ACP (`fx acp`), and `fx doctor`.
- Reported as `ConfigSource.process_override` (`StartupState.effort_source`), alongside the existing `model_source`.
- Never written back: `settings.json` keeps the configured effort, and the workspace/session preferences are seeded from the configured effort (`StartupState.configured_effort`), exactly as `configured_model` is used for the model. Resuming the same session later without the variable returns to the saved effort.
- Blank or unparseable values are ignored rather than failing startup (a debug-trace line records the ignored value). `auto`/`default`/`adaptive` select the default effort, matching `ReasoningEffort.parse`.
- `fx doctor` prints `effort=<label>` in the resolved `startup` check.

The resolution lives in one place, `config_runtime.processEffortOverride` / `resolveEffort`, and is used by startup, doctor, and the source marking.

  - `tui-startup.test.ts`: footer shows the env effort, the request carries it, and `--resume-last` without the variable shows and sends the saved effort.

title: Release the usage invocation slot when a generation identity is rejected
body:
## Problem

On a Codex (ChatGPT subscription) session, every prompt starts failing with:

```
System: request failed: UsageCapacityExceeded
```

Once it starts, it never recovers within that session. Restarting fx and resuming works — for another 64 requests.

`UsageCapacityExceeded` here is not a provider signal, it is the session usage ledger's own active-invocation cap (`max_active_invocations = 64`).

## Root cause

`GatewayObservation.begin` reserves an invocation slot per Gateway call and the slot is released by `finishInvocationUnlocked`. On the observed path, identity validation ran first:

```zig
pub fn finishObservedInvocation(...) !void {
    try validateGenerationId(id);   // returns here
    ...
    if (!self.finishInvocationUnlocked(sequence, duration_ms, outcome)) return;
```

`validateGenerationId` accepts only Gateway ids (`gen_` + 26 ULID characters). Codex returns OpenAI response ids (`resp_…`), so the early return stranded the reservation on every single request:

```
[session] usage generation checkpointed incomplete reason=InvalidGenerationId
[session] usage generation queued sequence=1 id=resp_02dd7a185a8e269d016a89d27cbe7487d2ac741377642d1acf
```

The 65th `reserveInvocation` then returns `error.UsageCapacityExceeded`, which propagates out of the prompt as a system error. Restarting clears it because `restore` resets `active_sequence_count` to 0.

A session that hit this four times shows the fingerprint exactly — `next_sequence: 257` (4 × 64 reservations), with no invocation ever accounted:

```json
{"billing":"incomplete","api_duration_complete":false,"api_duration_ms":0,
 "next_sequence":257,"settled_through_sequence":0,"request_count":0,"models":[]}
```


## Fix

* `finishObservedInvocation` finishes the invocation before an identity failure surfaces, so a rejected identity can never strand active capacity. The outcome is recorded as `possibly_billed_without_identity`, matching what the ledger already concluded through the error path.
* `GatewayObservation.complete` routes an id that is not a Gateway generation id through the same path as a missing id, instead of pushing an unusable identity into the observed path. Ambiguous transport evidence keeps `.ambiguous_delivery` as the recorded reason.

Billing semantics are unchanged: these sessions were already recorded as incomplete, and the ledger still files one `incident: incomplete` per subscription request exactly as before. Whether a subscription request should instead count as `.unbilled` is a separate decision, raised on #333.

## Verification

`zig build`, then two new focused tests in `session_usage.zig`, each running `max_active_invocations + 1` iterations to prove capacity no longer drains:

* `rejected generation identity releases the invocation slot` — also asserts the API duration of every rejected invocation is accounted
* `unsupported provider generation identity keeps invocation capacity` — also covers an ambiguous delivery with an unsupported id, and that every sequence settles

Exercised with `./zig-out/bin/fx ask` on a Codex subscription. Trace before/after:

```
before: usage generation checkpointed incomplete reason=InvalidGenerationId
after:  usage billing incomplete sequence=1 reason=generation_identity_unsupported
```

Persisted snapshot for that request now accounts the invocation, where it previously recorded nothing:

```json
{"billing":"incomplete","api_duration_complete":true,"api_duration_ms":1689,
 "next_sequence":2,"settled_through_sequence":1}
```

Full local suite: 8424 passed / 5 failed on this branch versus 8422 passed / 5 failed on `main` — the same five pre-existing failures, which are shell-profile tests that pick up local `zsh` startup noise.

Required label: `type: bug` (I cannot apply labels on this repository).

Fixes #333.

title: Bug: Codex sessions fail with UsageCapacityExceeded after 64 requests
body:
### Issue details

**Version:** fx 0.0.5, macOS arm64, provider `codex` (ChatGPT subscription, `gpt-5.6-sol`).

Partway through a Codex session every prompt starts failing with:

```
System: request failed: UsageCapacityExceeded
```

It never recovers inside that session. Quitting fx and resuming works — for another 64 requests, then it happens again.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. `fx login codex`, `fx provider codex`
2. Run 65 requests in one session (any prompts).
3. From request 65 on, every prompt fails with `request failed: UsageCapacityExceeded`.

**Cause**

The error is not a provider signal — it is the session usage ledger's own active-invocation cap (`max_active_invocations = 64` in `src/core/session/session_usage.zig`). `GatewayObservation.begin` reserves a slot per Gateway call, and `finishObservedInvocation` validates the generation identity *before* releasing it:

```zig
try validateGenerationId(id);   // returns here for Codex ids
...
if (!self.finishInvocationUnlocked(sequence, duration_ms, outcome)) return;
```

`validateGenerationId` accepts only Gateway ids (`gen_` + 26 ULID characters), while Codex returns OpenAI response ids (`resp_…`). So every Codex request strands its reservation, and request 65 fails in `reserveInvocation`. Restarting clears it because `restore` resets `active_sequence_count` to 0.

A session that had hit this four times shows the fingerprint exactly (`next_sequence: 257` = 4 × 64 reservations, nothing ever accounted):

```json
{"billing":"incomplete","api_duration_complete":false,"api_duration_ms":0,
 "next_sequence":257,"settled_through_sequence":0,"request_count":0,"models":[]}
```

Two side effects of the same path: API duration is never accounted on Codex sessions, and one `incident: incomplete` record is appended to `~/.fx/usage.jsonl` per request.

Fix proposed in #332.

### Trace

One `fx ask` request on Codex:

```
[session] usage generation checkpointed incomplete reason=InvalidGenerationId
[session] usage generation queued sequence=1 id=resp_02dd7a…
```

title: Bug: fx --resume aborts with InvalidTranscriptTransition on a healthy session
body:
### Issue details

**Version:** fx 0.0.5, macOS arm64, provider `codex`.

One saved session cannot be resumed: fx exits immediately with

```
$ fx --resume <id>
fx: InvalidTranscriptTransition
```

The session data itself is fine — `fx session <id>` prints the whole 8-turn transcript, and `fx session recover <id>` correctly refuses ("the session has a valid commit boundary"). What fails is the first frame after the resume projection, and the error escapes to the top level and kills the process instead of degrading to a plain repaint.

**What I narrowed down**

* Deterministic: fails on every launch of that session.
* Not terminal-size dependent in the usual sense — it fails at 80x24, 100x30, 120x40, 160x50, 200x100. It only succeeds when the terminal is tall enough for the whole transcript to fit without scrolling (~950+ rows for this session, restored offset 0–5).
* Not a general resume regression: other saved sessions resume fine at non-zero restored offsets (68, 90, 193).
* Isolated to a single turn. Rebuilding the checkpoint with `history[0:7]` resumes cleanly at `target_visual_offset=798`; `history[7:8]` alone (one user turn, 64 tool steps, ~2.1 MB of state, several file-diff presentations with 1461-line before/after content) reproduces the failure at `target_visual_offset=81`.
* Independent of the `resume-view.bin` cache — reproduces with the cache deleted (`outcome=stale` / cold).

The failing check is inside `resolveTransitionTarget` (`src/ui/transcript/runtime.zig`), reached from `resolveTranscriptTransitionTargetForFrame`; `attempt_restore` then reports the error rather than falling back.

Two things seem worth separating:

1. Whatever makes this turn's projection produce a target the transition rejects.
2. A resume that cannot paint its restored viewport should fall back (repaint from the bottom, or drop the restored offset) rather than aborting the process — a rendering invariant currently makes an otherwise healthy session unopenable.

### Trace

```
[session] event=resume_view_cache outcome=stale
[session] event=session_replay source=checkpoint checkpoint_seq=5 tail_bytes=0 elapsed_us=84327
[session] event=resume_projection turns=8 project_us=101865 finalize_us=157988 install_us=794
[render]  viewport_prepared cursor=37,64 last_visible_row=37 replaceable_row=1 reserved_rows=0
[scroll]  transcript_target_resolution_failed err=InvalidTranscriptTransition source_compatible=true geometry_rebase=false recovery_rebase=false normal_buffer_recovery_pending=false target_visual_offset=973
[frame_schedule] attempt_restore outcome=error err=InvalidTranscriptTransition reasons=first_frame,transcript,external_damage reason_count=3 invalidations=1 pending_reason_count=3
```

Restored offsets by terminal height for the same session (120 columns): 24 rows → 1037 (fail), 40 → 973 (fail), 100 → 887 (fail), 900 → 113 (fail), 950 → 5 (ok), 1000 → 0 (ok).

title: Stage transcript projections against the rows the frame granted
body:
## Problem

Some saved sessions cannot be reopened. `fx --resume <id>` exits immediately:

```
$ fx --resume <id>
fx: InvalidTranscriptTransition
```

The session is intact — `fx session <id>` prints the whole transcript and `fx session recover` correctly refuses because the commit boundary is valid. What fails is the first frame after the resume projection, and the error escapes the render attempt and ends the process, so the session is simply unopenable.

## Root cause

Transition staging measures the projection against a `types.Layout`, and the painter guards it:

```zig
if (prepared.selection.split_active or
    prepared.use_selected or
    area.isEmpty() or
    area.top == 0 or
    area.bottom > layout.content_bottom)
{
    return error.InvalidTranscriptTransition;
}
```

`area` is the transcript area **this frame** solved, while `self.layout.content_bottom` is the app layout's content bottom. They disagree whenever the frame reserves fewer footer rows than the app layout does — on the failing resume, the frame granted the transcript rows 1..37 while `content_bottom` was still 36:

```
[scroll] transition_resolve state=invalid target_offset=973 source_offset=0 total_rows=1010 area=1..37
[scroll] painter_reject site=stage_guard split=false selected=false empty=false top=1 bottom=37 content_bottom=36 rows=40 offset=64
[scroll] transcript_target_resolution_failed err=InvalidTranscriptTransition ... target_visual_offset=973
[frame_schedule] attempt_restore outcome=error err=InvalidTranscriptTransition reasons=first_frame,transcript,external_damage
```

Two of the staging sites in `resolveTransitionTarget` already handled this, rebasing the layout onto the frame's area before staging:

```zig
var projection_layout = self.layout;
projection_layout.content_bottom = target_layout.transcript_area.bottom;
```

The other five — the stable semantic-progress staging, the stable history projection, both recovering paths, and the invalid path — passed `self.layout` unchanged, so a frame whose transcript area reached past the app content bottom aborted the transition instead of staging into it.

## Fix

Resolve the projection layout once, from the rows the frame actually granted the transcript, and use it for every staging call in the transition. The two sites that already rebased keep exactly their previous behavior.

For the other five sites this changes two cases:

* **Frame area below the app content bottom** (the crash): the guard now passes and the projection stages into the frame's rows.
* **Frame area above the app content bottom** (a frame that reserves more rows than the app layout — an activity row, a banner): `content_bottom` now drops to the frame's bottom, so a terminated last line that fills the area exactly places the cursor on the area's last row instead of one row below it, outside the rows the frame granted. This matches what the two existing rebase sites already did; it is a deliberate alignment, not an accident of the fix.

### Why this layer

`self.layout` is the app's fixed-footer `types.Layout`; `frame_layout.solve` is the per-frame source of truth, and the two can legitimately disagree on where the transcript ends. The transition already acknowledged that by rebasing at two sites, so extending that to every staging call is the smallest change consistent with the existing design. Keeping `self.layout.content_bottom` in sync with the committed frame layout would remove the need for the rebase entirely; that is a broader change and out of scope here.

## Verification

`zig build`, plus a focused test — `frame transcript rows past the layout content bottom still stage` — that resolves a transition whose transcript area ends one row below `layout.content_bottom`. It fails with `error.InvalidTranscriptTransition` when `projectionLayout` returns the layout unrebased and passes with the fix.

Exercised with `./zig-out/bin/fx --resume` on the session that produced the report, driven through a pty at 80x24, 100x30, 120x40, 160x50 and 200x100: every size resumed, painted the transcript tail and status line correctly, and logged no transition rejection. Three other saved sessions resume unchanged.

Full local suite: 8425 passed / 5 failed, the same five pre-existing failures as `main` (shell-profile tests that pick up local `zsh` startup noise).

Fixes #334.

title: fix(napi): zeroize the copied API key before free
body:
## What

\`sdk/NAPI.md\`'s own "Secret handling" section documented this gap: the API key copied from JavaScript into native heap memory for the N-API core (\`src/napi_core_main.zig\`) was freed with a plain \`allocator.free()\`, with the doc stating plainly *"the allocation is not currently zeroized before free"* and asking for *"a future zeroization change [that] should cover all destruction and partial-construction paths and must not be optimized away."*

I found this while doing a broader manual security review of the repo (unrelated to any existing issue — I checked and didn't find one covering this).

## Where it's freed

Exactly two places, both covered here:
- \`Runtime.deinit()\` — normal teardown at the end of a runtime's life.
- the \`errdefer\` in \`createRuntime()\` — partial construction: fires if \`model\`/\`home\`/\`workspaceRoot\`/\`gatewayChatUrl\` validation fails, or the \`Runtime\` allocation/thread spawn fails, after \`api_key\` is already allocated.

No third path exists: \`createCore()\`'s own \`defer if (runtime_owned) runtime.deinit()\` routes every later failure (handle allocation, \`napi_wrap\`, etc.) back through \`Runtime.deinit()\`, so these two are jointly exhaustive.

## Fix

Route both frees through \`secret.zeroAndFree()\` (\`src/core/auth/secret.zig\`) instead of a plain \`alloc.free()\`. This is the same primitive already used for other credential material elsewhere in the codebase — not a new pattern. It wraps \`std.crypto.secureZero\` behind a \`noinline\` function operating on a \`@volatileCast\` slice specifically so the zeroing write cannot be elided by the optimizer — exactly the failure mode the doc's own comment called out.

Also updated the "Secret handling" section of \`sdk/NAPI.md\` to reflect the closed gap instead of describing it as future work.

## Verification

- \`zig fmt --check\` and \`zig ast-check\` pass on the changed file.
- \`zig build -Dnapi-surface=core -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe\` succeeds (\`zig-out/lib/libfx.node\` builds clean).
- \`npm run --prefix sdk test:node-napi\`: **11/12** native-surface test scripts pass, including the security-focused ones:
  \`\`\`
  native core misuse passed: argument, handle, stale, trace, backpressure, and closed-handle checks are enforced
  native core security passed: malformed creation is stable and ACP stdio MCP is blocked
  \`\`\`
  The 12th (\`test-libfx-loader.mjs\`) fails only on \`ENOENT\` for \`sdk/fx-core.wasm\` — the separate WebAssembly surface, which this change doesn't touch and which I didn't build locally (I only built \`-Dnapi-surface=core\`); unrelated to this diff.
- Full \`zig build test\` (whole-project unit suite): **8440/8443 passed, 2 skipped, 1 failed.** The one failure, \`core.tooling.tool_runtime.test.run_command timeout returns model-visible failure\`, lives in \`src/core/tooling/tool_runtime.zig\` (unrelated to \`src/napi_core_main.zig\` or \`src/core/auth/\`), asserts on a real subprocess's real wall-clock timeout, and failed "without output" (a flake signature, not a deterministic assertion diff) — consistent with scheduling jitter from 2+ concurrent ReleaseSafe zig compiles saturating my machine's CPU during that same run, not a regression from this change. Happy to re-run in isolation if useful for review.

Opening as draft per CONTRIBUTING.md, since I can't run the full 4-platform Full CI matrix locally — the change is small and self-contained (5 lines across 2 files) so should be quick to verify there.

Suggested label: \`type: security\`.

title: Wipe request-side credentials instead of leaving them in freed memory
body:
The device-code, refresh and revoke flows each build a form body that holds the credential itself, and the JS host encodes a Bearer token into its header JSON. Each of those buffers went back to the allocator without being overwritten, while the response in the same function was carefully wiped with `secret.zeroAndFree`. The token stayed readable in freed heap memory after the call.

Overwriting the final buffer is not enough on its own, which is what makes this more than a one-line change. Every one of these paths grows a buffer while holding the secret. The form writer starts near 132 bytes and reallocates as the body grows, which a JWT-sized refresh token easily triggers, and `allocPrint` sizes the Bearer header generously before shrinking to the exact length. Each growth step abandons an allocation that keeps its own plaintext copy. A scan of released buffers found five per form call, not one.

So each path now reserves the encoded worst case up front, or sizes the allocation exactly, and only then overwrites the single remaining buffer at scope exit. The overwrite goes through a new `secret.zero` helper beside the existing `zeroAndFree`, so every secret overwrite still greps as one convention.

`requestDeviceAuthorization` keeps its plain writer, because its form carries only the client id and the scope.

## Verification

The oauth test drives all three form calls through an allocator that inspects each buffer as it is released. Two details make it load-bearing rather than decorative: its credential is long enough to force the growth path, and it searches for a short needle at the head of the value rather than the whole credential, since a buffer abandoned mid-growth holds only a truncated prefix. An earlier version of the test missed both and passed against the unfixed code.

Measured per call site, with a 2 KiB credential, before and after:

| site | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `refreshToken` | 5 | 0 |
| `revokeToken` | 5 | 0 |
| `pollDeviceTokenBounded` | 5 | 0 |
| `executeBearerGet` (JS host) | 2 | 0 |

Removing the reservations while keeping the overwrite puts the test at `expected 0, found 9`, so it covers the growth path specifically and not just the final buffer.

Local `zig build test` and `zig build test -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe` both leave the failing-test set identical to the pre-change baseline on this machine. ReleaseSafe matters here because dead-store elimination is the thing `secureZero` exists to survive, and a Debug-only result would not have shown that.

## Not covered

The JS host path cannot run without a host, so its reservation is guarded by a bound test rather than an end-to-end one. The end-to-end measurement above came from a standalone harness with the host imports stubbed.

`headersJsonCapacity` accepts both call shapes, a comptime tuple and a runtime slice, and the test exercises both. Only the tuple shape is reachable in a native build today, so without that coverage the slice branch would have compiled purely by not being analysed.

The response side is a separate problem and is not addressed here. Tokens parsed out of a JSON response stay in the parser's own released allocations, which I have filed separately. Those counts are identical before and after this branch.


I cannot apply labels on this repo. The intended one is `type: security`.

title: Bug: OAuth tokens stay in freed memory after the response is parsed
body:
### Issue details

Tokens parsed out of an OAuth response stay readable in freed heap memory after the call returns.

`oauth.zig` is careful with the response buffer itself: `fetchJson` returns owned bytes and every caller wipes them with `secret.zeroAndFree`. The JSON parse in between is not covered. `std.json` allocates its own copies of the string values while decoding, and those allocations go back to the allocator without being overwritten, so the access token, refresh token or device code survives in released memory.

Observed on `04e0ae0b` with a wrapping allocator that scans every buffer at the moment it is freed:

- `refreshToken`, with the needle placed in the `access_token` the server returns: one released 674 byte buffer still contained `CRED_NEEDLE_aaaa` in plaintext.
- `requestDeviceAuthorization`, with the needle in the returned `device_code`: one released 814 byte buffer still contained it.

Both are the parser's own scratch, not the response buffer, which is wiped correctly.

Reproduction: call either function through an injected `oauth_transport.Provider` whose response body embeds a recognisable token, using an allocator that wraps `free` and searches the memory for that token before delegating. Any function that parses a secret out of a JSON response should show the same result, so `pollDeviceTokenBounded` is very likely affected too, though I only measured the two above.

For scope: this is separate from the request side, where the form body and the JS host header JSON had the same problem for the outgoing credential. That half has a fix in #364. The response side is untouched by it, and confirmed unchanged by that branch: the counts above are identical before and after.

A fix probably means parsing into memory the module controls, for example decoding through an arena that is wiped before release, rather than trying to chase individual parser allocations.

### Sensitive information

The tokens above are synthetic markers from a test harness. No real credentials appear in this report.

title: Bug: Saving an auth session leaves the tokens in freed memory
body:
### Issue details

Serializing a stored auth session leaves the access and refresh tokens readable in freed heap memory.

`oauth_session.stringify` builds the session JSON in a `std.Io.Writer.Allocating` opened with no reserved capacity. Each growth copies the plaintext into a larger block and releases the smaller one without overwriting it, and `toOwnedSlice` can relocate once more. The three callers wipe only the slice they get back (`publishAndVerifyKeychain`, `Mutation.saveFile`, `HostMutation.save`, each `defer secret.zeroAndFree(alloc, text)`), so every abandoned buffer goes back to the allocator with both tokens intact.

`grok_session.stringify` and `chatgpt_session.stringify` have the same shape and the same callers.

Observed on `41de7ab2` with an allocator that scans every block at the moment it is released:

- `oauth_session.stringify`: one released 165 byte block still contained `CRED_NEEDLE_aaaa` in plaintext. Zero after reserving the size up front.
- Through the real save path, `saveNewSession` to `Mutation.save` to `saveFile`, with `HOME` pointed at a temp directory: 5 blocks released, 1 carrying the token. No other stage of the save released it unwiped.
- The Grok and ChatGPT writers have fewer fields, so a short token fits inside the first allocation and nothing grows. From roughly 64 bytes of token they abandon 1 to 2 blocks per call, and these fields carry JWTs.

Two things that make this easy to miss:

A debug build reports nothing. `Allocator.free` overwrites the block with `undefined` before any wrapping allocator sees it, so the same measurement in a test build reads clean whether or not the bug is present. The numbers above are from a release build.

A regression test that scans freed memory is vacuous for the same reason, and a test with a short token is vacuous because the buffer never grows.

This is the same class as #365 on a different side. #365 is the response parse in `oauth.zig`, and #364 covers the request side. Serialization on save is untouched by both.

A fix is to measure the exact length first with a discarding writer, reserve precisely that, then write once, which is what `auth_runtime` already does for the API key entry buffer: "Reserve the entry ceiling up front so growth never abandons an unzeroed buffer holding part of the key".

### Sensitive information

The tokens above are synthetic markers from a test harness. No real credentials appear in this report.

title: Reserve the auth session buffer before writing the tokens into it
body:
Fixes #378.

`stringify` builds the session JSON in a `std.Io.Writer.Allocating` with no reserved capacity, so the buffer grows while it holds the access and refresh tokens. Each growth copies the plaintext into a larger block and hands the smaller one back to the allocator without overwriting it. The callers wipe only the slice they get back, so those abandoned buffers keep both tokens.

This measures the exact length first with a discarding writer, reserves precisely that, then writes once. The buffer never grows, so nothing is abandoned. `auth_runtime` already applies the same rule to the API key entry buffer, and says why in a comment: reserve the ceiling up front so growth never abandons an unzeroed buffer.

`grok_session` and `chatgpt_session` carry the identical shape with the same callers, so they get the same treatment. Three sites, one mechanism.

Measured with an allocator that scans every block as it is released, in a release build:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `oauth_session.stringify` | 1 released block carrying both tokens, 165 bytes | 0 |
| real save path, `saveNewSession` through `saveFile` to disk | 5 blocks released, 1 carrying the token | 0 |
| `grok_session` / `chatgpt_session`, JWT-length tokens | 1 per call | 0 |

The end to end run also clears the rest of the save path: no other stage released the tokens unwiped.

Output is byte identical before and after across every case, including values whose JSON encoding is longer than the input and multibyte values. That matters here because the size is computed in one pass and the bytes are written in another, so the two have to agree exactly.

On the tests, two traps are worth naming because both produce a green that means nothing:

A test that scans freed memory cannot work. `Allocator.free` overwrites the block with `undefined` before a wrapping allocator sees it, so in a test build the scan reads clean either way. The tests therefore assert that no block is released at all while the tokens are in flight.

A short token fits inside the first allocation, so the buffer never grows and the assertion passes on the unfixed code. The Grok and ChatGPT fixtures use lengths these fields actually carry. With the sizing removed, each of the three tests reports one released block; with a 43 byte token the sibling tests report none.

Verification: each test fails with the sizing removed and passes with it, confirmed by mutating the source and checking the mutation applied.
