title: Allow edits to files up to 16 MiB
body:
## Summary

- `edit_file` and `write_file` can change files up to 16 MiB, with up to 32 MiB of old and new content together. The limits were 4 MiB and 8 MiB, so large lockfiles had to be edited from the shell.
- A file over 16 MiB still fails with a limit error and stays unchanged. The error says to make the change with a shell command instead.
- An edit is saved to the session as the rows its diff shows, not as full copies of the file before and after. Session storage no longer grows by the file's size on every edit.
- Large-file edits use much less memory. Three edits to a 4 MiB file now leave the process at about 55 MiB instead of 225 MiB.
- After a session is resumed, Ctrl+O shows the same full diff as the live session, at every file size the limit allows.
- If one diff's rows exceed 4 MiB of text, the saved view ends with a line that says how many rows were not saved.
- Sessions saved by earlier versions still open and show their full diffs.
- Earlier versions open sessions saved by this one and show the short preview for its edits.

## Design

Raising only the limit made large edits expensive. Three edits to a 16 MiB file used about 830 MB of memory and saved 98 MB of session, because each edit kept both copies of the file and every checkpoint encoded them again. Saving only the preview keeps memory low but loses the full diff after a resume. The rows Ctrl+O shows grow with the change rather than the file, so saving them keeps the full diff at a bounded cost.

The rows go in a `file_review` item right after the edit's `tool_result` item. Earlier versions reject a tool result with a field they don't know but skip item types they don't know, so the tool result keeps the shape they read.

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  commit[Edit commits] --> result[tool_result keeps the old and new file]
  result --> checkpoint[Each checkpoint encodes both copies]
  result --> resume[Resume rebuilds the diff from the copies]
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  commit[Edit commits] --> capture[Diff rows captured once]
  capture --> result[tool_result item with the preview]
  capture --> review[file_review item with the rows]
  result --> resume[Resume]
  review --> resume
  resume --> full[Ctrl+O shows the full diff]
```

title: Reuse the prompt cache across workspaces and mid-session changes
body:
## Summary

- A session in a new directory or worktree reads the shared instructions from the prompt cache on Claude and on GPT-5.6 and later, instead of writing them again.
- The skills list and project rules show paths inside the workspace relative to it, so worktrees of one repository share their cached prompt.
- Permission reviews on GPT-5.6 and later no longer ask OpenAI for a cache write that no later request could read.
- Rules from a folder's AGENTS.md arrive at the end of the tool result that reached the folder, for every model, and the conversation before them stays cached.
- The instructions tell the model to follow rules delivered that way, and a later turn that reaches the same folder again gets a one-line reminder.
- Only fx opens the blocks it adds to the conversation (`<scoped-rules>`, `<fx-context-update>`, `<fx-skill-used>`). fx escapes their tags in tool output, in the text of instruction files, and in a named skill's text. An edit copied from tool output that shows an escaped tag still edits the file's `<`.
- When a later turn checks whether a folder's rules changed, it looks at the file the rules came from, through a symlinked AGENTS.md too, and in libfx at what the host's reader returns.
- Qwen 3.8 Max no longer fails after its first tool call with "System message must be at the beginning."
- After a restart, the note that earlier shell handles are gone rides on the resumed turn's message instead of the instructions. A queued prompt that is removed or refused before it runs gives the note back to the next prompt.
- The date, git branch, and permission mode are sent as they were when the session started. A change arrives as an `<fx-context-update>` block on the message where fx noticed it, and the model answers with the new values.
- A skill named with `$name` sends its text with that turn's message. Later turns get a short note naming the skill instead of its full text.

## How requests change

On main, every request rebuilds the instructions, so any change rewrites the start of the prompt and the provider throws away the cached conversation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E["Branch or permission change, folder rules reached, restart, named skill"] -- "rewrites" --> I
  subgraph R["A request on main"]
    I["Instructions: system prompt, project rules, runtime context, stale-shell note, skill text"] --> H["Conversation"]
  end
```

On this branch the instructions stay as the session's first request sent them, and a change rides on the newest message, after the cached conversation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph R["A request on this branch"]
    I["Stable instructions with a cache marker: system prompt, project rules, the session's first runtime context"] --> H["Conversation, cached"] --> N["Newest message: the user's turn or a tool result"]
  end
  E["Branch or permission change, folder rules reached, restart, named skill"] -- "adds a note to" --> N
```

Each note is saved with its turn, so a resumed session sends the same bytes. When a compaction cuts a turn, the saved ranges move each note with the steps it belongs to, and the compaction window counts the notes' tokens.

## Design record

D93 (context notes), D94 (the saved runtime context and its update notes), and D95 (named skills) in `tests/tla/session_manager/system-design.md` describe each mechanism and what was tried before it. `tests/tla/prompt_context/` models request prefixes, and the drivers in `tests/tla/drivers/prompt_context/` check the real requests along it.

## Why one pull request

The pieces share one mechanism: notes that ride on a message and are saved with its turn. Rules on tool results, the stale-shell note, runtime context updates, and named skills are each a kind of note, built on the same saving, resume, and compaction code. The cache markers alone keep the instructions cached, and the notes keep the conversation after them unchanged. Splitting the note kinds across pull requests would change the saved session format in several releases instead of one.

## Turning it off

Turning this off means reverting it. Sessions in fx's own store open both ways: a session main saved resumes here, and a session this branch saved resumes on main, which skips the item types it does not know. A libfx journal, checkpoint, or snapshot that holds a turn with notes or a saved runtime context is written as version 4, so an older libfx refuses it with `FxJournalVersionError` instead of reporting it as invalid.

## Measuring it

`tests/evals/prompt-cache-ab.test.ts` runs a branch switch, a permission change, folder rules, a restart, and a named skill on two fx builds, through a recording proxy. For each run it reports the requests that break the cached prefix, the new and cached input tokens, and whether the answers are right. `CONTRIBUTING.md` shows how to run it.

Earlier measurements, on 10 model families with two rounds of the same scenarios plus five more, against main at 7d854a42c: requests that broke the cached prefix went from 320 to 41, new input tokens from 6.77M to 3.84M, and cost from $19.48 to $14.84. The 41 that remain are the planned re-read on the turn after one that names a skill, where the short note takes the place of the skill's text, plus one Gemini request after fx's own recovery prompt. One run of a scenario varied by up to about 20% in new tokens between rounds, so compare several runs.

## Verification

- `zig fmt --check src/`, `zig build`, and `zig build test` pass.
- `tests/tla/prompt_context/check.sh`: all 43 configs give their expected verdict. `bun test tests/tla/drivers/prompt_context/`: 20 pass.
- SDK: `bun sdk/tests/test-checkpoint.mjs` and `bun sdk/tests/test-journal.mjs`, each `native wasm` and `wasm native`, and `node --experimental-wasm-jspi sdk/node/test-term-agents-md.mjs`.
- An older libfx: main's journal reader refuses a turn with notes or a runtime context written here with `UnsupportedJournalVersion`, and still reads a plain turn.
- E2E on this head: `sessions` (99) and `tui-resume` (67). Before the last rebase onto main: `gateway-stream-lifecycle` (206, 1 skip; the 5 that failed under heavy machine load pass when rerun), `auto-mode-reliability` (41), `tui-composer-edit-contracts` (34), `tui-gateway-stream-lifecycle` (69), and `acp` (168).
- Undoing each review fix in turn, such as writing a skill's text unescaped or dropping the edit fallback, fails a named test, 13 of 13.
- `zig build fuzz -Dfuzz-target=session_conversation_piece --fuzz=300K` finds nothing.
- Live, `prompt-cache-ab.test.ts` against main on 10 model families (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, GPT-6.1, GPT-5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Grok 4.7, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3) passes for each. Requests that broke the cache went from 80 to 10, new input tokens from 1,043,317 to 610,430 (41% fewer), and right answers from 28 of 50 to 48 of 50. On Qwen 3.8 Max main fails every scenario, and this branch runs all six, with the right answer in each of the five that check one.
- In a separate live run the model copied two escaped lines from `read_file` into `edit_file`, and both edits changed the file's own `<` lines.

title: Ask the user when a request needs them
body:
## Summary

- Status lines and error notices show errors in plain words, such as "couldn't make a secure connection" or "the disk is full". Raw error names go only to the trace.
- In the TUI, a rejected request, a content filter, or a conversation still too long after compacting now waits instead of ending the turn. Enter on an empty composer sends the request again, and one Esc ends the turn.
- While such a request waits, the provider's reason shows in the transcript and the status line says what to do.
- Running out of credits opens a picker: "I added credits, retry", "Switch to another model", or "Cancel this turn".
- "Switch to another model" puts the message back in the composer and opens the model picker.
- The out-of-credits picker replaces the old content-filter picker.
- When a request's fx login, Codex, or Grok sign-in has expired, fx opens that sign-in, and finishing it sends the request again with the new credential.
- One Esc while that sign-in is open closes it and ends the turn.
- fx ask, ACP, and subagents still end the turn on these errors.
- When an answer breaks off and fx resends the request, the TUI removes the half answer and streams the new answer in its place.
- A half answer that already holds a finished table or code block, or that scrolled off the screen, stays, and a short "↻ Restarted the answer" line marks the restart. fx ask and ACP always show that line in place of "[Response interrupted. Restarting.]".

Stacked on #1339.

title: Reconnect when an MCP server drops an idle connection
body:
## Summary

- An MCP tool call over HTTP after the server dropped an idle connection now goes out on a new connection, instead of failing with "the server went away" on every call until fx restarts.
- Renewing an MCP login after the sign-in server dropped an idle connection now goes through, instead of failing with "the sign-in server didn't answer" until fx restarts.
- A connection the server closed cleanly while idle is replaced before the call is sent, so the call no longer fails once with "the tool may have run".
- Connections unused for more than a minute are replaced instead of reused, so a call after the network silently dropped one no longer waits out its timeout.
- A request whose send fails goes out once more on a new connection. A request that was fully sent is still never sent twice.

title: Skill discovery walks past the home folder when HOME is not an ancestor of the workspace
body:
**fx version:** 0.0.14 (macOS arm64)

## What happens

The docs say project skill roots are checked "from the workspace upward,
stopping before your home directory". When `HOME` is not an ancestor of the
workspace, the walk never meets it and goes on to `/`. Every skill folder
on the way counts as a project root, including the real home folder's
`.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills` and `.codex/skills`.

We run fx over ACP (`fx acp`) as the agent of an unattended runner, and give
it its own `HOME` inside the project (`<project>/.tenaz/private/fx-home`)
so the user's fx settings and MCP servers are not touched. With the project
under the user's home folder, fx then finds every skill the user has
installed for other agents: 354 in our case.

Setting `context_limits.skill_catalog_bytes` to `0` keeps them out of the
prompt (fx reports `skill catalog omitted 354 entries … effective=0 bytes`),
but:

- `capability_search` still returns them, and
- the `skill` tool loads any of them, without a permission request, even
  with `permission_mode: "ask"`.

So a session can load a skill that runs a cloud service, which an
unattended local run must not do.

## How to reproduce

1. `mkdir -p ~/probe && cd ~/probe && git init` (any folder under your home
   folder that has skills in `~/.claude/skills` or `~/.agents/skills`).
2. Make an isolated home with a settings file pointing at an
   OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for example
   `HOME=/tmp/fx-home` with `/tmp/fx-home/.fx/settings.json`, and
   `"context_limits": {"skill_catalog_bytes": 0}`.
3. Run `HOME=/tmp/fx-home fx acp` in `~/probe`, send `initialize`,
   `session/new` and a prompt, and have the model call
   `capability_search` (we used a scripted endpoint that returns that tool
   call).
4. The result lists the skills from `~/.claude/skills` and
   `~/.agents/skills`. A following `skill` call with one of their names
   completes with the skill's content and no `session/request_permission`.

The same steps in a folder outside the home folder (`/tmp/probe`) return
`"skills": []`. A symlink from `/tmp` to the project does not help: the
workspace is resolved to its real path.

## What we would like

Any one of these would solve it for us:

1. Stop the upward walk at the repository root (or the workspace root)
   instead of only at `HOME`.
2. A setting to turn off project-ancestor and user skill roots, or to list
   the roots fx may use.
3. With `skill_catalog_bytes: 0`, leave skills out of `capability_search`
   too, and refuse `skill` for skills that were not advertised.

A permission request for `skill` in `ask` mode would also let a client
decide, as it does for other tools.

## Workarounds we found

- Running fx with `HOME` set to the workspace's parent folder stops the
  walk, but makes fx write `.fx/` into a folder that is not ours.
- Denying reads of the skill folders above the workspace (macOS
  `sandbox-exec`) empties the list, but fx then reports that a root "could
  not be read … fix access to the root and reload skills", which invites
  the model to try.

title: Preserve Claude prompt caches when workspace context changes
body:
## What changed

- Mark the end of stable instructions as a request-local cache boundary before live runtime context. The native Gateway serializer emits Anthropic's ephemeral cache-control hint when prompt caching is enabled.
- Keep instruction roles, message order, live runtime context, automatic Gateway caching, and session affinity unchanged. Do not persist the new hint.
- Read Gateway cache-read and cache-write usage and expose it in `fx ask --json`, preserving unavailable counts as `null` and reported zero as `0`.
- Add regression coverage for boundary placement, empty stable prefixes, input immutability, caching disabled, usage parsing, and CLI JSON output.

## What fx users get

With Claude through Vercel AI Gateway, fx can reuse cached stable instructions when workspace context changes while still sending the current context. This changes fx's request construction, not the models themselves.

In the tested branch-change workload, cache reuse increased from **0% to 98.32% on Haiku 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Sonnet 5.5**. The Opus and Sonnet result repeated in two parallel comparisons: **24 live requests, all current-branch answers correct**, with approximately **94% lower reported model cost on the changed-context turn**.

These are workload-specific measurements, not guaranteed savings on every request. Latency was inconsistent, so this PR does not claim a speedup. The other tested providers showed no proven improvement from this marker. Callers can inspect the new `fx ask --json` cache counts to measure reuse in their own workloads.

## Why

Gateway's automatic cache points can occur after mutable runtime context. Changing that context can invalidate a large stable instruction prefix for providers that use explicit cache boundaries. In the bounded experiment below, changing the workspace branch reduced Claude's cache-read share from almost all input tokens to zero. The extra stable boundary retained that prefix without freezing context or changing instruction authority.

This uses Anthropic's documented per-message `providerOptions.anthropic.cacheControl` rather than moving runtime instructions into conversation history or keeping stale environment data. Other tested vendors retain their existing implicit caching behavior. Their fluctuations are not evidence of an improvement caused by this hint. Cache thresholds, expiry, routing, and provider capacity still apply.

## Experiment

The committed report is [`benchmarks/gateway-cache-prefix.md`](https://github.com/justrach/fx/blob/feat/gateway-stable-prefix-cache/benchmarks/gateway-cache-prefix.md).

The initial experiment made 30 live requests through fx's native Vercel Gateway adapter: five model vendors, three turns per arm. Each sequence starts with a long stable instruction containing public Vercel AI SDK source, resumes with unchanged context, then resumes after the synthetic workspace's actual Git branch changes. The question asks for the current branch; this measures cache retention and context freshness, not coding-task quality.

The public source was pinned to `vercel/ai` revision `20c4031d1fc59aab54b67c16679e3981374690ab`. Each model and arm used an isolated session and unique synthetic system prefix. The local observer replaced private environment values and the local skills inventory with synthetic data without moving or dropping the runtime-context message. It allowed at most 30 upstream requests, capped output at 1,024 tokens, disabled model tools, and made no paid retries. All baseline sequences preceded the changed sequences.

| Model | Unchanged-context cache read, before / after | Changed-context cache read, before / after | Changed-context process time, before / after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | 99.05% / 87.19% | 87.06% / 97.49% | 2.273s / 2.568s |
| Kimi K3.1 Pro | 98.24% / 98.31% | 96.63% / 96.70% | 7.752s / 5.658s |
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | 99.89% / 99.89% | 0% / 98.32% | 2.110s / 7.303s |
| GPT-5.4 mini | 92.03% / 92.03% | 91.90% / 91.89% | 2.253s / 2.155s |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | 67.59% / 67.62% | 0% / 0% | 6.404s / 3.453s |

Cache-read percentages describe input tokens, not successful requests. Resolved providers were Fireworks, Moonshot AI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Vertex respectively.

### Limitations and failures

- In the initial five-model run, only Haiku showed the explicit cache-retention gain. Its changed-context request read 34,259 tokens from cache instead of zero. Its reported model cost fell from $0.0043579 to $0.00041874, but process time increased. This does not establish a latency improvement.
- In the initial five-model run, 29 of 30 branch answers were correct. Gemini returned the previous branch once despite receiving the new branch in current context and reporting zero cache-read tokens. The patch does not resolve that model response failure or Gemini's cache miss.
- All 30 requests exited successfully with clean stderr. Native fx cache counters matched Gateway on every request.
- This is one three-turn sequence per model per arm, without randomized ordering or statistical confidence. Shared tool prefixes can already be cached: the changed OpenAI arm's initial request read 3,584 cached tokens despite its unique system prefix.
- Gateway metadata summed to approximately $0.236 in `cost` and $0.239 in `gatewayCost`. These are reported metadata, not an invoice. DeepSeek's resolved provider charged more than the public catalog estimate.
- The live comparison used a development checkout with cache-usage instrumentation before this contribution was isolated into its PR branch. It is not represented as a live benchmark of the eventual PR commit. Local checks on the isolated branch are listed separately.

### Opus and Sonnet follow-up

Twelve additional live requests tested `anthropic/claude-opus-5.5` and `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5` in parallel. Each model ran three baseline turns followed by three improved turns, with separate sessions and unique synthetic prefixes. Both arms used the same built `./zig-out/bin/fx` at `cfa5de350e0bffc0eca4bfa7d962bf84770a272d`; the observer removed only the explicit stable marker for the baseline and retained it for the improved arm. Automatic Gateway caching, live context, instruction roles, and session affinity remained unchanged.

The follow-up reused the pinned public source, branch-change task, low reasoning effort, disabled Fast and Ultrafast, 1,024-token output cap, privacy filtering, and no-tools/no-paid-retry policy. Two six-turn loopback preflights passed, and their normalized request pairs differed only by the marker. No product code changed for this follow-up.

| Model | Unchanged-context cache read, baseline / improved | Changed-context cache read, baseline / improved | Changed-context process time, baseline / improved | Changed-context reported model cost, baseline / improved |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Opus 5.5 | 99.89% / 99.89% | 0% / 98.32% | 4.775s / 3.058s | $0.174316 / $0.009897 |
| Sonnet 5.5 | 99.89% / 99.89% | 0% / 98.32% | 4.799s / 2.311s | $0.0871705 / $0.0049487 |

Both models resolved to Anthropic. All 12 branch answers were correct, every process exited successfully with clean stderr, and all native cache counters matched Gateway. Opus's changed-context cache reads rose from zero to 34,255 tokens, and Sonnet's rose from zero to 34,257; both improved requests wrote only 582 cache tokens.

Gateway reported approximately $0.820 in model `cost` and $0.821 in `gatewayCost` for the follow-up. These are metadata, not an invoice. This is one sequence per model per arm, with concurrent model runs and no randomized ordering. The lower process times are observations, not a general latency guarantee. Full methodology and token counts are in the committed experiment report.

### Independent fx repeat

A second 12-request run used the same product code at `3ebaac74`, with Opus and Sonnet again running concurrently. Both conditions used the same built fx binary; the observer removed only the new marker in baseline requests. The initial five-model run and both Claude follow-ups remain separate in the committed report.

| fx model | Changed-context cache read, without / with boundary | Changed-context reported model cost, without / with | Changed-context process time, without / with |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Opus 5.5 | 0% / 98.32% | $0.1743310 / $0.0098976 | 2.649s / 3.092s |
| Sonnet 5.5 | 0% / 98.32% | $0.0871655 / $0.0049485 | 1.808s / 2.109s |

Both resolved to Anthropic. All 12 current-branch answers were correct, stderr stayed clean, and fx's native cache counters matched Gateway. Reported totals for this repeat were $0.8201124 in model `cost` and $0.8213124 in `gatewayCost`, not an invoice. Cache retention and lower reported cost repeated, but changed-context latency worsened in this run. These fx measurements therefore support cache reuse, not a general speedup or a guarantee of savings for every request or provider.

## Verification

The development checkout passed a ReleaseSafe build and 84 focused prompt-context and Gateway protocol tests. The freshly built `./zig-out/bin/fx` also passed a three-turn loopback preflight. Comparing the before and after serialized requests showed identical roles, ordering, context, and options except for the added stable cache marker.

On the isolated branch at `cfa5de350e0bffc0eca4bfa7d962bf84770a272d`, based on upstream `main` at `f0732a02`:

- `zig fmt --check src/` and `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe --summary all` passed.
- 100 focused Zig tests passed using a temporary filtered copy of the project build definition. Coverage included prompt construction, Gateway serialization, cache-usage parsing, and CLI JSON success and error contracts. No build configuration changes are included in this PR.
- `FX_SOUND=0 bun test cli.test.ts --test-name-pattern 'fx ask usage|saved ask resumes|ask --help|oversized'` passed 7 tests from `tests/e2e`, with inherited live credentials removed. A separate run with `--test-name-pattern 'fx ask help renders documented options through both aliases'` passed the help snapshot test.
- A separate three-turn loopback smoke test drove this branch's freshly built `./zig-out/bin/fx`: start, resume, change the workspace branch, and resume again. It verified a single stable system cache marker before current runtime context, updated branch data, unchanged session affinity, parsed cache counters, successful exit, and empty stderr on every turn. This smoke test made no paid requests; the later Opus and Sonnet follow-up is reported separately above.
- `scripts/check-public-surface.sh` and `git diff --check HEAD^ HEAD` passed. The existing CLI E2E corpus entry and shard weight remain appropriate; no new root E2E file was added.

The follow-up commits change only the experiment report; the product code exercised above is unchanged. The CI, Benchmarks, macOS, and Binary Size runs for the current head, `e84cbcf1240e35da9d1c1032b22a7dd2fa8e161c`, report `action_required` and need upstream maintainer approval. The required checks must pass for that exact commit before this draft is marked ready.

## Docs

The manual lives in a private repository. A maintainer needs to update:

- https://fx.sh/docs/using-fx/fx-ask, **Use `fx ask` in scripts**: add `"cache_read_tokens": 800` and `"cache_write_tokens": 0` to the example `usage` object. Replace the usage paragraph with: "`usage.input_tokens`, `usage.output_tokens`, `usage.cache_read_tokens`, and `usage.cache_write_tokens` sum the counts reported by main-agent completions, including usage recorded before an error. A count is `null` when no completion reported it; reported zero remains `0`. Cache counts are included in input totals, not added to them. These totals exclude subagent, helper-model, and provider-tool usage. Use `fx usage` for the usage and spend your provider reports."
- On that page after the usage paragraph, add: "With prompt caching enabled, Gateway requests mark the end of stable instructions for Anthropic's explicit cache. Live runtime context stays after that boundary and is refreshed for each request. Other providers keep their existing cache behavior; hits depend on the provider, prefix size, routing, and expiry."

## Contribution notes

Created with Codegraff. This PR was read by a human at commit `cfa5de35`. The Opus and Sonnet report was added after that review; product code is unchanged. Suggested maintainer label: `type: improvement`.

title: Link a waiting sign-in in one line on the server screen
body:
**Summary**
---
- While a sign-in waits, the server's screen in `/mcp` reads "Waiting for the browser. Didn't open? Open the sign-in page." in one line, with the label linking the whole address. It used to wrap the address over as many rows as it took, so a long one like Supabase's filled the panel and scrolled past it ("2 more below").
- This follows #1453, which links the address the same way in the transcript. Both now take the label from `menu.sign_in_link_label`, so they can't drift.
- Like the Vercel row in #1453, the screen falls back to the whole address, with a link on every row, when the address can't be a link target or the screen is too narrow for the label. Narrow screens drop "Waiting for the browser." and then "Didn't open?" before falling back.
- Tests: inline tests cover the one-line link at several widths, the narrow fallback, and an address that can't be a link target. The two `mcp-auth.test.ts` tests for the waiting screen now check the label and that the address isn't spelled out, and one of them completes the sign-in from the link's target.

title: Show the session's cost and context on the status line's right side
body:
**Summary**
---
- The status line's right side now shows the session's cost next to the context, such as `$0.90 · 37k/1000k 3%`, and updates after every model step. The cost is what AI Gateway reports for each response in `providerMetadata.gateway.cost`, which fx now reads at `finish`. Providers that don't price responses, such as ChatGPT and Grok plans, show only the context.
- `/statusline` gets a Usage item, on by default and saved globally as `statusLine.usage`. Workspace overrides do not override this preference. With Usage and Context both on, the context shows once, on the right; with only Usage it reads `37k tokens`; with only Context it moves from the left to the right. Notices, such as an armed Esc, update ready, the full access warning, and the MCP startup notice, still take the spot while they last.
- `/statusline` and `/settings` show the status line in place of their key hints, so each change shows as it's made.
- After the first prompt, the status line no longer brings up MCP servers, including one that fails later on. Only a sign-in the user started from `/mcp` still shows there. This replaces the "only new problems" rule and removes `Seen`.
- The cost counts the main agent's requests, retries included, and lives in memory: it starts at zero on a new or resumed session. Subagents, auto-mode reviews, compaction, and titles aren't counted yet.
- Cost additions, UI snapshots, and resets share a mutex in the session runtime. Each priced response is counted before recovery or cancellation branches, including failed attempts that are retried. A pending Ctrl+C confirmation hides ordinary right-side notices so the exit instruction stays readable in narrow terminals.
- Tests cover Gateway cost parsing, context placement, concurrent cost updates and snapshots, global-only Usage settings, and Ctrl+C priority at 32 columns. A fake-Gateway TUI regression verifies that a priced failure and retry total `$0.60`, Usage toggles preserve that total, and `/new` resets it. Existing menu waits now use the menus' own rows instead of the removed key hints.

## Docs

- Usage and costs (`/docs/using-fx/usage-and-costs`): add that the status line shows the current session's cost as AI Gateway reports it for each response, counting main-agent requests only, kept in memory, and starting at zero on a new or resumed session. Billing stays authoritative in `/usage` and the Gateway dashboard.
- Configuration (`/docs/configure-fx/configuration`): add `statusLine.usage` (global-only boolean, default `true`) and note that context usage now shows on the status line's right side.
- Slash commands (`/docs/using-fx/slash-commands`): `/statusline [context|session|workspace|usage]`, and `/statusline` and `/settings` preview the status line while open.
- MCP (`/docs/capabilities/mcp`): the status line's MCP notice shows at startup and goes away for the rest of the session after the first prompt.

title: Split libfx into platform packages and load only what each runtime uses
body:
## Summary

This branch now holds the whole libfx packaging change. #1468, #1469, #1475, #1478, and #1485 were merged into it, and each keeps its own description and measurements.

- In Node.js, importing libfx loads the engine and the native loader. The WebAssembly host loads only when the native addon is unavailable (#1468).
- Each native addon ships in its own platform package, `@libfx/libfx-<os>-<cpu>[-<libc>]`, so an install or a Vercel function carries one binary (#1468, #1469).
- `require("libfx")` loads the same files as `import`, and needs Node.js 20.19, 22.12, or newer (#1469).
- A browser app ships only the `.wasm` it uses, and importing `libfx/browser` does no work (#1475).
- The `.wasm` files are 13% smaller (#1478).
- CI fails when what Node.js loads, what browser bundles carry, the package sizes, or the manifest and types regress (#1485).

| | `main` | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libfx` packed | 18,574,909 B | 3,674,131 B |
| Next 16 webpack standalone function | 44.7 MB | 18.2 MB |
| Next 16 Turbopack function | 61.9 MB | 17.8 MB |
| Next 15 webpack standalone function | 43.9 MB | 17.3 MB |

The live Vercel test passed against a real project with Next 16 Turbopack, Next 16 webpack, and Next 15, each 12 of 12 turns on the native backend (Node.js 24.21, glibc 2.34).

## Step 1: split the engine from the WebAssembly host

- `libfx/wasm` keeps the same exports and behavior. The engine both backends share, the WebAssembly host, the WebAssembly terminal, and the xterm.js adapter now live in separate modules (`engine.js`, `wasm-runtime.js`, `wasm-terminal.js`, `xterm.js`), and `engine.js` imports no WebAssembly code.
- The npm package carries those four modules, so it has 49 files instead of 45.
- The packaged terminal demo includes every module its page imports. It used to leave out six of them, so the page failed to load.

A later change uses the split to load the WebAssembly host in Node only when the native addon is unavailable, and moves each native addon into a package for its platform.

## Native addon packaging

Before this split I compared three ways to ship the native addons, each run through `sdk/tests/test-next-package.mjs` on Next 16 with Turbopack and with webpack and on Next 15 (dev, `next build` and `next start`, and a standalone build with `assetPrefix` started from a copy with the source removed), and through `sdk/tests/test-node-tracing.mjs`:

| Layout | Next config needed | webpack build | Addons in a route's trace |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One package per platform, bundled with the app | none | no warnings | 1 |
| One package per platform, libfx in `serverExternalPackages` | `serverExternalPackages: ["libfx"]` until Next lists libfx | no warnings | 1 |
| All four addons in `libfx`, as today | none | no warnings | 4 with webpack, 1 with Turbopack |

The bundled platform packages build cleanly only in one shape. webpack sees a `webpackInclude` context over the installed `@libfx/*` packages, and Turbopack, Node, and file tracers see one literal `import()` per platform inside `try`. A literal `import()` without `try` fails the Turbopack build when a package is missing, and with `try` alone webpack warns once for each missing package. The packages will be named `@libfx/libfx-<os>-<cpu>[-<libc>]`.

Standalone trace of the test app's `app/api/fx` route on macOS arm64, with today's layout and with bundled platform packages:

| Bundler | Traced bytes | Addons | Isolated standalone directory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Turbopack, Next 16 | 68.3 MB → 31.7 MB | 5 → 1 | 103.1 MB → 66.5 MB |
| webpack, Next 16 | 49.1 MB → 21.0 MB | 4 → 1 | 94.7 MB → 66.6 MB |
| webpack, Next 15 | 48.3 MB → 20.2 MB | 4 → 1 | 96.9 MB → 68.8 MB |

A Linux x64 install goes from 47.7 MB to 21.0 MB, libfx plus one platform package. Turbopack evaluates `process.platform` at build time in every layout, so a Turbopack build carries only the build machine's addon. Turbopack also traces the whole `node_modules/libfx` directory into each route, including both `.wasm` files, which the Node loader change addresses.

## Module sizes

| File | Bytes | Gzipped |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fx-sdk.js` on main | 166,717 | 42,382 |
| `fx-sdk.js` | 821 | 449 |
| `engine.js` | 118,052 | 31,431 |
| `wasm-runtime.js`, `wasm-terminal.js`, `wasm-module.js` | 47,567 | 11,149 |
| `xterm.js` | 4,697 | 1,454 |

`dev-release.yml` still uploads only part of the module graph for the web artifacts. It already left out the provider and subscription modules `fx-sdk.js` imports before this change, and I'll fix it separately.

title: ACP: a sub-agent that needs approval waits forever; the request never reaches the client
body:
With `fx acp` in `ask` mode, a sub-agent that needs tool approval never finishes. fx moves the child to `awaiting_approval`, but never sends the ACP client a `session/request_permission`, or anything else. The parent's `subagent` tool call stays `in_progress`, and `session/prompt` never returns. The only way out is cancelling the turn.

## Repro

fx 0.0.14. The code path is unchanged on `main` at e71a663b.

1. Set `"permission_mode": "ask"` in `~/.fx/settings.json`.
2. Create a workspace containing a `package.json` and a `tsconfig.json`.
3. Run the attached probe: `node acp-subagent-probe.mjs <path-to-fx> <workspace> out.ndjson`. It:
   - sends `initialize` and `session/new`;
   - prompts "Spawn 2 subagents, one to read package.json and one to read tsconfig.json";
   - approves any `session/request_permission` with `allow_once`;
   - logs every frame.
4. One child finishes in about 6 s: its `tool_call_update` is `completed`. The other's tool call stays `in_progress`. No permission request or other frame follows, and the prompt never returns; the probe gives up after 240 s.
5. The session's `subagent/children.json` shows that child with `"phase":"awaiting_approval"` and `"permission_mode":"ask"`.

It happened every time: three of three runs, from this probe, from T3 Code, and from T3 Code's replay recorder. In `auto` mode, the same prompt completes.

## Where it seems to come from

- [`runSubagentChild`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/blob/v0.0.14/src/acp/prompt.zig#L1268) runs the child with the parent's tool context.
- When the child needs approval, [`TurnContext.registerApproval`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/blob/v0.0.14/src/core/subagent/execution.zig#L516) moves it to `awaiting_approval` and registers the request in the sub-agent approval registry.
- Only the terminal app drains that registry, via [`pendingApprovalRequest`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/blob/v0.0.14/src/core/subagent/tool_host.zig#L256) / `resolveApproval` in [`input_approval_runtime.zig`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/blob/v0.0.14/src/core/app/input_approval_runtime.zig#L339) and `app_worker_runtime.zig`. Nothing under `src/acp` calls either function, so over ACP the request is never shown to the user and never resolved.

## Expected

The child's approval reaches the client as a `session/request_permission` on the parent session, ideally saying which sub-agent asks, and the client's answer resolves it. If fx can't route it, the child should fail rather than wait forever.

## Attachments

- [fx-0.0.14-acp-subagent-supervised.ndjson](https://gh-file-drop-api-prod-mi5fy3sowv63ufte.pinglabs.workers.dev/f/962538e09f3e76e0/fx-0.0.14-acp-subagent-supervised.ndjson): every ACP frame from the probe run, with home paths replaced and the host's skill list omitted. The last frames are the stuck call's `in_progress` and the other call's `completed`.
- [acp-subagent-probe.mjs](https://gh-file-drop-api-prod-mi5fy3sowv63ufte.pinglabs.workers.dev/f/a2303ff27d87d88f/acp-subagent-probe.mjs): the probe client.
- [children.json](https://gh-file-drop-api-prod-mi5fy3sowv63ufte.pinglabs.workers.dev/f/b59593cc87e90643/children.json): the session's sub-agent state after the hang.

Found while adding fx to T3 Code ([pingdotgg/t3code#18277](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/pull/18277)). T3 Code shows fx sub-agents in their own threads, and for now tells users to switch to Auto when delegating.

title: Run MCP tools across turns and recover from empty cut-off replies
body:
## Summary

- A later turn, or a resumed session, can call an MCP tool that an earlier turn loaded. The terminal app and `fx ask` no longer fail the call with "Dynamic MCP tool not selected for this model step".
- A call to an MCP tool name that no live server has still fails without reaching any server.
- Tool group summaries count MCP calls as "MCP call" instead of "command", and the status line counts MCP calls made.
- When the model catalog failed to load, a request waits up to two seconds for the retry its prompt starts, so the retry's limits reach that request.
- A reply that runs out of the provider's default output limit before any text is sent again once with an explicit limit, and fx says it is retrying. The limit is 32,768 tokens, or an eighth of the model's context window when that is smaller. The ChatGPT Codex provider sets its own limit, so fx does not retry there.
- An empty cut-off reply that is not retried ends with "The reply ran out of output tokens before any text." instead of "Done.".
- Commands with identical output get different `full_output_handle` values, and each handle reads back, including after a resume.

title: Pluralize subagent counts in tool group summaries

title: Ship each libfx native addon in its own platform package
body:
## Summary

- Each platform's native addon ships in its own package, such as `@libfx/libfx-linux-x64-gnu`, which libfx pins as an exact-version optional dependency. npm installs only the one for the machine.
- A Next.js route that bundles libfx carries one addon, for the platform it was built on, with both Turbopack and webpack.
- Importing libfx in Node loads the engine and the native loader only. The WebAssembly host loads only when the native addon is unavailable or `backend: "wasm"` is requested.
- A missing platform package is reported as `LIBFX_NATIVE_ARTIFACT_MISSING` with the package name, and the errors say to install it or to run Node with `--experimental-wasm-jspi`.
- Turbopack no longer copies the whole libfx package into each function.
- webpack no longer warns about the import of a caller-supplied `nativeAddon` module.
- The publish job refuses to publish libfx while a platform package it pins is missing from npm.

Merge this together with #1469, which publishes the platform packages. The dev channel publishes after every push to `main`, and until the platform packages exist, that job stops instead of publishing.

## Sizes

Both sides use the same four addons and `.wasm` files, built with Bun 1.4.2 as in CI.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libfx` package | 18,574,909 B packed, 43,296,407 B unpacked, 49 files | 3,396,623 B packed, 9,955,982 B unpacked, 47 files |
| Platform packages | none | 3.6 to 4.0 MB packed, 7.7 to 9.0 MB unpacked, 5 files each |
| Linux x64 install | 43.3 MB | 19.0 MB |

What the fx route in the Next.js fixture traces:

| Setup | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Next 16 webpack, `next build` | 37.2 MB, 4 addons | 11.6 MB, 1 addon |
| Next 16 webpack, standalone | 44.7 MB, 4 addons | 19.1 MB, 1 addon |
| Next 16 Turbopack | 61.9 MB, 5 addons | 18.7 MB, 1 addon |
| Next 15 webpack, `next build` and standalone | 36.5 MB and 43.9 MB, 4 addons | 10.9 MB and 18.2 MB, 1 addon |

The remaining 7 MB in the standalone and Turbopack traces is the two `.wasm` files the fallback uses.

## Not in this change

- `node.cjs` is still one bundle. It includes the WebAssembly host and drops the `webpackInclude` hint, so a webpack app that calls `require("libfx")` sees every file in the `@libfx` scope. Plain Node is unaffected. #1469 makes `node.cjs` a wrapper around `node.js`.
- Publishing the platform packages, which #1469 adds.
- CI guards for the load graph and trace contents.

Stacked on #1463.

title: Publish the libfx platform packages and make node.cjs a wrapper
body:
## Summary

- The publish workflow publishes each `@libfx` platform package before libfx, from the same commit and with provenance. A rerun after a partial publish skips the versions npm already has. Afterward the workflow downloads every package and compares it byte for byte with the archive it tested.
- Before publishing, the package job checks that the platform archives match the versions libfx pins and contain only the addon, its loader, the manifest, the README, and the license. `test-node-package.mjs` runs that check on a correct set and on three broken ones.
- `node.cjs` is now `module.exports = require("./node.js")`, so `require("libfx")` loads the same modules as `import`. With the native addon installed, neither loads WebAssembly host code. The Bun build of `node.cjs` is removed.
- `engines` is now `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`, the Node.js versions that load an ES module with `require()`. On older versions, `require("libfx")` fails with a message that names the versions it needs. `import` works as before.
- The package declares `"sideEffects": false`. No libfx module does work when imported.
- The durable bundles ship linked sourcemaps. Each map names its sources relative to `sdk/durable` and leaves the source text out.

## Before merging

The platform packages are not on npm yet, and npm trusted publishing cannot create a package. Before this merges, an owner of the `@libfx` scope publishes a placeholder version of each of the four packages by hand. They then add a trusted publisher for `publish-libfx.yml` with environment `npm` and `npm publish` allowed, as `sdk/NAPI.md` describes. Until then the publish job stops before libfx and reports which package failed.

Merge this right after #1468.

## Decisions

- `durable.js` and `fx-harness.js` stay static imports. Importing `node.js` takes about 7.3 ms, and `durable.js` accounts for about 1.5 ms of that. Most of `fx-harness.js`'s cost is `engine.js`, which libfx loads anyway. Loading them lazily would help only apps that never call `createFxAgent`, and `memory()` and `wakeHandler()` are synchronous exports of `durable.js`, so it would mean splitting that module.
- The durable bundles stay minified. Unminified, a cold import of `durable/vercel.mjs` took about 88 ms instead of 68 ms. Sourcemaps without the source text add about 450 KB packed. With the source text they would add about 2.8 MB.
- This adds no musl package, because the README claims glibc only.

## Sizes

Both sides use the same four addons and `.wasm` files, built with Bun 1.4.2 as in CI.

| | #1468 | This change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libfx` package | 3,396,623 B packed, 9,955,982 B unpacked, 47 files | 3,755,972 B packed, 11,514,720 B unpacked, 50 files |
| Each platform package | 5 files | 5 files, about 40 B larger |
| Linux x64 install | 18,993,248 B | 20,552,027 B |

The three sourcemaps add 1,875,220 B unpacked, and `node.cjs` drops from 317,465 B to 568 B.

The Next.js fixture's fx route traces the same files as in #1468, with one addon each: Next 16 webpack 11.6 MB, 19.1 MB standalone; Next 16 Turbopack 18.7 MB; Next 15 10.9 MB, 18.2 MB standalone.

Files Node loads for `createFxEngine()` with the default backend:

| | `import "libfx"` | `require("libfx")` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform package installed | engine and native loader, no WebAssembly host | the same, plus `node.cjs` |
| Platform package missing | adds `node-wasm.js`, `wasm-runtime.js`, `wasm-module.js` | the same, plus `node.cjs` |

`require("libfx")` on the official Node.js builds for macOS arm64:

| Node.js | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 20.18.3, 22.11.0 | Fails with the version message |
| 20.19.0, 22.12.0, 22.21.1, 24.21.0 | Works, with no warnings |

## Not in this change

- The browser entry and its `.wasm` assets, which #1475 changes.
- CI guards for the load graph and trace contents.

Stacked on #1468.

title: Tell the model how to keep a service running after fx exits
body:
## Summary

- The shell tool description no longer forbids detaching. It tells the model to start a service that must keep running with `setsid <cmd> >log 2>&1 &` on Linux, or `perl -MPOSIX -e 'fork&&exit;setsid;exec@ARGV' <cmd> >log 2>&1 &` on macOS, which has no `setsid` command, and to check that it is ready in the same call.
- The description now tells the model that owned shell sessions end when fx exits and that `&` and `nohup` jobs end with their command.
- The startup-files sentence is shorter so the macOS description fits the 1024-byte tool description limit, and a shell description over the limit now fails the build instead of being cut off.

title: Prepare v0.0.15 release
body:
## Summary

Bring the 0.0.15 notes up to date with the newly merged fixes. Keep the approved summary and existing entries.

- MCP tools work across turns and resumed sessions.
- Tool summaries count MCP calls separately from shell commands.
- Saved command results remain distinguishable when their output is identical.
- Empty replies cut short by output limits can recover through one retry.

Verified the changelog validator, formatting, and a local build. Ran fresh `./zig-out/bin/fx --version` and `help`, then checked the interactive 0.0.15 header, `/help`, and clean `/quit`.

title: Record token usage in saved sessions and report cached tokens
body:
## Summary

- Gateway replies now report cache read and cache write token counts instead of dropping them.
- Saved sessions write their running token totals after every model reply, so a run that is killed or times out keeps the usage of every reply it received.
- Resumed and forked sessions keep adding to the totals they saved.
- A subagent saves its own token totals in its own session log. The parent's totals still leave the subagent's out, as `fx ask --json` does.
- `fx ask --json` usage includes `cache_read_tokens` and `cache_write_tokens` when the provider reports them, and leaves them out otherwise.

title: Overlap durable admission reads without starting sends early
body:
## Summary

Overlap the sender's log read with the viewer's stream-position lookup when a prompt supplies a `messageId`. The same operations still run, but the sender no longer waits for that lookup before starting its read.

This is a latency improvement, not a fix for a shipped data-loss bug. The stream position must still resolve, and cancellation must still be checked, before admission begins. The input is persisted before its queue message is sent, and acceptance still waits for both. Queue delivery, leases, and World APIs are unchanged.

The speculative read carries its log object and `newest` position into the existing sender-to-worker handoff. It does not skip history checks or assume a newly created session is empty.

## Regression coverage

- A gated stream-position lookup proves that the sender reads concurrently but cannot write or enqueue before that position resolves.
- Aborting during that lookup stores neither a prompt nor a targeted cancel. A later prompt can reuse the same `messageId` and runs normally.
- The native acceptance test now targets the retry observer's log object. Holding an arbitrary next read could instead block the preceding worker's tail read or the sender's speculative read after this ordering change. It still proves that acceptance and turn execution do not wait for the observer's retry check.
- A bounded TLA+ model checks the viewer-before-write boundary. Removing that boundary must produce a counterexample. This is a focused safety model, not a replacement for the existing session, intake, or isolation models.

## Measurements

8 balanced A/B pairs on Vercel previews, with one warmup per side excluded. All 16 measured prompts completed with complete traces and no failures. Each prompt created a new chat and asked for the same short reply without tools.

Both packages use SDK base `7f2383af7`, the same freshly built native/WebAssembly engines, and the same World bundles. Only `durable.js` and its generated CommonJS bundle differ. The measured candidate is `4570701a6`; the follow-up changes only comments and model documentation. Minifying the measured and final `durable.js` produces identical executable output. Raw trace artifacts remain local.

| Metric | Baseline p50 | Candidate p50 | Median paired delta | Candidate faster |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SDK admission (`prompt.accepted`) | 537 ms | 511 ms | -47 ms | 5/8 |
| HTTP POST to acceptance (`sendingMs`) | 822 ms | 786 ms | -56 ms | 6/8 |

The delta column is the median of candidate-minus-baseline within each pair, not the difference between the two p50 columns. Traces show the initial reads overlap in all 8 candidate runs and none of the baseline runs; both still make 6 World calls during new-chat admission.

These are small, noisy samples, not a statistical significance claim. Two baseline runs paid backend initialization costs despite the nominal warm setup. Excluding those pairs leaves 6 pairs: admission's paired median remains -47 ms (4/6 faster), while POST-to-acceptance becomes -26 ms (4/6 faster).

No time-to-first-text improvement is claimed: its overall p50 worsened from 2,126 to 2,638 ms, while its paired median moved -113 ms. That disagreement and the large per-pair variation make an end-to-end claim unsupported. Follow-up chats and a controlled cold-start cohort were not benchmarked in this run.

## Validation

- The durable core passes on memory, local, World, and queue backends.
- The real-engine durable suites pass on memory, local, and World with native and WebAssembly engines.
- Native and WebAssembly builds pass.
- Focused TLC checks cover the new viewer boundary and existing session/intake/isolation models.

The earlier prototype that queued the backstop before persistence is not included. Recovery review found a failed-write/retry sequence that could leave an accepted input without a pending backstop. Its larger latency reductions are not results for this PR.

title: Update examples for libfx 0.0.16
body:
## Summary

- Pin published `libfx@0.0.16` and its matching native packages in all four examples, using `createFxEngine()` for one conversation.
- Update Vite, Next.js, Nuxt, and their compatible dependencies from the older example versions.
- Update Nuxt to 4.6.3, which fixes the dev server and server route advisories that affect 4.6.2.
- Point each demo's setup link at the signed 0.0.16 example source.
- Preserve the raw interfaces, direct browser-key path, free-token proxy, and existing limits.

Verified the examples' 19 offline tests, all three framework builds, formatting, a local `zig build`, and fresh `./zig-out/bin/fx help`. The streaming regression uses the published engine with mocked transport. Next.js and Nuxt build output includes the native addon. No live model calls were made.

Node, browser, and Next.js lockfile audits have no findings. Nuxt's audit reports six low and six moderate findings in nitropack's build tooling (glob, minimatch, and deepmerge), which the example's request path doesn't use.

Companion website: https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx-web/pull/231.

title: Make libfx/browser emit only the WebAssembly module an app uses
body:
## Summary

- `browser.js` now only re-exports. `createFxAgent` and `createFxEngine` live in `browser-agent.js`, which imports the engine and the WebAssembly host directly and names `fx-core.wasm` inside `createFxEngine`. `createFxTerminal` lives in `browser-terminal.js`, which names `fx-term.wasm`.
- Importing `libfx/browser` does no work. Neither URL is built until a factory runs, so a server can render a client component that creates an agent at module scope.
- A browser build emits only the `.wasm` its code reaches. With Next.js, an agent page gets `fx-core.wasm` and no `fx-term.wasm`, with both Turbopack and webpack. Vite 8 does the same when Rolldown's lazy barrel optimization is on.
- `createFxAgent` is marked pure, so a bundle that never calls it drops the durable session code.
- The README says which bundlers copy the `.wasm` files and which headers a CDN must send.

## Tests

- The Next.js fixture has a new client page whose component creates an agent at module scope. In dev, production, and standalone with `assetPrefix`, `test-next-package.mjs` checks that the page renders on the server. It also checks that each client build carries exactly one `.wasm`, the package's `fx-core.wasm`.
- `test-browser-import.mjs` checks that importing `libfx/browser` and creating an agent makes no fetch and no WebAssembly compile. It also checks that its modules reach no Node.js code, that `browser.js` only re-exports, and that each `.wasm` is named in exactly one module. It runs in the Node and Bun N-API lanes.

## What each build emits

The same apps were built against the package from #1469 and from this change. Vite 8.3.5 bundles with Rolldown 1.2.15. The other tools were esbuild 0.28.2 and Next.js 16.4.3. `fx-core.wasm` is 2.6 MB and `fx-term.wasm` is 4.4 MB.

| Build | Agent-only app | Engine-only app | Terminal app |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Next.js, Turbopack | both → `fx-core.wasm` | both → `fx-core.wasm` | both → `fx-term.wasm` |
| Next.js, webpack | both → `fx-core.wasm` | both → `fx-core.wasm` | both → `fx-term.wasm` |
| Vite 8, lazy barrel on | both → `fx-core.wasm` | both → `fx-core.wasm` | both → `fx-term.wasm` |
| Vite 8, default | both → both | both → both | both → both |
| esbuild | none → none | none → none | none → none |

| JavaScript | Agent-only app | Engine-only app | Terminal app |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vite 8, minified | 137 → 137 KB | 137 → 84 KB | 140 → 27 KB |
| esbuild, not minified | 280 → 280 KB | 280 → 164 KB | 287 → 55 KB |

Next.js with webpack also builds client components for the server. That build used to emit both `.wasm` files, and it now emits only the one the page reaches. The page function's trace includes neither. Every Next.js page above rendered on the server with status 200. Vite's dev server serves `fx-core.wasm` from the package as `application/wasm` with no configuration.

The package grows by 606 B and two files, to 3,756,578 B packed. The Node.js route traces are unchanged.

## Not in this change

- By default, Vite 8 still copies `fx-term.wasm` into an agent-only build, although the app never references it, so browsers never download it. Rolldown documents that it plans to remove the `lazyBarrel` option.
- esbuild doesn't copy `new URL` assets, so esbuild apps still pass `wasm` themselves.
- CI builds with Vite and esbuild, and the other load-graph and trace guards.

## Docs

`/docs/lib/webassembly`: after the paragraph that starts "The browser entry point resolves `fx-core.wasm`", add that Next.js copies only the `.wasm` an app's client code uses. Vite 8 copies both unless `build.rolldownOptions.experimental.lazyBarrel` is `true`, and esbuild copies neither. Also add that a CDN serving the files, for example through Next.js's `assetPrefix`, must send `Content-Type: application/wasm` so the browser can compile while it downloads, and CORS headers when the files come from another origin.

The companion docs change is vercel-labs/fx-web#225.

Stacked on #1469.

title: Resume interrupted requests when a session reopens
body:
## Summary

- When a crash or a closed window interrupts a model request, reopening the session in the terminal app sends the request again without a prompt and shows "Resuming the interrupted request".
- While the resumed request waits for its first byte, the status row shows "Resuming the interrupted request · attempt N" with a clock.
- A tool that was running when fx stopped comes back answered as possibly run, and the model is told to check what finished and rerun only what is safe.
- Closing the terminal window during a request counts as a clean close, not a crash, so repeated closes keep resuming without asking.
- A request that crashed fx twice asks first: Enter sends it again, and Esc ends the turn so nothing resends it.
- A request interrupted more than a day ago, or dated ahead of the clock, asks before it is sent again.
- A turn whose answer was saved, or that the user cancelled, is never sent again.
- When a full disk lost a turn's answer, the next launch sends the request again and saves the answer.
- Replayed history, in the terminal app and in ACP `session/load`, shows a resumed turn as its resume line instead of a user message.
- `fx ask`, ACP prompts and subagents keep ending an interrupted turn as before.

Stacked on #1456.

title: Make model search fuzzy across provider and model names
body:
## Summary

- The model menu and the inline `/model <query>` suggestions match each query word against the full `provider/model` ID, so `anthropic opus` and `claude sonnet 4.5` find their models.
- Punctuation inside a query word is ignored, so `sonnet45` finds `claude-sonnet-4.5` and `z.ai glm` finds the `zai/glm-*` models.
- A query word also matches when its letters appear in order from the start of a word in the ID, so `cs45` finds `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5`.
- Results that contain the query as typed come first, then word matches, then fuzzy matches, each in catalog order, so queries that already worked keep the same top results.

title: Shrink the libfx WebAssembly modules with wasm-opt
body:
## Summary

- CI and the publish workflow run `wasm-opt -Oz` on both WebAssembly modules after `zig build`, through `sdk/scripts/optimize-wasm.mjs`. binaryen 132.0.0 is pinned in `sdk/tools` with a lockfile.
- The pass enables only the WebAssembly features Zig already builds with, so the modules need nothing new from a browser or Node.js.
- CI optimizes before its SDK jobs, so every SDK test runs on the modules the package ships. A local `zig build` skips the pass.
- `bundle-durable.mjs` records why the durable modules bundle their Workflow Worlds instead of depending on them.

## Sizes

Both modules were already built ReleaseSmall and stripped. This adds `wasm-opt -Oz` to the same source:

| Module | Before | After | gzip | brotli |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fx-core.wasm` | 2,590,065 B | 2,240,868 B (−13.5%) | 923,421 → 893,693 B | 715,999 → 709,289 B |
| `fx-term.wasm` | 4,446,398 B | 3,866,560 B (−13.0%) | 1,632,436 → 1,579,852 B | 1,243,515 → 1,232,994 B |

| | #1475 | This change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libfx` package | 3,756,578 B packed, 11,516,505 B unpacked | 3,674,131 B packed, 10,587,470 B unpacked |
| Next 16 webpack standalone trace | 19.1 MB | 18.2 MB |
| Next 16 Turbopack trace | 18.7 MB | 17.8 MB |
| Next 15 webpack standalone trace | 18.2 MB | 17.3 MB |

Browsers download compressed modules, so downloads shrink by only 1 to 3%. Compiling either module in Node.js takes the same time as before, about 2 ms for `fx-core.wasm` and 3.5 ms for `fx-term.wasm`. Locally the pass takes about 60 seconds for both modules.

## Why `fx-term.wasm` is larger than `fx-core.wasm`

Function bodies take 2,250 KB in `fx-core.wasm` and 3,879 KB in `fx-term.wasm`. Most of the 1,629 KB difference is the terminal itself: the interactive app runtime in `core.app` (553 KB), the terminal UI in `ui` (618 KB), and the composition root in `main` (110 KB).

About 380 KB more is Zig's TLS and HTTP client, which `/usage` reaches through `gateway.client.fetchUsageGet`. WebAssembly cannot open network connections, so `/usage` in the browser terminal sends no request and shows zero usage. A separate fix will send it through the host's `fetch`, which also removes that code.

## Why the durable modules stay bundled

The esbuild metafiles of the durable modules attribute 63% of `durable/vercel.mjs` and 86% of `durable/local.mjs` to undici and zod. Installed as dependencies, the Worlds and their dependencies take 28.9 MB, which every libfx install would carry, including apps that never use durability. Bundled, they add about 2 MB. Optional peer dependencies would make each app install them itself. libfx also loads each durability module through an ignored import of a single file, which bundlers copy without following its imports.

## Not in this change

- A separate package for the `.wasm` files. Node.js functions that only use the native addon still carry them.
- The `/usage` fix.
- Size budgets and the other CI guards, which are in #1485.

Stacked on #1475.

title: Fail ChatGPT sign-in for an unusable account ID
body:
## Summary

- ChatGPT sign-in with an account ID that fx cannot save now fails as a sign-in error ("failed to sign in") instead of "Credential could not be saved. Check authentication storage before signing in again." Nothing is saved in either case.
- Valid account IDs sign in as before.

title: Kill a terminal's whole process tree when it stops
body:
## Summary

- A `tty: true` terminal that timed out was killed by process group only. Session teardown and a graceful close that runs out of time did the same. The final kill when fx exits also reached the process tree it saved before hanging up, but only after killing the group. Job control or a nested shell such as `bash -i` moves processes out of that group, so they survived, and a shell that saw its job end ran its next command. With `bash -i -c 'sleep 3; touch after'` and a 1-second timeout, `after` appeared right away.
- These kills now go through one helper, `killTerminal`, which reaches the process tree the way a forced stop already did: the terminal's process group and every process that left it. If the tree can't be read, it falls back to the process group, as forced stop does.
- Before a kill, every process in the tree is stopped, parents first. Killing the group ends the launcher, which hangs up the terminal's foreground job, and a shell outside the group that sees that job end would otherwise run its next command before its own kill arrives.
- Other signals are unchanged, including the SIGTERM a graceful close sends first.

## Testing

- A new `tui-terminal-tool.test.ts` test times out `bash --norc --noprofile -i -c 'printf %s $$ > pid; sleep 3; touch after'` after 1 second and requires the nested bash to be gone and `after` to be absent. It fails on `main`, where `after` appears about 1.6 seconds in.
- The rest of `tui-terminal-tool.test.ts` passes, except "force stop settles a stubborn captured command and permits later work", which is flaky on macOS on `main` too: it failed 2 of 3 runs without this change. It covers captured commands, which this change does not touch.
- `native_session.zig` and `process_tree.zig` unit tests pass, 421 passed and 1 skipped. `tests/tla/terminal/check.sh` passes; `TerminalLifecycle.tla` only changed its shutdown comment from the process group to the process tree.

title: Load a symlinked global AGENTS.md that points elsewhere in home
body:
## Summary

- Load `~/.fx/AGENTS.md` when it is a symlink to a file anywhere in the home directory, such as a dotfiles checkout or a Nix `mkOutOfStoreSymlink` target.
- Keep omitting a global `AGENTS.md` symlink whose target is outside the home directory.
- Keep project and nested `AGENTS.md` symlinks limited to their own directory.

title: Run the libfx model check on pull requests only when libfx changes
body:
## Summary

- Pull requests run the libfx durable-session model check only when they change code libfx owns: `sdk/`, the SDK models and drivers, the Node-API and WebAssembly core entry points, `src/acp/`, `src/core/hosts/`, `src/core/session_manager/`, `build.zig`, `build.zig.zon`, or `ci.yml`.
- Other pull requests skip the check, which takes about 40 minutes, so their CI finishes in about 25 minutes instead of about 50.
- Every push to `main` and every manual `ci.yml` run includes the check, so Publish libfx still waits on it.
- `Build & Test` fails when the detector can't read the change.

title: Use a smaller square for the cancelled marker
body:
Use the smaller `▪` (U+25AA) for the cancelled marker instead of `■` (U+25A0).

**Why**

The cancelled marker (`■ Cancelled · What can fx do differently?`, cancelled questions, cancelled tools) renders noticeably larger than the `●` status marker beside it in the transcript. The filled square fills most of the cell and looks heavy next to the other markers.

**Approach**

Swap the glyph everywhere fx draws it: tool status in the transcript runtime, the question footer, and the compact command row. `▪` keeps the same shape and color and stays one column wide (a text-default emoji variation base, so it renders as text without U+FE0F).

The two parsers that read a status marker back from recorded transcript bytes (`normalizeCanonicalStatus` and the connected row in `render_input.zig`) accept both `▪` and the old `■`, so sessions saved by earlier versions still group and restyle on resume.

**Validation**

- `zig build` succeeds on Zig 0.17.0 (Linux x86_64).
- `zig fmt --check src/` passes.
- Unit and e2e expectations updated to the new glyph.
- Not yet driven end to end in the TUI; please check a cancelled tool row in `./zig-out/bin/fx` before merging.

title: fix(gateway): allow EOF after finish_reason in OpenAI chat completions stream without [DONE] sentinel
body:
Closes #1334

### Summary
Some OpenAI-compatible backends (e.g. MiniMax, custom proxies) close the SSE connection cleanly after delivering the final chunk with  inish_reason:  stop instead of emitting a trailing data: [DONE] sentinel.

Previously, consume_stream treated any stream EOF without [DONE] as error.IncompleteStream even if the turn was already finished.

### Changes
- In src/gateway/chat_completions_protocol.zig:
  - When  raming.next() returns EOF (data == null), if educer.phase == .finished, transition to .done and call educer.finish().
  - Streams cut off before  inish_reason continue to fail with error.IncompleteStream as expected.
  - Added unit test cases in chat completions stream framing handles chunks trailers truncation and wire limits verifying completion without [DONE] (both with and without trailing usage chunks).

title: Guard the libfx package layout in CI
body:
## Summary

- A new `SDK package guards` job packages libfx with all four platform packages and fails on a regression in what the earlier changes fixed. `Build & Test` now requires it.
- `test-node-load-graph.mjs` records every module Node.js loads from an installed libfx, through a module hook, in seven scenarios:
  - `import` and `require` with the platform package load the engine and the native loader, and no WebAssembly host code.
  - Without the native addon, the fallback loads only the core's WebAssembly host, and a turn completes.
  - With only another platform's package installed, libfx never loads it. Its error names the package the machine needs, and it tries the fallback only when the runtime supports JSPI. On the Linux runner that package is `@libfx/libfx-darwin-arm64`, which covers a build made on macOS and run on Linux.
- `test-browser-bundles.mjs` builds an agent-only and a terminal app:
  - With esbuild, the agent bundle carries `browser-agent.js` and not the terminal, and the terminal bundle carries `wasm-terminal.js` and not the durable code.
  - With Vite, each app's code names only its own `.wasm`. With `lazyBarrel`, each emits only that file.
  - No bundle names a platform package or imports a Node.js built-in.
- `test-package-size.mjs` checks the sizes in `sdk/tests/package-size-budgets.json`.
- publint and attw check the manifest and the types.
- `test-next-package.mjs` now also checks, with Turbopack, webpack, and Next 15, that native turns load none of the WebAssembly fallback. In `next start`, the first WebAssembly turn must load the fallback as a chunk of its own.
- `sdk/tests/tools` pins vite 8.3.5, esbuild 0.28.2, publint 0.3.25, and @arethetypeswrong/cli 0.18.5 with a lockfile.
- `test-vercel-package.mjs` ships no lockfile when it deploys a local package. pnpm 11 can't install from a lockfile that names another platform's local tarball, so the deployment's install failed with ENOTDIR. The live test now passes against a Vercel project with Next 16 Turbopack, Next 16 webpack, and Next 15: 12 of 12 turns each on the native backend.

## Budgets

Each budget is about 10% above the size it was set at, from this stack's package:

| Entry | Now | Budget |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libfx` packed / unpacked | 3,674,131 / 10,587,470 B | 4,042,000 / 11,647,000 B |
| `fx-core.wasm` | 2,240,868 B | 2,465,000 B |
| `fx-term.wasm` | 3,866,560 B | 4,254,000 B |
| `engine.js` gzip | 31,421 B | 34,600 B |
| `wasm-runtime.js` gzip | 9,940 B | 11,000 B |
| `fx-sdk.js` gzip | 439 B | 490 B |
| `@libfx/libfx-darwin-arm64` packed / unpacked | 3,628,733 / 7,745,061 B | 3,992,000 / 8,520,000 B |
| `@libfx/libfx-darwin-x64` packed / unpacked | 3,961,879 / 8,927,802 B | 4,359,000 / 9,821,000 B |
| `@libfx/libfx-linux-arm64-gnu` packed / unpacked | 3,695,108 / 7,686,709 B | 4,065,000 / 8,456,000 B |
| `@libfx/libfx-linux-x64-gnu` packed / unpacked | 3,910,221 / 9,037,307 B | 4,302,000 / 9,942,000 B |

Since #1463, `fx-sdk.js` only re-exports, and the WebAssembly host it used to hold is in `wasm-runtime.js`, so both have budgets.

## What each guard catches

I ran each guard against code that has the regression it guards against:

| Guard | Run against | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node load graph | #1468's `node.cjs`, which bundled its own copy of the library | Fails: `require` never loads `node.js` |
| Node load graph | `node.js` importing `node-wasm.js` statically | Fails: a native `import` loads the WebAssembly host |
| Next fallback checks | The same static import, with Turbopack and webpack | Fails: the WebAssembly turn loads no fallback chunk of its own |
| Browser bundles | #1469's `browser.js`, which named both modules | Fails |
| Package sizes | #1475's modules, built without `wasm-opt` | Fails: both `.wasm` files are 105% of budget |

## attw

attw runs with the `node16` profile and ignores `cjs-resolves-to-esm`:

- `node16` leaves out `node10` resolution, which ignores `exports`. libfx requires Node.js 20.19 or later.
- Every subpath other than `libfx` and `libfx/node` has always been an ES module only, which `require()` loads on the Node.js versions libfx supports.

`libfx` and `libfx/node` pass every resolution mode, and any other problem fails the job.

## Timing

Locally the job's steps take 51 seconds, including installs and packaging. The checks themselves take 6 s for the load graph, 3 s for the browser bundles, under 1 s for the sizes, and 4 s for publint and attw. The job runs in parallel with the other SDK jobs, after the same builds.

## Not in this change

- The `/usage` fix for the browser terminal.

Stacked on #1478.

title: Read /usage through the host in the WebAssembly terminal
body:
## Summary

- `/usage` in the WebAssembly terminal reads usage through the host's `fetch`. Before, it showed only cached numbers: on a fresh start, `$0.0000` and "nothing fetched today".
- `r` refreshes and Tab changes the period in the WebAssembly terminal's `/usage`. Before, both did nothing there.
- While a usage read waits, the WebAssembly terminal keeps drawing and reading keys.
- Ctrl+C aborts a waiting usage read and keeps the numbers already shown, and quitting the terminal cancels it.
- `fx-term.wasm` no longer includes Zig's HTTP and TLS client, and is 8% smaller.

## How it works

- The usage dashboard ran each fetch on a worker thread and skipped the fetch in single-threaded builds. Without a worker thread, `open` and `refresh` now queue the fetch, and `tick` runs it in the event loop with the dashboard unlocked. They only queue because a key read during a model turn can call them. `fx usage` runs the fetch from `waitForFetch`.
- In WebAssembly, each usage GET goes through the host's streaming `fetch` with the new `host_stream_provider.get`. It sends the headers the native client sends, built by one shared function, with the same 1 MiB limit and 15-second deadline. While it waits, it pulses the terminal, as a model turn does.
- The cooperative launch now calls `rebindAfterInit`, as the native launch does. The WebAssembly app uses it to give the usage host the app's final address. `rebindAfterMove` does nothing in WebAssembly, which has no v2 session store or subagent host.
- The WebAssembly profile allows `profile_usage`, which gates `r` and Tab in `/usage`.

## Size

| `fx-term.wasm` | `main` | This change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ReleaseSmall | 4,451,957 B | 4,094,541 B (−8.0%) |
| gzip | 1,633,809 B | 1,500,692 B (−8.1%) |
| After `wasm-opt -Oz` | 3,871,201 B | 3,543,943 B (−8.5%) |

## Behavior to know

- A bare Esc pressed while a read waits takes effect when the read ends, as during a model turn: the cooperative pulse doesn't resolve the escape timeout. Ctrl+C takes effect at once.
- A fetch queued during a model turn starts when the turn ends, because `tick` runs from the event loop's fact collection, which a turn's pulses don't run.
- Redirects are the host's. `fetch` follows them and drops `Authorization` when one leaves the origin, where the native client refuses them.
- In a browser, AI Gateway's `/v1/report` and `api.vercel.com/ai-gateway/usage-report` answer CORS preflights for any origin with `Authorization` and `x-vercel-ai-gateway-team` allowed. Codex and Grok usage needs whatever proxy the app's `fetch` already uses for those providers.

title: Reuse main's base binaries in the binary size check
body:
## Summary

- Each push to `main` builds and caches that commit's binary for every Binary Size target.
- Binary Size on a pull request restores its base binary from that cache instead of building it, so most jobs build fx once instead of twice.

title: Bound the nesting of provider JSON before fx serializes it
body:
## Summary

- A streamed Gateway event nested more than 64 levels deep now fails the request as an invalid event instead of aborting fx. This covers a deep tool-call input, a provider-executed tool result, and provider metadata.
- A streamed Responses event from OpenAI Codex or xAI nested more than 64 levels deep, such as a reasoning item, now fails the request the same way instead of aborting fx.
- A provider error body whose `param` path nests more than 16 levels now shows the expected and received kinds without the path instead of overflowing the stack.
- Chat Completions providers keep the 64-level limit they already had.

title: Read backslashes inside double quotes the way the shell does
body:
## Summary

- Inside double quotes, fx now keeps a backslash unless the next character is `$`, `` ` ``, `"`, `\`, or a newline, as the shell does. `"a\&b"` reads as `a\&b`, not `a&b`.
- In auto mode, a routine command with such a word, like `npm "te\st"`, now goes to review. fx used to check it as `npm test` and run it without review, while the shell passed `te\st` to npm.
- `git push origin "fe\at"` no longer counts as a push to the current branch `feat` in the evidence fx gives the security reviewer.
- Arguments typed after `/mcp` keep a double-quoted backslash the same way.
