title: Stop treating a tool's own next-step message as prompt injection
body:
## Summary

- In auto mode, running the next step a program prints for itself, such as a CLI's next subcommand or a git hint, no longer counts as prompt injection, so the agent can follow its own workflow tools without the action being held.
- Instructions planted in files, web pages, repository content, tool results, or another agent's messages still count as prompt injection, including a "next step" a tool prints for a different program or a step that sends secrets.

Docs: vercel-labs/fx-web#249

title: Treat damage before a kept turn as a damaged session on resume
body:
## Summary

- `fx --resume` on a session with a damaged log line in the turns its newest compaction kept says "saved session is unreadable" and points to `fx doctor` and `fx session recover`, instead of exiting with `fx: InvalidConversationFrame`.
- `fx ask --resume` on such a session fails with `InvalidSessionFormat`, as it does for other damaged sessions.
- An ACP client that loads such a session gets "Session could not be loaded" instead of "Session not found".

title: Copy and free shared types through one walker
body:
## Summary

- `types.zig` had 58 hand-written functions that copy or free a value field by field. Each repeats the same steps: duplicate every slice, copy its elements, undo the copies made so far when one fails, and free them all again. The new `src/core/shared/owned_copy.zig` describes each type once at compile time and walks the description to copy or free any value, the way `json_decode` shares one parser across types.
- The rule is simple: a value owns every slice and optional payload it reaches, and copies everything else bit for bit. A struct lists borrowed fields that copies leave out in `pub const copy_omits` (here `ToolCall.resolved_skill` and `resolved_display_target`). Any other pointer is a compile error, so a type whose ownership the walker can't read keeps hand-written code. `FinishedPrompt` keeps its pair because it retains and releases snapshot file ownership.
- The 57 public functions keep their names and signatures and call the walker, so no caller changes. Four private helpers are gone. `AGENTS.md` points new code at the walker.
- Two copy bugs go away with the hand-written code:
  - A copied interrupted turn keeps `stopped_by_exit`. This is the same fix as #1608, which can merge first.
  - Copying several context notes no longer leaks the sources of earlier notes when a later copy runs out of memory.

## Size

Measured on a local replay of the macOS release build, against `363327a6e`:

| | Change |
|---|---:|
| Machine code | −7,296 bytes |
| Descriptor tables | +3,160 bytes |

That's not enough to cross a 16 KB page, so the file size is unchanged on its own. This is the first of 158 files with hand-written copy and free pairs; the rest migrate in follow-ups.

## Speed

Copying a whole history runs on prompt submission, compaction, and resume. A ReleaseSafe benchmark that copies and frees three fully populated turns, 142 allocations, makes the same allocations as before but spends about 3 ns more per allocation walking the descriptors. That's about +35% for copying and +45% for freeing in isolation, or roughly 30 µs per copy of a 100-turn session. Strings, most of what these types own, are copied without a call per type.

## Testing

- `owned_copy.zig` tests: a copy equals its source and shares none of its memory, `copy_omits` fields are reset, values that own nothing copy as they are, and an allocation-failure sweep through `testing_allocator.no_resize` leaks nothing. Ten bugs planted one at a time in the walker each fail a test.
- New `types.zig` tests build every history-turn kind with every owned field set, then check the copy and run the same allocation-failure sweep. On the old code they fail on `stopped_by_exit` and on the context-note leak.
- A comptime dump of every migrated type's fields, compared against each hand-written copy, finds no ownership difference other than the intended ones above.
- CI's full unit suite passes in ReleaseSafe. Locally, 10,388 of 10,391 unit tests pass and 2 are skipped. The one failure is a command-runner test that races a cancel 25 ms before a 2-second timeout. It doesn't use this code and ran while the E2E suites were loading the machine. All 271 tests in `types.zig` and its imports pass in Debug and ReleaseSafe. `zig fmt --check src/` and every boundary and public-surface script pass.
- 16 E2E files pass on the release replay with API keys unset: `sessions`, `session-recovery`, `compaction-policy`, `tui-compaction-activity`, `tui-resume`, `tui-resume-brutal`, `acp`, `tui-interrupt-recovery`, `tui-host-instances`, `tui-host-switch`, `gateway-stream-lifecycle`, `cli`, `ask-presentation`, `file-tool-paths`, `tui-decision-prompts`, and `prompt-history`. There are two exceptions. `cli`'s `update_channel` check fails the same way on `main`'s local replay builds. A delegation-cancel test in `gateway-stream-lifecycle` failed once under load, then passed 13 of 13 times alone, as it does 3 of 3 times on `main`.
- On the release replay, one `fx ask` turn with a tool call against a fake gateway sends the same requests and saves the same session files as `main`, apart from IDs, times, and the temporary path.

title: ACP: declare an auth method so fx can be listed in the ACP registry
body:
we run fx through OpenBot, which only adds ACP agents from the ACP registry (no custom agent form on our setup). fx isn't in it yet.

two PRs already try to add it (agentclientprotocol/registry#540, #590) but they're stuck on the registry's auth check: it needs `initialize` to return at least one `authMethods` entry of type `agent` or `terminal`. right now `fx acp` returns `authMethods: []`, and without saved credentials `initialize` errors instead (details in agentclientprotocol/registry#591).

a terminal auth method that runs `fx login` (or `fx setup`) would probably be enough. then an official registry entry could ship with the releases.

happy to test on linux x86_64 once it's in. thanks for fx, it's been light on our server (~20 MB per session vs ~270 MB for what we had).

title: fix(journal): keep at most one resume notice per turn across queued checkpoint resumes
body:
Closes #1584

### Summary
When a planned queue hand-off resumes the same checkpoint repeatedly, each resume was previously appending another `"Resuming from unexpected session interruption."` to `steering`, causing notices to stack on every hop.

### Changes
- In `src/acp/libfx_journal.zig`:
  - Filter out existing `resume_notice` entries from `pending.execution.steering` before appending the fresh notice so that a turn never stacks them.
  - Added unit test cases in `"resuming the same checkpoint twice adds one notice, not two"` asserting exactly one notice remains across repeated resumes and zero when yielded.

title: Close an agent from the agent list with delete
body:
## Problem

Subagents belong to the session they started in. After a subagent finishes, it stays in the agent list as `idle`, and resuming the session brings it back. A session that delegated work over a few days ends up with a list like this:

```text
fx 1 · Subagent Task Completion Report · main · idle
  uno · No hagas nada. No uses herramientas. Responde solo · main · idle
  dos · No hagas nada. No uses herramientas. Responde solo · main · idle
  cinco (on screen) · No hagas nada. No uses herramientas. Responde solo · main · idle
  cuatro · No hagas nada. No uses herramientas. Responde solo · main · idle
  tres · No hagas nada. No uses herramientas. Responde solo · main · idle
```

You can't remove a single subagent today. Asking the main agent to stop one only ends its turn, and `/close` closes the whole instance with all of its subagents. The only way to get a clean list is `/new` or `/close`, which also drops the conversation you are working in.

Other agents give you a way out. Codex lets the main agent close a subagent with `close_agent`. Claude Code removes finished subagents from `/tasks` after a short time and lets you stop a running one with `x` in its subagent panel.

## Proposal

With the agent list open, pressing `delete` on a row closes that agent. While the list is open, other keys do nothing today, so `delete` doesn't conflict with typing or the draft.

### Behavior by row

| Row | First `delete` | Second `delete` on the same row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Idle or finished subagent | Closes it | Not needed |
| Working subagent, or one that needs approval or has a question | Shows a confirmation such as `del again to stop and close tres` | Stops its turn and closes it |
| Instance other than the last open one, such as `fx 2` | Shows a confirmation, because this closes its conversation and subagents | Same as `/close` on that instance |
| The only open instance | Nothing, and the hint stays hidden | Nothing |

Any other key cancels a pending confirmation.

### What closing a subagent does

1. Stops its turn if it is working, and drops the messages waiting for it, as a stop does today.
2. Removes it from the session, so it doesn't come back when you resume. See the open questions for what happens to its saved conversation.
3. Discards a report it still owed. You closed it because you no longer need its result.
4. Adds a note to the main agent's next message, such as `You closed subagent tres`. Without the note, the main agent could try to message a subagent that no longer exists. A later `subagent` call to that name starts a new subagent.
5. Frees the name, so the main agent can start a new subagent with it.

### List and screen updates

- The key hint row shows `del close` next to `↑↓ preview · enter switch · esc back` when the selected row can be closed.
- If you close the agent that is on screen, such as `cinco (on screen)`, fx shows its instance's screen, and `esc` returns there.
- After a close, the selection moves to the next row, or to the previous row when the closed row was last.

## Open questions

- Should a closed subagent's conversation be kept on disk for a while for debugging, as Claude Code keeps subagent transcripts for 30 days, or deleted right away?
- Should the main agent also get a tool action to close a subagent, like Codex's `close_agent`, so it can clean up after itself? This proposal covers only the user-facing key.
- The note to the main agent needs a format that the `subagent` tool and the recovery path already understand. That depends on how reports are stored today.

## Tests

- A TUI E2E test that starts subagents, opens the agent list, closes an idle one with `delete`, and checks that it is gone from the list and stays gone after resume.
- A TUI E2E test for the two-step confirmation on a working subagent.
- A test that the only open instance can't be closed from the list.
- A unit test that the main agent receives the close note once.

## Docs

- `fx.sh/docs/using-fx/instances`: add `delete` to "Switch between instances" and the agent list description.
- `fx.sh/docs/capabilities/subagents`: in "Switch to a subagent", explain that closing removes the subagent from the session and discards a pending report.
- `fx.sh/docs/using-fx/keyboard-shortcuts`: add the key.

## References

- [fx instances](https://fx.sh/docs/using-fx/instances)
- [fx subagents](https://fx.sh/docs/capabilities/subagents)
- [Claude Code subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)
- [Subagents comparison across agents](https://harnessnotes.com/subagents)
- [Codex: closed subagents remain visible in Desktop](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/23931)

title: Fix request recovery gaps under network and gateway faults
body:
## Summary

- Retry 529, 520, 524 and every other 5xx except 501 and 505 the way 503 is retried, and name the status the server sent instead of HTTP 502. 501 and 505 end the turn.
- Resend an AI Gateway request when its stream carries an event that is not JSON, shown as "Unreadable reply". After three such replies the turn ends with "unreadable reply". An event nested too deep to read still ends the turn.
- Spread retry waits over their jittered range instead of rounding each one up to a whole second.
- Show Offline, with offline backoff, when a connection times out before it opens.
- After a crash or a closed window, answer the original message on resume, and keep every later message consistent with it. The model no longer gets a "do not continue" note, hears about a possibly-run tool only when the stopped turn ran one, and sees one resume note after repeated closes.
- On Esc while an AI Gateway connection in the terminal app or `fx ask` is stuck in a DNS lookup or connect, end the turn at once so the next prompt starts right away. The connection that opens later goes back to the pool unused.
- Honor Retry-After from the browser SDK's host and from the direct Codex and xAI providers, counting only a plain number of seconds.
- End a browser SDK turn at once when it is cancelled during a retry wait.
- Retry the model catalog on the same server statuses as model requests.

title: Free copied context notes whole when a later copy fails
body:
## Summary

- When `dupePersistedContextNotes` ran out of memory partway through a list, its cleanup freed the text of the notes copied so far but not their sources, so those source paths leaked.
- The cleanup now frees each copied note in full with `freePersistedContextNote`.

## Testing

- New test `dupePersistedContextNotes leaves nothing behind when a later note fails to copy` copies two notes with sources under an allocation-failure sweep backed by `testing_allocator.no_resize`. It reports a leak without the fix and passes with it.
- All 267 tests in `types.zig` and its imports pass in Debug and ReleaseSafe.
- `zig fmt --check src/` and `zig build` pass, and `./zig-out/bin/fx --version` and `help` run.

title: Wait while another fx saves or refreshes a login
body:
## Summary

- A refreshed MCP login is saved instead of dropped with "another fx kept it busy" when other fx processes read or write the saved logins in the Keychain at the same time, such as several idle windows refreshing their logins together.
- Each Keychain call an fx makes while it holds the saved logins gets its own 10 seconds, so one fx on a slow Keychain still saves a login or signs out.
- A Keychain helper that stops reading what fx writes to it is stopped after 10 seconds, and the write fails, instead of holding the saved logins until it resumes.
- A waiting fx process gives up on the saved logins only when the process holding them has started no Keychain call for 12 seconds, as when that process is stopped with ctrl+z. It then shows the same notice as before.
- While an fx process from an older build holds the saved logins, a waiting process gives up 12 seconds after it started waiting.
- An fx that needs a login another fx is refreshing waits for that refresh, even one the sign-in server takes up to 30 seconds to answer, and then uses the login it saved instead of refreshing again with a token already used. Behind an fx stopped mid-refresh, it refreshes on its own about 32 seconds after that fx's last step.
- `fx mcp login` and `fx mcp logout` wait for the saved logins the same way.
- Logins kept in a file, with `FX_DISABLE_KEYCHAIN=1` or when no default Keychain exists, still wait 2 seconds.
- An fx whose fx login expired waits while another fx refreshes it, however slowly the Keychain or the issuer answers, and uses the login that fx saved, instead of failing its model request with "Credential refresh is temporarily unavailable."
- An fx whose Codex or Grok login expired waits the same way while another fx refreshes it.
- An fx waiting on one that froze while holding the fx, Codex, or Grok login lock (ctrl+z) gives up 17 seconds after that fx's last step, instead of 2 seconds after it started waiting.

## Why a lease

A longer fixed wait doesn't fix this. Several fx windows can take the saved logins in turn, each making Keychain calls of up to 10 seconds, so enough of them outlast any fixed wait, and a long one makes every window wait that long behind one that's stopped.

Instead, the fx holding the saved logins writes the time into the lock file before each Keychain call, and each call ends within its own 10 seconds. A waiting fx gives up only once that time is 12 seconds old: it waits as long as the holder keeps going and stops soon after the holder stops. A login's refresh lock works the same way. The refreshing fx stamps it when it takes it, before it sends the refresh, and before it saves, and a waiting fx goes ahead only 2 seconds after both the refresh's 30 seconds and the saved logins' 12 seconds ran out.

The fx, Codex, and Grok login locks use the same lease. The fx refreshing a login stamps its lock before each Keychain call and each request to the issuer, and a waiting fx gives up 17 seconds after the last stamp: the 15 seconds a request to the issuer may take, plus 2.

`tests/tla/mcp_host/StoreLockBudget.tla` and `tests/tla/mcp_host/RefreshLease.tla` model the MCP locks, and their drivers check real fx processes against them, on macOS for the Keychain.

title: Stop waiting on a fifo in place of the MCP config or a sign-in file
body:
## Summary

- When `~/.fx/mcp.json` was a fifo, `fx status`, `fx mcp add`, `fx mcp list`, and `fx mcp show` opened it for reading and waited for a writer that never came, so each one hung until killed.
- The three readers of the profile MCP config now share `config_file.read`, which opens through `io_mod.openExistingReadOnlyRegularFile`. A regular file, or a symlink to one, reads as before. Anything else fails with `DurablePathUnsafe` at once.
- `fx mcp` now says what is wrong. `list` and `show` print "an MCP config file isn't a plain file; replace it with one", and `add` says "it isn't a plain file" instead of blaming a hard link. `fx status` reports the error in its `mcp` section and finishes.
- `fx ask` and the shell hung at startup the same way. They now stop at once with `fx: DurablePathUnsafe`, as they already do for an `mcp.json` that is unreadable (`fx: AccessDenied`) or isn't valid JSON (`fx: McpConfigInvalidJson`).
- The MCP sign-in store had the same wait: with `~/.fx/mcp-credentials/credentials-v3.json` a fifo, `fx mcp list` hung. The store now opens it the same safe way, and a file that isn't a regular one counts as an unreadable store, as a damaged one does. A lookup finds no login, `fx mcp logout` says fx can't read the saved sign-ins, and the file is left as it is.
- The sign-in files had it too: with `~/.fx/auth.json`, `chatgpt-auth.json`, or `grok-auth.json` a fifo, `fx status` hung. Their four readers opened the file before checking what it was. They now open it the same safe way, and a fifo counts as no usable sign-in.

| `~/.fx/mcp.json` is a fifo | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `fx status --json` | hangs until killed | exit 0, `"inspection_error":"DurablePathUnsafe"` |
| `fx mcp list` | hangs until killed | exit 1, `fx mcp: an MCP config file isn't a plain file; replace it with one` |
| `fx mcp add probe -- /bin/echo hi` | hangs until killed | exit 1, `Couldn't add probe to ~/.fx/mcp.json: it isn't a plain file; replace it with one.` |
| `fx ask "say hi"` and `fx` | hang at startup | exit 1, `fx: DurablePathUnsafe` |

| A sign-in file is a fifo | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `fx status --json` with `auth.json`, `chatgpt-auth.json`, or `grok-auth.json` a fifo | hangs until killed | exit 0, auth `"missing"` |

A regular, a symlinked, and a missing `~/.fx/mcp.json` behave as before, and so do regular and missing sign-in files.

## Testing

- The new unit test "read returns a file's text, follows a symlink, and refuses a fifo without blocking" passes 20 of 20 runs.
- `FX_SOUND=0 bun test cli.test.ts -t "MCP profile"` passes, including the new test "status, list, and add finish when ~/.fx/mcp.json is a fifo".
- `FX_SOUND=0 bun test mcp-verbs.test.ts` passes.
- The credential store test "the credential file is private, and one this fx can't read is never written over" now also covers a fifo, and passes 20 of 20 runs.
- The new unit test "a private sign-in file is present, and a fifo in its place is unavailable without blocking" passes 20 of 20 runs.
- Ran `./zig-out/bin/fx` with a fifo `mcp.json`, alone and together with a fifo `settings.json`: `status`, `usage`, `mcp add`, `mcp list`, `mcp show`, and `sessions` each finished within a second. With each of nine files under `~/.fx` in turn a fifo, `status --json`, `mcp list`, `usage`, and `sessions` all finished.

title: Close subagents from the agent list, and show their titles and models
body:
## Summary

- Each agent list row ends with the agent's model, and its reasoning effort when that isn't the default, such as `reviewer · Review the parser · main · working · opus 4.7 high`.
- A subagent's first task gets a generated title, as the user's first prompt does, when the subagent runs on main's credential. One with its own credential keeps the title from its task's first words.
- An agent's title reaches the list as soon as it is generated, whether or not that agent is on screen.
- The footer counts subagents working off screen, such as `1 subagent working · main ↓`, when no agent needs the user, no instance finished unseen, and there's no upgrade or MCP status to show.
- In the agent list, `x` (or `X`) on a subagent's row shows `x again to close it for good` at once, a second `x` closes it, and any other key keeps it. The hint row shows `x close` on a subagent's row. `x` does nothing on an instance's row. After a close, the highlight is on the agent shown, the one that started the closed subagent.
- Closing a subagent stops its turn, drops the messages waiting for it, and removes it and the subagents it started from the list. It stays closed after a resume.
- When the user closes a subagent working on something main sent, main's report says the user closed it and how many of main's messages waiting for it were dropped. A report still owed after a restart names the closed subagent.
- The subagent tool has a `close` action. Main's close sends no report, its tool row reads `closed tester`, and a later message to that name starts a new subagent. If the close can't be saved, main gets `close_not_saved` and the subagent stays open.
- A message to a subagent while it is closing is refused with `child_closing`.
- An older fx opening a session with a closed subagent shows that subagent as idle.
- A subagent started without a profile is recorded as running in `main`, fx's own profile, as fx itself is without `--profile`. `main` sets nothing, so the subagent is still a copy of the agent that started it.
- A subagent's row shows the profile it runs in. Before, every subagent's row said `main`, because a subagent's own agent never loads its profile.

## Design

A close is saved in the parent's log as one more work item of the child, under the id `fxclose:<child id>`: a spawn line with the child's name and profile and no report rule, then a finish line whose data is `{"closed":true}`. fx writes it once the child's running work has ended, so a close never splits a work item. When fx folds the log, a child whose newest work item finished closed is left out of the registry, so it isn't listed, resumed, or messaged again. A new kind of log line would have changed the session format libfx owns. This pair needs no format change, and an older fx shows the closed subagent as idle.

title: Keep a startup file's builtin function out of fx's shell setup
body:
## Summary

- zsh and bash run a function before a builtin of the same name. A `.zshrc` or `.bash_profile` that defines `builtin` therefore took over every `\builtin` line fx adds: the zsh preludes that turn off `equals` and reset the TERM trap, the snapshot capture's `printf` lines, and the terminal bootstrap's `eval`. In zsh, a command such as `echo ======` failed with `zsh:1: ===== not found`.
- fx now removes such a function before its own lines. zsh runs `(( ${+functions[builtin]} )) && \unfunction builtin`, which runs no command when there is no such function, so `setopt errexit` in a startup file can't stop it. bash runs `\unset -f builtin`, which succeeds either way, at the top of the snapshot capture and before the terminal's `eval`.
- The capture removes the function before it lists the user's functions, so a snapshot replay never brings it back. The command fx runs then runs without that function too, since fx can't keep the user's `builtin` and still rely on the real one. The `user` profile's zsh prelude now runs the removal and `unsetopt equals` before resetting the TERM trap.

| Startup file defines `builtin() { ... }` | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| zsh, `echo before; echo ======; echo after` | `zsh:1: ===== not found`, and the function runs | prints all three lines; the function never runs |
| bash, same command | the snapshot capture runs the function | prints all three lines; the function never runs |

Without such a function, the commands fx runs are the same apart from the added line.

## Testing

- The new unit test "a startup file's builtin function never runs in place of fx's shell setup" runs a command through a real zsh and bash, from a snapshot and from full startup. It passes 20 of 20 runs, and with main's `shell_resolver.zig` it fails 20 of 20 with `zsh:1: ===== not found`.
- The `shell_resolver` tests that pin the exact zsh and bash command lines are updated and pass 20 of 20 runs.
- `zig build` passes.

title: Outline cold code on Linux x86_64 PGSO candidates
body:
## Summary

- Linux x86_64 PGSO candidates now run LLVM's machine outliner on code the training profile marks cold (`-enable-machine-outliner=conservative-pgo`). AArch64 already does this by default for the functions profile use compiles for size.
- Hot code, code without profile data, and the `nooutline` startup functions stay inline, so the startup commands keep their code in place.
- The x86_64 benchmark candidates get the same flag, so the heavy workloads measure its cost.
- Linux arm64 and macOS candidates are unchanged.
- In a local model of the current x86_64 fx code (every function except the ones the arm64 profile keeps hot compiled for size), outlining shrank the code from 8,758,454 to 8,426,381 bytes (−3.8%).
- On this PR's Linux x86_64 PGSO run, the candidate is 8,364,192 bytes (7.98 MiB), 0.77 MiB under the 8.75 MiB ceiling. #1649's run, without outlining, produced 8,568,336 bytes, and the plain build grew by 105,312 bytes between the two runs' bases, so at the same plain size outlining saves about 272,000 bytes (0.26 MiB).

title: Add an embedded JavaScript engine
body:
## Summary

- Add fx's own copy of quickjs-ng v0.18.0 in `src/js/quickjs/`, without its file, process, and timer modules. This is the first third-party C code fx builds. The maintainers agreed to add it for code mode, which needs a JavaScript runtime that every fx binary carries and that gives a program no file, network, or process access. `FORK.md` records the release, its checksum, a script that compares the copy with upstream, and the changes fx makes to it.
- Make the copy's array loops, such as `join`, `reverse`, `sort`, and `slice`, check the deadline on each pass. They walk an object up to its `length`, which a program can set as high as 2^53 - 1, and before this change `Array.prototype.join.call({ length: 2 ** 27 }, '')` ran for more than a second against a 200 ms limit.
- Make the copy's `cutils.h` include `<stddef.h>`. A static musl build, which is how fx ships on Linux, doesn't define `offsetof` before that header runs, so the header's fallback `((size_t) &((type *)0)->field)` stood in. The C undefined-behavior checks read that as a member access through a null pointer, so every `container_of` trapped and the engine stopped at its first allocation. Compiled for `aarch64-linux-musl` with the include, `quickjs.c` has the same 3,090 undefined-behavior checks as the glibc build, not 3,595.
- Add `src/js/engine.zig`, which runs one program in a fresh runtime with limits on its heap (64 MiB), its time (30 s), and its native stack (4 MiB in Debug builds, 1 MiB otherwise). A program that hits the heap limit stops with an error it can't catch. The heap also has a cap of its own, because QuickJS's limit doesn't count the 4 KiB arenas it carves small blocks from.
- Report a timeout, not a thrown error, when the deadline passes while a program's own `toJSON` or `toString` runs, and keep thrown text valid UTF-8 when a program throws a lone surrogate.
- Run the engine's tests with `zig build test-js`, which `zig build test` also runs. Nothing in the fx binary uses the engine yet.
- Run the macOS check for any change to the engine's C.
- Describe `src/js/` in `AGENTS.md`, and add quickjs-ng's license to `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`.


## Architecture

Before, fx had no JavaScript engine:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  test["zig build test"] --> fxtests["fx unit tests"]
  fx["fx binary"]
```

After, the engine is its own module, built and tested by `zig build test-js`. The fx binary doesn't link it yet:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  test["zig build test"] --> fxtests["fx unit tests"]
  test --> testjs["zig build test-js"]
  testjs --> engine["src/js/engine.zig: run"]
  engine --> bindings["src/js/quickjs.zig"]
  engine --> heap["src/js/capped_heap.zig"]
  bindings --> fork["src/js/quickjs/: quickjs-ng v0.18.0 fork"]
  heap --> fork
  fx["fx binary"] -.-|not linked yet| engine
```

title: Leave out built-ins code mode does not need
body:
## Summary

- Give programs only the built-ins code mode keeps. `Proxy`, `WeakRef`, `FinalizationRegistry`, the typed arrays, `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer`, `Atomics`, and `DataView` are left out. None of the 30 programs that models wrote in fx's code-mode evals used them.
- Reading a left-out name, `typeof` included, throws `TypeError: <name> is not available in code mode`, so a model learns why its program failed and can rewrite it.
- Make `eval` and the four Function constructors stand-ins with the same names. A program can still use `instanceof Function`, `typeof eval`, or `fn.constructor.name`, but calling one throws, for example `TypeError: The Function constructor is not available in code mode`.
- Make `import()` throw `TypeError: import() is not available in code mode`.

## Why a prelude

Leaving intrinsic groups out of the context can't remove `eval` or the Function constructors. `JS_AddIntrinsicBaseObjects` installs `Function`, `GeneratorFunction`, and the global `eval`, and `JS_AddIntrinsicPromise` installs the async constructors. Every program needs both groups, because it runs as the body of an async arrow function. QuickJS also has no hook like the one V8 gives Node's `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings` and Cloudflare Workers for refusing code generation from strings.

So a short prelude runs before each program and swaps in the stand-ins. Its properties are neither writable nor configurable, so a program can't undo them. Direct `eval(...)` compiles code only when the callee is QuickJS's own `eval`, which no program can reach.

The other left-out names throw when read rather than going missing, so a model sees that a name was left out on purpose instead of `ReferenceError: Proxy is not defined`. The cost is that `typeof Proxy` throws too, so feature detection doesn't work for these names.

## Architecture

Before, `run` built a context with every built-in QuickJS offers:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  run["engine.run"] --> ctx["JS_NewContext: every built-in group"]
  ctx --> program["program"]
```

After, `run` refuses every `import()`, builds a context with only the kept groups, and runs the prelude before the program:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  run["engine.run"] --> loader["module loader: refuseImport"]
  run --> raw["JS_NewContextRaw"]
  raw --> groups["kept groups: base objects, Date, compiler, RegExp, JSON, Map and Set, Promise, atob and btoa, performance"]
  groups --> prelude["cut_prelude: throwing getters for left-out names, stand-ins for eval and the Function constructors"]
  prelude --> program["program"]
```

## Testing

- `zig build test-js` passes 22 tests in Debug and ReleaseSafe. They cover the 30 eval programs run against stand-in tools, every path to code generation, attempts to undo the prelude, and the patterns that must keep working, such as `instanceof Function`, `fn.constructor.name`, and `typeof eval`.
- The deep-nesting test now nests the program's own text, because its `eval` call had been throwing before it reached the parser.

Stacked on #1634.

title: Fuzz the JavaScript engine
body:
## Summary

- Add three fuzz targets, `js_program`, `js_regexp`, and `js_json`, seeded with programs models wrote, and list them for the nightly Fuzz workflow.
- Fix a crash in `String.prototype.normalize` and `localeCompare`. The engine's C called its realloc callback through the wrong function type, which the function-type check traps on in release builds. The fork now wraps the callback, and `FORK.md` records the patch.
- Leave the engine's C uninstrumented in fuzz builds, since Zig's fuzzer can't read C coverage. The targets follow the Zig code's coverage.

Stacked on #1635.

## Architecture

Before, `tests/fuzz/targets.json` could name targets in fx or the session manager, and the engine was only tested by `test-js`:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["tests/fuzz/targets.json"] --> B["build.zig reads targets and saved inputs"]
  B -->|"fx targets"| F["fuzz"]
  B -->|"session manager targets, in its build options"| S["fuzz-session-manager"]
  E["src/js engine"] -.->|"not fuzzed"| X["test-js"]
```

After, the engine is a third fuzz module with its own binary:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["tests/fuzz/targets.json"] --> B["build.zig reads targets and saved inputs"]
  B -->|"fx targets"| F["fuzz"]
  B -->|"session manager targets, in its build options"| S["fuzz-session-manager"]
  B -->|"js targets, in the engine's build options"| J["fuzz-js"]
  J --> P["js_program, js_regexp, js_json in engine.zig"]
  P --> C["QuickJS C: no coverage instrumentation, function-type check traps"]
```

The engine imports nothing from fx, like the session manager, so its saved inputs travel in its own build options as `fuzz_corpus_<target>`.

### Why wrap the callbacks

The function-type check found a real bug, so the fork fixes the calls instead of turning the check off for the engine's C, which would also hide the next mismatch. The fix is two wrappers, `fx_dbuf_realloc_ctx` and `fx_dbuf_realloc_rt`, with the exact `DynBufReallocFunc` type. `FORK.md` records them for the next upstream update.

Zig's sanitizer runtime has no handler for this check, so Debug builds used to leave it out. Trapping on it keeps the check in Debug, where the tests and the fuzzer run.

## Testing

On #1635, a ReleaseSafe build that calls either method crashes:

```
error: 'probe-normalize.test.normalize and localeCompare return' terminated with signal TRAP
```

A Debug build of #1635 runs the same program without a trap, because it doesn't check the call. Built with this branch's flags, #1635's code traps in Debug too.

On this branch, the same program returns:

```
"\u00e9".normalize("NFD").length                            2
"e\u0301".normalize("NFC").length                           1
"\ufb01".normalize("NFKD")                                  "fi"
"\u1e9b\u0323".normalize("NFKC").length                     1
["b", "a", "\u00e9", "e"].sort((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y))  ["a","b","e","é"]
```

- `zig build test-js` passes in Debug and ReleaseSafe, 26 of 26.
- `zig build fuzz -Dfuzz-target=<target> --fuzz=500` is clean for all three targets, and 2,000 more inputs each on `js_regexp` and `js_json`.
- In a Debug build with these flags, a program that calls every function reachable from the globals, their constructors, and their prototypes (391 functions, 17,220 calls) finishes without a trap.

title: Build the JavaScript engine's C for size
body:
## Summary

- Compile the engine's C with `-Os` in release builds. At the top of this stack (#1639), a ReleaseSafe `fx` is 192,704 bytes (188 KiB) smaller, and a binary with only the engine is about 181 KiB smaller.
- The engine runs about 6% slower. On a workload of 40,000 objects through JSON, filtering, a regex test, and a sort, `-Os` was 4% to 9% slower on the best run across three alternating comparisons, and 6% slower on the median of 84 runs.
- Keep the C unoptimized with full checks in Debug builds.

Stacked on #1636.

## Measurements

ReleaseSafe builds on macOS arm64, in bytes:

| Binary | Default (`-O2`) | `-Os` | Saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fx` at #1639's head | 13,635,344 | 13,442,640 | 192,704 |
| `zig build test-js` test binary | 1,834,376 | 1,649,464 | 184,912 |

To repeat the `fx` row, run `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe` at #1639's head, then again with the `-Os` entry removed from `quickjs_release_flags`, and compare `zig-out/bin/fx`.

title: Show the fork notice after the replayed conversation
body:
## Summary

- After `/fork`, the `session forked` notice and the command that reopens the original session appear after the replayed turns, just above the input box, instead of above the whole replay.
- On a session longer than the terminal's scrollback, the notice and the command stay on screen after the fork instead of scrolling out of reach.
- The command sits alone on the line under `Resume the original session with:`, so selecting that line copies only `fx --resume <id>`.

title: Make the shared sort faster than std.mem.sort
body:
## Summary

- `sort_utils.sort` swapped elements one byte at a time and merged runs only by rotating them in place. On the lists fx sorts it ran 2 to 14 times slower than `std.mem.sort`.
- It now sorts runs of 16 by insertion and merges them through an 8 KB stack buffer, back and forth between the list and the buffer when the whole list fits.
- Only the insertion and merge loops, which compare elements, are compiled per element type, so comparisons inline as they do in `std.mem.sort`. The run schedule, the buffer handling, and the in-place fallback for runs larger than the buffer stay shared. Lists of 16 or fewer don't reserve the buffer.

## Speed

ReleaseSafe on macOS arm64, best of 15 runs, allocator hidden from the optimizer, shuffled input. Each cell compares against `std.mem.sort` on the same list.

| List | n=16 | n=200 | n=1000–3000 | Old shared sort, n=200 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `Ranked` as in capability retrieval (24 B, score) | 67% faster | 21% faster | 25–29% faster | 11.6× slower |
| `SessionSummary` (120 B, newest first) | 83% faster | 67% faster | 49–70% faster | 7.4× slower |
| Indices compared through records, as in `host_record` and `tool_group_projection` | 78% faster | 46% faster | 49% faster | |
| 48-byte rows by string key | 79% faster | 13% faster | 5–11% faster | 13.7× slower |
| Strings | 61% faster | 12% faster | 15% faster | 4.9× slower |

The one case still slower than `std.mem.sort` is bare integers compared with a plain `<` at 50 to 2000 elements (14 to 34%). No call site in fx sorts that, and it's 4 to 20 times faster than the old shared sort there.

## Size

The comparing loops compiled per element type cost size. Insertion, the merge from the buffer, and the whole-list merge pass are compiled for each of the 27 sorted types. Plain ReleaseSafe build for macOS arm64, against `main` at `921268063`:

| | File | `__text` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `main` | 11,100,880 | 9,802,376 |
| This PR | 11,133,728 (+32,848) | 9,842,356 (+39,980) |

The first version also compiled a merge from the right; dropping it saved 16,416 bytes at the same speed. Moving these 27 sorts to `std.mem.sort` instead would compile a block sort of 6.6 to 8.4 KB for each. The PGSO release size is in PGSO run 41946191135.

## Testing

- The module's tests compare every result against `std.mem.sort` element for element, which is exact because both sorts are stable. New tests cover runs larger than the buffer (2,000 elements of 64 bytes in random, sorted, reversed, equal, and sawtooth order), elements larger than the buffer, and over-aligned elements, which skip the buffer.
- 13 bugs planted one at a time in the insertion, merges, merge pass, ordered-run skip, rotations, and swaps each fail a test. Six of them are caught only by the new tests.
- `zig test` passes in Debug and ReleaseSafe. `zig fmt --check src/`, every boundary and public-surface script, and `zig build` pass, and `./zig-out/bin/fx --version` and `help` run.
- The local full unit and E2E runs were too loaded to judge: their failures are timing tests, and the two `skill_runtime` failures reproduce on `main` in the same harness. CI is the clean check.

title: Speed up the shared JSON parser
body:
## Summary

- `json_decode` ran 4 to 12% slower than `std.json`, mostly from matching object keys and from the call and dispatch made for every value.
- Keys: fx writes fields in declaration order, so the parser tries the field after the last one matched before scanning. Names up to 16 bytes compare as two overlapping words instead of a byte loop.
- Values: strings, numbers, and optionals inside an object or list are parsed in place, without a call through `parseInto`. An optional number, enum, or string payload skips that dispatch too.
- Results and errors stay identical to `std.json`.

## Speed

ReleaseSafe on macOS arm64, best of 41 runs, with std and this parser taking turns going first. Each cell compares against `std.json`.

| Document | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| 100-event session log, 54 KB | 4–7% slower | 3–5% faster |
| One session record, 534 B | 6–10% slower | within ±1% |
| Tool arguments with optional numbers, 61 B | 9–12% slower | about 4% slower (about 5 ns) |
| Plain tool arguments, 43 B | | 3–4% slower (4–7 ns) |

The rest of the gap on tiny objects is the shared integer parse and one dispatch per object. Closing it would mean reproducing every `std.fmt.parseInt` error case in a generic integer path, which this change doesn't attempt.

## Testing

- Two new differential tests run every input through `std.json` and this parser under all six option sets. They cover keys in declaration, reversed, and shuffled order, repeated keys, unknown and near-miss keys, names of every length class that differ in one middle byte, an escaped key, and strings, numbers, nulls, and optionals parsed inline, including wrong-type and out-of-range values.
- Five bugs planted one at a time in the name comparison, the expected-field shortcut, mutable string copies, and inline nulls each fail a test. Four of them are caught by the new tests.
- `zig test` passes in Debug and ReleaseSafe. `zig fmt --check src/`, every boundary and public-surface script, and `zig build` pass. `./zig-out/bin/fx --version`, `help`, `config --json`, and `sessions --json` run on a fresh profile.

title: Count tui-transcript-window in the PGSO corpus test
body:
## Summary

- `scripts/pgso/corpus.json` classifies `tui-transcript-window.test.ts` as a verification file. The corpus test still listed the verification files and counted the candidate scenarios from before it was added.
- The PGSO driver tests therefore fail on `main`, and with them every macOS arm64 PGSO run, the stable release's included. This adds the file to the test's list and raises the candidate count from 66 to 67.

## Testing

title: Keep diff counts visible on clipped grouped edit rows
body:
## Summary

- Grouped Edited and Wrote rows that are too wide for the terminal now cut the path with an ellipsis and keep their `+N / -M` line counts at the end of the row.
- When the counts would fill more than half of a very narrow row, the row is cut from the right as before.

title: Compare only the defined reasoning effort options in tests
body:
## Summary

- Model capability tests compare the defined reasoning effort options, the option count, and every other field, without reading the undefined tail of the options buffer.
- The input runtime defaults test does the same for the effort menu's options.

title: Work around two more IR outliner miscompiles
body:
## Summary

- PGSO builds no longer let LLVM's IR outliner replace an outlined function's exit selector with a lifted parameter, which sent callers down the wrong branch. A unit test hit this as an `orelse` panic on a non-null result.
- PGSO builds find outlined functions whose output stores the outliner left in unreachable blocks, exclude their callers from outlining, and outline again, failing after four rounds. A macOS arm64 candidate rebuilt from #1600's inputs had one such function, in the footer row builders, whose callers lost the error code on `OutOfMemory`. This PR's own macOS arm64 candidate had none in its first round.
- `check-outlined` fails the build on either pattern.

title: Run the unit tests on PGSO-transformed code on Linux
body:
## Summary

- The Linux arm64 and x86_64 PGSO workflows run fx's unit tests on code built through the candidate's transforms, with every function marked `minsize`, and fail if any test fails.
- A failed run is retried once, and a pass on the retry prints a warning naming the tests that failed first.
- The PGSO control and bitcode builds time out after 30 minutes instead of 15.
- The step adds about 30 minutes to the Linux x86_64 PGSO run and 37 to the Linux arm64 one, measured on this branch's last green runs.

title: Order Linux PGSO candidates by function again
body:
## Summary

- Linux PGSO candidates place the startup functions first, in first-use order, followed by the profile order. Since #1548, every fx function reached code generation without a symbol, so lld's symbol ordering silently dropped all of them: #1627's Linux x86_64 run mapped 0 of its 4,710 profile functions, and #1566's arm64 run 0 of 4,719.
- The fx candidate's private functions get internal linkage before code generation. The code is the same, and each function keeps a local symbol that lld orders and the final `-s` link strips.
- A Linux PGSO build fails when an fx function section reaches the ordered link without a symbol, instead of shipping an unordered candidate.
- macOS candidates, which order sections, and Linux benchmark candidates are unchanged.
- On this PR's runs the order applies again, and Linux startup commands come closer to the plain build. On x86_64, 4,809 functions were ordered (720 of 4,821 profile functions unmapped), and `fx --version` p50 is +2.4% against +7.4% on #1627's run on the same runner type. On arm64, 4,804 were ordered (717 of 4,837 unmapped), and `fx --version` p50 is +2.2% against +6.1% on #1566's run. The x86_64 candidate's `fx --version` now touches code in 10 64 KB windows, as the plain build does, against 18 before, measured with valgrind's memory trace.

title: Let tmux answer the theme test's background query
body:
## Summary

- The theme-change E2E test no longer races fx's 200 ms background-color query. tmux answers it from the pane's background, so the test settles on light and then dark without injecting replies.

title: Remove the unused external handoff and stale audit rules
body:
## Summary

- Remove `App.runExternalInteractive`, which nothing calls, and the direct-write audit rule that named it.
- Remove six more direct-write audit rules that classify no write site, and the two categories only they used.
- The direct-write audit fails when, run on this repository, a rule classifies no site.

title: Keep eight unit tests passing on a busy machine
body:
## Summary

- The two skill refresh unit tests wait up to ten seconds for the background refresh instead of a fixed count of yields.
- Two auth inventory tests and two full-transcript tests wait up to ten seconds for their background task instead of a fixed count of yields.
- The output-drain deadline unit test times its command's exit by the wall clock, so a slow Python start can't push it past the deadline.
- The MCP SIGTERM unit test waits for each server script to set its trap before stopping it.

## Testing

I built just these eight tests and ran them five times with one busy loop per CPU. On `main`, three of the five runs failed, each time in the output-drain deadline test. On this branch, all five passed.

title: Start /launch instances with their own profile's model and effort
body:
## Summary

- `/launch <profile>` inside `fx --profile <name>` starts the new instance with the launched profile's model and effort instead of the first profile's.
- A launched profile that sets no model or effort starts from the configured ones.

title: Say when fx can't remove a saved MCP login
body:
## Summary

- `fx mcp logout` and `/mcp logout` say when the saved login couldn't be removed, and why, instead of printing "Signed out" while every other fx keeps using it. `fx mcp logout` exits 1.
- A logout while another fx keeps the saved logins busy says nothing changed, and why, instead of "fx mcp: something went wrong".
- `fx mcp remove` says when it removed the server but couldn't delete its saved login, why, and how to delete it once that's fixed, instead of printing only "Removed X from ~/.fx/mcp.json." It exits 1, since the login stays with no server left to sign out of.
- The notice for a login that can't be saved, and these messages, give the reason in words, such as a store fx isn't allowed to write, a full disk, or a Keychain that refused the change, instead of the error's name.

title: Wait while another fx refreshes the same login
body:
## Summary

- An fx whose fx login expired waits while another fx refreshes it, however slowly the Keychain or the issuer answers, and uses the login that fx saved, instead of failing its model request with "Credential refresh is temporarily unavailable."
- An fx whose Codex or Grok login expired waits the same way while another fx refreshes it, instead of failing its model request with the same error.
- An fx waiting on one that froze while holding one of these locks (ctrl+z) gives up 17 s after that fx's last step, instead of 2 s after it started waiting.

Stacked on #1619.

title: Keep the provider picker key column test's labels in a live buffer
body:
## Summary

- The provider picker's key column test reads each row's label from a buffer the test owns. Before, the label pointed into a helper's dead stack frame, and the test failed on a Linux x86_64 PGSO build of the unit tests.
