| `fx mcp show NAME` for a saved login the server refuses | `status needs login`, JSON `"error": null` | the same status, plus `error  NAME refused the saved login (invalid_token: "No authorization provided").` and the same text in the JSON `error`; exit 1 as before |
| the `/mcp` status line | `NAME needs login · /mcp` | `NAME refused the saved login · /mcp` |
| `/trace`, the problem record for the server | `issue: needs_login`, with nothing about the refusal | the same `issue`, and `error` carries the same words |
| `capability_search`, `authentication_required.message` | `Run /mcp login NAME, then search again.` | `NAME refused the saved login (invalid_token: "No authorization provided"). Run /mcp login NAME, then search again.` (the search answer is escaped for HTML, so a quote reaches the model as `"`) |
| `fx mcp call` from the agent's shell, for a server that is waiting for a login | `MCP server 'NAME' needs a login. Ask the user to …, then try again.` | `MCP server 'NAME' needs a login: NAME refused the saved login (invalid_token: "No authorization provided"). Ask the user to …, then try again.` |
| a tool call the model makes that gets the 401 itself, on a login that worked until then | `MCP server 'NAME' needs a login. Ask the user to …, then try again.` | the same words as the row above, with the server's own |

A server that gives no error says `NAME refused the saved login`. No saved login at all, and a refused refresh, keep their own words.

## Behavior notes

- A new login is saved when the server accepts a request that carries it. The engine holds the new tokens in memory, fx sends the same request `fx mcp show` uses, and the answer ends the sign-in. When that request can't be checked (no answer, a 5xx, a dropped connection, a 403 that isn't a step-up, or the 45 second wait ending with no 401 held), the login is kept with a note. A login the server refused with a 401 that reached fx before the save is never saved. The check request's own 401 can come after the save only for a server whose `startup_timeout_ms` is over 45 seconds and that sends it after the wait ended: fx holds no 401 then and keeps the login with the note. That late 401 reaches the host after the sign-in has ended, so it refuses the login as a saved one, not a new one, and the server shows as needing a login.
- A refused new login is not kept: it is dropped, nothing is saved, and nothing is revoked for it. It is not a logout, so it shows nothing from a logout.
- A 401 to a request that carried the new token refuses the login, unless the refresh that the 401 starts brings a token the server then accepts: that retry is accepted, and the login is saved. When the refresh gets no usable answer (a 5xx, a 429, none), the engine ends the request as failed but still holds the 401, and the host reads it (`Engine.loginRejected`) before it decides the check "couldn't be made". The 45 second wait for the check ends the same way: with a 401 held (a refresh or a retry is still pending) the login is refused and nothing is saved, otherwise it is kept with the note. The wait only comes into play when a server's `startup_timeout_ms` is longer than 45 seconds, since the engine's own start timer (30 seconds by default) ends the check first. The first version of this change saved the refused token in these cases.
- A 401 counts against the new login only when the request carried the newest token. A late 401 to a request that went out with a token since replaced is answered by sending the request again with the new one.
- A check request that fails without a 401 on the token still signs in, with the note above. A 403 that is not a step-up is one of these: the server answered, but not about the token.
- The server's words are quoted inside fx's sentence, with a quote or a backslash in them escaped, so a description such as `x). Signed in to NAME` can't close the sentence or start one of fx's own. The error shows only when it is a plain token (letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.`, up to 64 bytes). The same words reach the model, so the model's text is covered too.
- After `/mcp login`, the server is connected, because the request that checks the login connects it. `/mcp list` shows `ready, 1 tool` right after, where it showed `signed in`.
- After a refused re-login of a server that is already up, the host takes the saved login that worked before back into use. That is not a sign-in, so it says nothing: the footer no longer says `Signed in to NAME.` right after `Couldn't sign in to NAME`. A login another fx saved within 30 seconds of the refusal is taken the same way, without the notice. One saved later is a new login, and fx says "Signed in to NAME.". The same 30 seconds bound the older saved login that comes back: if nothing picks it up within 30 seconds of the refusal, it gets "Signed in to NAME." too, though it is not a new sign-in.
- A logout while a login waits for that request ends the login: nothing is saved and "Signed in" is not said.
- When the saved logins can't be read, a refusal is kept, and it shows once they read. The status says the store can't be read until then.
- A server's words with typographic quotes (“ ”) are shown as they are. Only the straight quote and the backslash are escaped, because only they can close fx's sentence.
- The server's error and description are cut (64 and 240 bytes, the engine parser's own bounds) and made terminal-safe before they are shown. Logs name the server and a plain error code, never the server's text or a token.

## How it is checked

- `tests/tla/mcp_host/SignIn.tla` gains a check request before "Signed in", with `SignedInOnlyAfterCheck`, `NoticeMatchesAnswer`, `RefusedNeverSaved`, `NeverTakeRefused`, `AnsweredKeptAndReported`, `NoPendingWithoutHost` and `ConfirmingEnds`. It also models the host's read again of the saved logins (`Reread`, `HeldNeverReplaced`), the order of a sign-in's answer and the unreadable-store branch (`UnreadFirst`), a logout during the check (`Logout`, `LoggedOutNeverSaved`), a 401 whose refresh then gets no usable answer (the answer `refuse_unrenewed`, with `RefreshFailAsUnchecked`), and the 45 second wait for the check (`ExpireCheck`, with `DeadlineKeepsRefused`). Five findings configs show fx before this change breaking the properties. 25 planted bugs are caught, among them "the deadline saves a refused login" (`RefusedNeverSaved`). The smoke config has 77,824 distinct states and the stress config 23,332,864. `AuthGate.tla` records why a request needed a sign-in, with four invariants and four planted bugs.
- The model owner is `SignIn.tla` and not a new model, because it already holds the check request, its answers, and what is saved.
- Bun drivers run the built binary against a fake OAuth server and have TLC check each trace: a refused login, a refused login whose refresh answers 500, a garbage challenge, a 500, a dropped connection, a check that gets no answer, fx killed mid-check, and refused sign-ins in a row. The stress test runs 6 sign-ins by default (`FX_TLA_SIGNIN_STRESS`). A run with `FX_TLA_SIGNIN_STRESS=50 bun test ./tests/tla/drivers/mcp_host/sign-in.test.ts -t "repeated sign-ins"` ran 50 and passed on a Linux x86_64 build of this head.
- `tests/e2e/mcp-auth.test.ts` has the cases above through the CLI, the TUI, `capability_search` and `fx mcp call`. It includes the re-login of a server that is already up (with a check of the footer), a refusal while the store can't be read, a saved login another fx made while a new one waits for its check, a logout during the check, a new login refused with a refresh that answers 500 or 429 (exit 1, no store file; and with a saved login, the store file unchanged), a tool call that gets the 401 itself, and a description that tries to close fx's sentence. The tests of the review fixes fail on the head they were written against and pass on this one. The second review added three more: a new login refused while the check's retry is held past the 45 second wait (the server's `startup_timeout_ms` is 120 s so the engine's own timer doesn't end it first; exit 1, no store file), a login another fx saves 35 seconds after a refusal (the notice is shown), and a Zig test that a late 401 for a replaced token is no refusal, plus one for the 30 second bound.
- A new fuzz target, `mcp_challenge`, reads a `WWW-Authenticate` header within its bounds, with 8 saved inputs. One of them is a header that spells `insufficient_scope` with an escape (`insuffic\ient_scope`), which a server may send and which the parser reads as that word; a first version of the fuzz law rejected it.
- Eleven planted bugs in the code were each caught by one of the tests, in a run of a script that is not in the repository. They were: the sign-in reported as signed in on the exchange again; a refused login saved before it is dropped; a refresh during the check saving the unconfirmed login; the engine dropping the reason a refused token carried; the challenge's description kept without a bound; a sign-in the server couldn't be asked about saying plain "Signed in"; the check request served from a tool list kept from an earlier login; the status line saying "needs login" for a refused login; the unreadable-store branch answering the check request first; a re-read of the store taking a login in place of the one a sign-in holds; and a logout leaving the login that waits for its check request going. The two new planted bugs for the unrenewed 401 are in `SignIn.mutants.json`.
- The `TLA+ MCP models and drivers` job no longer runs `tests/tla/mcp_host/check.sh` on top of `models.test.ts`, which runs the same catalog and checks more. The job had reached its 40-minute limit with the larger `SignIn` model. The script stays for local use.

## Where the checks ran

- macOS arm64, ReleaseSafe build, no model keys: `mcp-auth.test.ts` and `mcp-verbs.test.ts` whole, the Zig tests for the changed code by name, `zig fmt --check src/`, `scripts/check-public-surface.sh`, and `ci-shards.test.ts`.
- Linux x86_64: `tests/tla/mcp_host/check.sh` whole, the sign-in drivers on a build made there (23 tests), and the 50-sign-in stress run.

## What was not checked

- A real third-party server such as ClickState. Only fakes were used.
- ThreadSanitizer. The Linux run of the first version was not repeated for this repair, which adds no thread or shared state: the host reads the engine's held 401 on its owner thread. The macOS ThreadSanitizer build was never run.
- A server that answers 401 to `initialize` for a reason other than the token.

## Merge notes

`origin/main` moved the trace report to `src/core/app/trace_report.zig` and its format to JSON Lines while this was open. The `/trace` change in `app_commands.zig` is gone with the code it edited, and the `error` field of the problem record carries the words instead. `tests/tla/README.md` merged by keeping both sides.

## Docs

The troubleshooting page gets a row for a server that refuses the login, and one for a sign-in that couldn't be checked. The MCP page says when the login is saved. Companion PR: https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx-web/pull/272

title: Send the user's own words with a subagent's message to main
body:
## Summary

- When the user asks a subagent on its screen to pass something on, main now gets the lines the user typed there with the subagent's message, so it can see the request came from the user.
- A line the user types into a turn main started counts the same way. Main's own messages and other subagents' reports never count as the user's.
- A subagent's own text can't add or change those lines.
- Each message carries at most the user's last eight lines, each cut to 2 KB.

title: Show a restored subagent's own title after a resume
body:
## Summary

- After a resume, the agent list shows each subagent from before the restart with its own saved title, not "new session", before its conversation is opened.
- A restored subagent that main messages before the list is opened gets its saved title too.

title: Say what main's wait, status and stop calls do
body:
## Summary

- Main's `wait` call shows as "waiting for subagents", then "waited for subagents", not "Managing subagent" and "Managed subagent".
- A `status` call shows as "checking subagents" or "checked tester", and a `stop` call as "stopping tester" or "stopped tester".
- A call that fails reads "couldn't check tester", and one that is interrupted reads "wait for subagents interrupted".
- A group of subagent calls counts them as calls: "4 tool calls · 4 subagent calls", not "4 subagents" when two subagents got four calls.

title: Tell main when the user closed a subagent it calls again
body:
## Summary

- When the user closes an idle subagent from the agent list, main hears nothing today. Its next message to that name starts a new subagent with no history, and main treats it as the old one.
- Main's `status` now lists the name as `tester: closed by the user; a message to it starts a new one with no history`.
- The message that starts a new subagent under that name adds: "The user closed the earlier tester, so this one starts with no history." The note is given once.
- A close by main itself adds nothing. The note lives in memory, so a restart forgets it.

## Tests

- Unit: `after the user closes a subagent, main's status and the message that starts a new one under its name say so, once` fails on main and passes here.
- E2E: `after the user closes an idle subagent, main's next message to its name says the new one starts with no history` fails on main and passes here.
- `zig build test` and `tests/e2e/tui-host-switch.test.ts` (39/39) pass.

title: Name the files a stopped subagent changed in its report
body:
## Summary

- When a subagent's work ends early (the user stops it, it fails, or fx quits), its report gives main the text it had written, but not the files it already changed. Main can then redo the work or miss a half-made edit.
- The report now ends with `Files it changed before it ended: notes.txt, src/a.zig`, from the saved turn's file record.
- Only `write_file` and `edit_file` record changes, so only their successful writes and edits are listed, each path once. A file a shell command changed (`echo >`, `rm`, `mv`) is not listed.
- A finished report is unchanged. If the list can't be read, the report goes without it and a trace line says why.

## Tests

- E2E: `a subagent the user stops tells main which files it changed before it ended` fails on main and passes here.
- Unit: `an early-ended work names each file it changed once, without reads or failed changes`. A mutant without the repeat check fails it.
- `zig build test` and `tests/e2e/tui-host-switch.test.ts` (41/41) pass.

title: Show an instance only the MCP servers its profile names
body:
## Summary

- An instance started with a profile that sets `mcp_servers` (for example `fx --profile nomcp` with `mcp_servers: []`) can call only those servers, but its toolbox menu still listed every configured server. The model was offered servers it could never use.
- The menu now keeps only the servers the profile allows. It uses the same check that limits the calls, now in one helper, `instanceMcpProfile`.
- Subagents were already right: their menu comes from their captured view, which their profile narrows.

## Tests

- E2E: `an instance's profile decides which MCP servers it can use` now also checks the first request's menu. It fails on main (the `nomcp` menu lists `fixture`) and passes here.
- `zig build test` and `tests/e2e/tui-host-instances.test.ts` (43/43) pass.

title: Switch agents in the agent list only on Enter
body:
## Summary

- Up and Down in the agent list move only the highlight. The agent on screen stays until Enter.
- Enter shows the highlighted agent. Esc and Ctrl+X close the list and leave the agent on screen as it was.
- The highlight stays on its agent while subagents start, finish, and reorder, and moves to the agent on screen when its own agent closes.
- A paste while the list is open closes the list and lands in the composer of the agent on screen.
- The list's hint row says "↑↓ move" instead of "↑↓ preview".
- A queued message no longer paints over the last line of a subagent's conversation right after switching to it.

title: Show control bytes in MCP tool errors and unknown tool names as text
body:
## Summary

- `fx mcp call` shows control bytes in an MCP server's text as visible escapes, such as `\x1b`, `\x07`, `\x0d` and `\u{009b}`. That covers the text of a tool error and the text of a failed, denied or refused reply, which includes the message of a JSON-RPC error that answers a tool call. It used to print them as they came, to the terminal and, through the shell tool, to the model. Plain text prints as before, with its lines and tabs. A CRLF line end prints as a line feed.
- The answer to a call of a tool fx does not know, `Unsupported tool: <name>`, writes the model's tool name as visible text in the encoding the toolbox messages use, such as `` and `�`. A plain name reads as before.
- That answer reads the same everywhere fx writes it: the turn loop, the tool runtime and its workspace call path, and the registry of tools kept by name.

## Left as it is

- `unknown tool: <name>` in `tool_dispatch.zig` is a different message. The dispatcher writes it only for a tool missing from the registry it was handed, and its callers look the tool up first.
- A C1 control other than U+0085 and invalid UTF-8 in a tool name stay as they are in the answer. fx refuses an empty name, a name over 256 bytes and a name with invalid UTF-8 before any tool runs.

title: Send an attached file's folder rules as a note, not in the instructions
body:
## Summary

- An ACP client that attaches a file from a folder with its own AGENTS.md no longer changes the instructions for that request. The folder's rules arrive as a note at the end of the turn's own message, so the provider's cached prefix keeps matching for the rest of the conversation.
- A later attachment from the same folder gets the short reminder line instead of a second copy of the rules, and a saved session that is loaded again does not send them again unless the file changed.
- A resource that is not a local file (a remote URI, or a file URI with a parent segment) keeps its omission record, and the record now rides in the same note instead of the instructions. A local file outside the workspace still brings no rules.
- The step that queues an image folder's rules for the TUI and `fx ask` is now the one step for attached workspace files: it takes the images a host names by path and the files a host attaches. Images in ACP still carry no workspace path and are left out.
- A turn that continues an earlier one, such as the turn after a subagent report, does not send the first turn's attachments again.
- The instructions' context input no longer has fields for attached files or omission records, so a host cannot put an attachment back into the instructions: the compiler refuses it, and a test checks it. Attachments have one path, the note.
- libfx hosts reach the same prompt path and can send `file://` resources, but the libfx cores register no project instructions, so nothing is selected there and their behavior does not change.

## Notes for review

- The change in `src/core/agent/runtime/orchestrator.zig` is `queueImageFolderRules`, renamed `queueAttachedFolderRules`, and its call in `processQueuedPromptLoop`. `QueuedPrompt.attached_files` is borrowed from the host for the turn, and `enqueuePromptLocked` asserts a queued prompt carries none.
- The existing ACP test that counted remote-resource omissions now expects 33 omission blocks and a summary of 96: the initial gather's own omission (the workspace is not below home) stays in the instructions, and the 32 retained resource records and the summary of the other 96 ride in the note.
- The `tests/tla/drivers/prompt_context` driver is not part of the evidence. It already fails on the unmodified `origin/main` binary with `instruction groups base,project,ctx,rt differ from base,skills,project,mcp,ctx,rt` and `marker inside the base group`, because the toolbox menu from #1658 replaced the separate skills and MCP sections. A separate PR repairs the driver. The model gets an `attach` event and a planted mutant (`p6-mutant-attach-in-instructions.cfg`, caught by `MidSessionKeepsHistory`), `prompt_context/check.sh` passes, and `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts` checks the same prefix rule on the built binary.
- ThreadSanitizer was not run. The only edit in a concurrent path is one assignment on a by-value copy of the job in `runReportTurns`.
- The `project_instruction_guidance` text is unchanged and still names tool calls. The block that arrives with an attachment has the same `<scoped-rules>` form.

## Review

The full review ran on 07503185c. The later commits 94a0153d6 and 2119fab21 merge main and resolve the tests/fuzz/targets.json conflict, and were checked on their own.

title: Keep failed tool calls whole in traces
body:
## Summary

`/trace` now writes JSON Lines, so this PR adds its changes as records in `src/core/app/trace_report.zig`. The schema comment at the top of that file documents each new record and field.

- `failed_tool_call` records keep the 32 newest tool calls that did not succeed, so later successful calls no longer push them out of the trace. `tool_calls` counts them in `failed_retained`, and `failed_complete` says whether they are every failure of the session.
- Each `failed_tool_call` keeps up to 8 KiB of its arguments and 8 KiB of its result. A longer value keeps its first bytes in `args` or `result`, its last bytes in `args_tail` or `result_tail`, and counts the bytes between them in `args_omitted_bytes` or `result_omitted_bytes`. All four text fields are masked.
- Each kept failure has `dir`, the folder its tool ran against, where a shell command starts when it has no `cwd`. A failed shell run whose command ran with the startup files the snapshot holds, which fx decides from the resolved command (a `run` in the user environment of the login shell that left a command result), also has `redefined`, the common commands it used that the startup files redefine.
- `tool_call` records, and the `call` of `tool_call` problems, carry `call_id`, the provider's ID, which matches `call_id` in the session's `log.jsonl`. A window `tool_call` whose failure is also kept has `failure_kept: true`.
- `tool_call` problems come from the kept failures, so they include failures that the 64-call window no longer holds.
- A new `shell` record shows the login shell, the shell fx runs, how `user` profile commands start and the command line before `-c`, the snapshot state or why its capture failed, and which common commands the startup files redefine, such as `ls` as an alias of `eza`. `alias_of` is masked.
- Cuts of tool call arguments and results no longer end inside a UTF-8 character.

A `failed_tool_call` record from a real trace:

```json
{"type":"failed_tool_call","at":"2026-11-12T19:37:39.629Z","at_ms":1794512259629,"name":"shell","outcome":"command_failed","duration_ms":707,"source":"parent","call_id":"call-d1b097a5-e657-4071-b71f-7e23ac8c225f-0","dir":"/private/tmp/fx-trace-demo/ws","redefined":[{"name":"ls","kind":"alias","alias_of":"eza"}],"args":"{\"action\":\"run\",\"command\":\"ls -d /nonexistent-fx-trace-dir\"}","args_bytes":60,"result":"{\"state\":\"completed\",\"full_output_handle\":\"fx-command-replay-d049c41b0983-e0849304bedb02b529b6aef3e63de891731e06abee35dc050ed0a6d538959369.bin\",\"exit_code\":127,\"duration_ms\":150,\"output_delta\":\"(eval):1: command not found: eza\\n\"}","result_bytes":230}
```

## Tests

- Unit tests in `trace_report.zig` read the records back: a failure that left the 64-call window keeps its own record with its head and tail, a window call points at its kept failure, problems list a failure the window no longer holds, and the `shell` record says how commands start in each snapshot state.
- `tool_call_metrics.zig` tests the failure ring and its cuts. Every trace test that records a failed call records it with `recordToolCallResult`, the path tool calls take.
- E2E tests in `tui-command-permissions.test.ts` read the trace with `tests/e2e/trace-report.ts`: the failed call is still in the trace after 70 later calls, its `call_id` is in the session log, and the `shell` record names the alias from the startup files or says why the capture failed.

## Docs

vercel-labs/fx-web#276

title: Apply provider routing and the review model to fx acp turns
body:
## Summary

- An `fx acp` turn on AI Gateway prefers the providers in `provider_order`, from `~/.fx/settings.json` or the project's `.fx.json`, as a TUI turn does.
- With `provider_strict`, an `fx acp` turn's requests go only to those providers.
- Auto mode reviews in `fx acp` use the `review_model` setting in place of the default reviewer.

title: Revoke the Codex login at OpenAI on logout
body:
## Summary

- `fx logout codex` and `/logout codex` now revoke the Codex login at OpenAI, so its refresh token stops working after the sign-out.
- When OpenAI doesn't confirm the revocation (an error answer, no connection, or no answer within 15 s), the local login is still removed and fx warns that the remote revocation could not be confirmed.
- A saved Codex login that can't be read is removed without being sent, with the same warning.
- `/logout codex` signs out at once and revokes in the background, and quitting right after waits at most 2 s for it.

When the revocation isn't confirmed, `fx logout codex` still exits 0. It writes the warning to stderr and the result to stdout:

```
fx logout: local Codex session removed, but remote revocation could not be confirmed
Signed out of Codex.
```

`/logout codex` shows `Signed out of Codex.` and then the warning notice `The local Codex session was removed, but remote revocation could not be confirmed.`

The revocation request is built by `oauth.revokeToken`, the same function that revokes an fx login, with the refresh token and OpenAI's Codex client ID.

A revocation answer that is still arriving when the 15 s limit ends no longer crashes fx: that is fixed by #1867, which this branch is rebased on.

Docs: vercel-labs/fx-web#278

title: Send MCP arguments as the types their schemas name
body:
## Summary

- A model sometimes writes a number, boolean, array, or object argument of an MCP tool as text, such as `"limit":"40"` or `"queries":"[\"...\"]"`. When the tool's schema gives that field one type other than string and the text is exactly a value of that type, fx now sends the value, so a server that checks types, such as Datadog's, takes the call instead of rejecting it with `-32602`.
- Fields whose schema accepts a string, nested values, and text that isn't exactly a value of the field's type still reach the server as the model wrote them. Numbers keep the digits the model wrote, and a call with nothing to change sends the model's arguments unchanged.
- With `FX_TRACE_LOG` and the `mcp` trace scope, fx logs each changed field with its server, tool, field name, and new type, never its value.
- This covers the MCP servers fx connects to. A libfx host that passes its own MCP client to `createMcpAdapter` still sends the model's arguments unchanged.

title: Keep a tool's notice and a Stop hook's message in the saved turn
body:
## Summary

- A tool's notice to the model, such as the one Vision sends when it cannot read an image, now stays in the saved turn. The next prompt in a session, `fx ask --resume`, and the next prompt of an ACP session start with every message the last request carried, so the provider's prompt cache keeps hitting past that point.
- A Stop hook's message to continue the turn stays in the saved turn the same way. No host registers a Stop hook today, so flow tests cover this and the binary cannot reach it yet. Two tests pinned the message as unsaved, and they now pin it as saved, because the saved turn has to match the request that carried it.
- A notice raised by a call of a step joins the turn once all of that step's tool results and its permission feedback are in, never between two results. Between two results it ended the step in the saved turn and dropped the later results and the feedback (the finding of #1881's seeded test); a flow test now fails on `main` and passes on this branch. A scoped `AGENTS.md` a call of the step reached joins before the notice, as every boundary's notes join before its steering.
- A turn that is cancelled, hits the step limit, stops after repeated tool failures, or whose process dies, after a notice keeps the notice. A step that ends on a repeated shell failure or a repeated shell validation error and takes typed steering keeps the order notes, notice, steering.
- The transcript, Ctrl+O and ACP `session/load` still show neither message, and compaction still counts them as fx's messages, not the user's words.

## How it works with #1881

#1881 puts a boundary's notes (the gate's rules, a changed runtime context) before the steering the last step ended with (`insertBoundaryNotes`, `boundaryNotesStart`). A notice and the hook's message are marked like the other prompts fx sends (`recovery_prompt`), so they are steering to it, and the notes go before them with no further code. This branch's earlier version held the notice until the next step's start and added the step's notes itself at the repeated-failure exits. With #1881 that hold is not needed, so this branch no longer has it: the notice joins when its step's results are in (the existing drain), and the next step's notes go in front of it. The simpler design stays because the flow tests, #1881's seeded round trip, the saved-turn model and its driver all pass without the hold, including a notice raised by the first of two results and the repeated-failure exits.

The saved-turn checks now describe fx with both messages saved:

- `SavedTurn.tla` has `Notices = "end"` (the notice joins once its step's results and feedback are in) in place of `"held"`, and no `held` variable.
- `saved-turn-main.cfg` (the known limit of both messages unmarked) and `saved-turn-kept.cfg` are gone; `saved-turn.cfg` is the design fx implements. The README row, the `check.sh` header and the planted-defect comments say so.
- The seeded test in `execution_memory.zig` builds the hook's message and the notice as marked steering and expects every message kept.
- The saved-turn driver has no Vision scenario, so the real binary is checked against the notice by the E2E tests below, not by the model.

`PR1092Steering.tla` also gains `notice` and `hook` message kinds, with two planted bugs. That model has no driver or trace check that ties it to the Zig code, and no notion of a position inside a step, so it does not check the order of a notice and a context note. The flow tests, the E2E cases and the saved-turn model do.

The first message that differs between the last request and the next turn's request, as an index into the last request's 11 messages. The turn is one step that raises the Vision outage notice, then `ask --resume`:

| | Notice only | Notice and a scoped `AGENTS.md` read in the same step |
|---|---|---|
| `main` before this PR (`a83fa7c1e`) | 10 | 9 |
| First push (`afbb5e2d1`) | none | 9 |
| This head | none | none |

"None" means the next request starts with the last one, message by message. The numbers come from a scratch comparison of the two requests in the same flow as the E2E cases in `tests/e2e/vision-route-fake-gateway.test.ts`, which assert that the next request extends the last.

## Review

The full reviews ran on afbb5e2d and db078b751. The later commits were checked on their own: f97f7f34f (the repeated-failure exits), the merges of main that bring in #1881, 21d5b6f9f (the notice hold removed, since #1881 places boundary notes before the steering tail) and 773f8fecc (the model and tests updated to match).

title: Open a resumed session at the end of its history
body:
## What changes

`fx --resume` on a long saved session now opens at the end of the conversation. Before, fx wrote the saved history to the terminal 64 rows per frame, about one frame every 12 ms, so the screen scrolled through every earlier message before it reached the last one.

The change has three commits:

- **Write a resumed session's history in one frame.** Removes the 64-row cap (`resume_publication_rows_per_frame`), so a resumed transcript plans its rows the way every other transcript frame does.
- **Bound a resumed session's history frames by bytes.** fx wraps a frame in one synchronized update, and the terminal engine fails on one over 1 MiB (`max_sync_bytes`), so `fx replay` rejected a tape of a long resume with `synchronized update too large`. A resume frame now writes at most 512 KiB of saved history. A shorter history opens in one frame, and a longer one continues in the next.
- **Publish a resumed history longer than 65,535 rows.** This bug is also on `main`. The first frame recorded the rows still to write as at most 65,535, the most one frame can scroll. A longer history stopped matching what the next frame expected, so fx jumped to the last screen and left the rows between out of terminal scrollback. The first frame now records every history row.

## Trade-off

A history over 512 KiB takes more than one frame, so a very long session still shows one or two intermediate jumps. Raising `max_sync_bytes` would allow one frame for any length, but that limit also bounds memory for hosted terminal sessions, so this change leaves it alone.

## Verification

Measured in tmux at 100x32 with the debug build of `./zig-out/bin/fx`, on sessions seeded through the fake gateway and resumed with `--resume last` under `FX_RECORD`. "Time to last line" includes about 1 s of process startup.

| Saved history | `main` | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 lines | 64 frames, 1.4 s to last line | 1 frame, 1.1 s |
| 20,000 lines | 626 frames, 8.5 s | 2 frames, 1.1 s |
| 35,000 lines (70,000 rows) | 40 of 35,000 lines in scrollback | 3 frames, all 35,000 lines |

In every run on this branch, each saved line was in tmux scrollback once and in order, stderr was empty, and `fx replay` of the recorded tape exited 0. The branch was also run against a real long saved session.

Tests:

- New and changed Zig tests, each of which failed before its fix: `pending resume publication bounds one frame by its history bytes`, `oversized resume publication starts without a prior committed frame`, and `core.app_render_runtime resume publication preserves the pre-scroll origin through the coordinator`, which now covers 500, 40,000, and 70,000 rows.
- 875 Zig unit tests passed, filtered to `resume`, `publication`, `recover`, `scroll`, `history`, and `transcript window`. The full `zig build test` suite was not run locally.
- `zig fmt --check src/` and `zig build` exit 0.
- `tests/e2e/tui-resume.test.ts`: `new and resumed sessions preserve native terminal scrollback while fx is active` now also checks that the first frame carrying saved history holds both its first and last line. It failed before the fix.
- `FX_SOUND=0 bun test tui-resume-brutal.test.ts`: 1 pass, 3 opt-in tests skipped.
- `FX_SOUND=0 bun test tui-resume.test.ts` on macOS arm64: 87 pass, 1 fail. The failure is `interactive resume aliases restore history and return to a live composer`, in its live Markdown table check, which runs before that test resumes anything. It fails the same way locally with a build of the base commit `204da96ec`.

Not verified: a release build, and terminals other than tmux.

title: Keep blank rows out of scrollback after a long tool-heavy turn
body:
## Summary

- After a long turn with many tool batches, terminal scrollback no longer gets a block of hundreds of blank rows.
- The final answer of such a turn appears once in scrollback, not twice.
- The Ctrl-O stress E2E also fails when scrollback holds a long run of blank rows.

## Before and after

The gap shows on Linux under CPU load and did not show in 98 loaded runs on macOS. Linux setup: Ubuntu 24.04, tmux 3.4, bun 1.3.14, 4 CPUs with 6 busy loops.

| Check | main | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 120 runs of the history phase of the stress test, longest blank run in scrollback | 99 runs with a gap of 416 to 1418 blank rows | 0 runs with a gap (longest blank run 1) |
| The committed stress E2E, author's runs | 15 of 20 failed at the blank-row check | 6 of 6 passed |
| The committed stress E2E, reviewer's runs | 15 of 20 failed, with 416 to 1394 blank rows | 20 of 20 passed |

Under heavier load this branch alone does not remove every gap. On 8 CPUs with 8 busy loops it still failed 4 of 8 runs with a 458-row gap, against 2 of 4 on main with the same test. That gap comes from a second path, a stable-source plan with a recovery rebase, which #1877 fixes. With #1877 and #1889 on top, the same loaded run passed 7 of 7. Land the three together.

Before this change the stress test failed its first CI attempt in about 5 percent of recent jobs, for example run 42760378255, because the done marker appeared twice.

## Review

The full review ran on 74e40b471. The later commit b34d06949 changes only the test bound and this text, and was checked on its own.

title: Close an agent from the list with the Delete key too
body:
## Summary

- The agent list's hint says `delete close`, but only Backspace armed and closed the highlighted subagent. The forward Delete key (`ESC [3~`), which the decoder sends as the `delete_next` action, did nothing.
- The list now takes `delete_next` as its close key: the first press arms, the second closes, and any other key disarms, as with Backspace.

## Tests

- E2E: `Delete, then Delete again, in the agent list closes a working subagent for good…` now presses the forward Delete key for its last arm and close (Backspace still for the first). It fails on main (the press arms nothing) and passes here.
- `zig build test` and `tests/e2e/tui-host-switch.test.ts` (45/45) pass.

title: Test four MCP login and logout edge cases
body:
## Summary

- Adds e2e tests for a held server's logout, which sends no revocation, and for a revocation endpoint that refuses the connection.
- Adds macOS e2e tests for a login read again after a slow first Keychain read that the server refuses, or that the server asks more scopes of.
- Lets the test auth server ask for more scopes on a valid token, as a step-up does.
- Says the unreadable-store and revocation-answer facts once in the MCP host and engine doc comments.

title: Retry a refused fresh login instead of asking to sign in again
body:
## Summary

A user's turn stopped for half an hour on "Sign-in expired" while their login was fine. AI Gateway answered 401 twice for a login fx had just refreshed. fx then opened a Vercel sign-in code and waited. The code expired unused, and the same login worked on the next send. A refresh that works shows the login is good, so signing in again can't fix that 401. The gateway-side cause is tracked in #1858.

- A 401 for an fx login on AI Gateway that fx has just refreshed now retries with the same login on the usual backoff, with the status `Gateway refused the login · next try in 4s · attempt 3`. It retries until the gateway takes the login or the user presses Esc, because the refusal comes and goes on the gateway's side and the request is still the user's. Each resend that gets a 401 refreshes the login again, so a login whose refresh stops working moves to the sign-in wait. Codex and Grok subscriptions keep asking for a sign-in as before.
- The gateway's reason for the 401 shows once in the transcript, with the credential fx sent masked, so the user and we can see why it was refused.
- While a request waits for a sign-in, fx resends it with the saved login every 3 minutes, and the status counts the wait: `Sign-in expired · waiting 4m 10s · next try in 1m 50s`. Before, a wait with nobody at the keyboard never ended, even after the gateway stopped refusing or another fx process signed in. Every 3 minutes keeps it to 20 requests an hour.
- When the sign-in code fx opened for a waiting request expires, fx tries the saved login once without opening a second sign-in, because that login is often still good, as it was here. The notice says Enter retries with the current login and `/login` signs in again.
- One of those resends that fails on the way, for example on a dropped connection or a 5xx, keeps the sign-in wait and its time instead of opening a second sign-in. If the user signs in while it's on the wire, fx resends with the new login: at once when the resend fails with a sign-in error, and after the usual short wait when it fails on the way.
- `/trace` network lines for failed calls carry `error="..."` with the provider's message, the call's own credential masked for every provider, because trace output gets pasted into chats.
- The Codex and Grok transports mask the token they sent in a provider's error body, as the AI Gateway path does. The host-run providers never hold the key inside fx, so there's nothing for fx to mask there.
- Picking the Vercel team the login already uses prints `Using Vercel team <name> (<slug>).` instead of `Changed Vercel team to ...`, which read as if something had changed.
- `fx ask` and ACP still end the turn on a refused login, since nobody can stop a retry there.

The same-team notice and the `/trace` field are small and came out of the same report, so they stay in this PR instead of two more.

Docs: vercel-labs/fx-web#277

title: Draw a subagent's own subagents under it in the agent list
body:
## Summary

- The agent list put every subagent of an instance on one branch, sorted by work and reply. A subagent's own subagent (lead's helper) looked like lead's sibling, and a working helper sorted above lead.
- After the usual sort, each subagent's own subagents now come right under it, in that sorted order (`nestSubagents`), and draw on a branch of their own:

```
  main         Fix the login bug   working         main
  ├ lead       Plan the fix        idle            main
  │ └ helper   Check one fix       working         main
  └ tester     Run the auth tests  idle            tester
```

- The switch order follows the list, so ↑ and ↓ go through the tree as drawn.

## Tests

- Unit: the order (`a subagent's own subagents come right under it, in their sorted order`, and a 10,000-host random check that nesting keeps every agent, keeps instances in place, and puts each subagent's own right under it) and the drawing (`a subagent's own subagents hang off its branch…`).
- E2E: `an idle agent waits only on its own subagents…` now opens the list and expects `└ helper` under `└ lead`. It fails on main (the list shows `├ helper` above lead) and passes here.
- `zig build test`, `tests/e2e/tui-host-switch.test.ts` (45/45) and `tests/e2e/tui-host-instances.test.ts` (46/46) pass.

title: Keep "needs approval" on a subagent's row while main shows its prompt
body:
## Summary

- While main's screen shows a subagent's approval or question for it (the prompt is lent to main), the agent list said main `needs approval` but called the subagent `working`. Lending swaps the prompt off the subagent's own agent, so its row only saw a running turn.
- `stateOf(app, target)` now answers what an agent waits for or does: the subagent whose prompt is lent waits on it (`needs approval` or `has a question`), otherwise as before. Every row, the busiest state, and the busy-elsewhere check read it, in place of six copies of `instanceState(…, requestWaitsForUser(…))`.
- A subagent waiting on a lent prompt no longer counts as working, so the list sorts it with the others that wait.
- The footer's `N subagents working` counts through the same state, so a subagent that waits for the user shows in the waiting note, or on screen, and not as working.

## Tests

- E2E: `a subagent's approval can be answered on its own screen, and main's clears` now also expects the writer's row to say `needs approval` while main shows its prompt. It fails on main and passes here.
- `zig build test`, `tests/e2e/tui-host-switch.test.ts` (45/45) and `tests/e2e/tui-host-instances.test.ts` (47/47) pass.

title: Keep fx mcp call working for commands left running in the background
body:
## Summary

- A command that keeps running after its shell run call returns, such as a loop that polls a long MCP job, can keep using `fx mcp call` until it ends. Before, every call after the run call's yield exited 3 with "no running fx shell call to reach".
- While the agent is not watching the command, its calls wait. They run once the agent watches it again with shell interact, under that call's permission check, prompt, and automatic review.
- An interact keeps waiting while one of the command's calls runs, so its result shows the command after the call.
- When the command ends or is stopped, its token is revoked: a call still waiting is refused, and a process it left behind exits 3.
- The exit 3 message, `fx mcp call --help`, and the agent's toolbox hint say a background command's calls wait until the agent watches it.

Docs: vercel-labs/fx-web#279

title: Count a resumed session's subagents before the agent list opens
body:
## Summary

- After `fx --resume`, `/resume` or `/fork`, the subagents the session had started came into the switch list only when the agent list first opened (`syncChildList` ran from `openMenu`). Until then the footer had no `main ↓` and counted no subagent.
- The resume's warm-up step now lists them (`listRestoredSubagents`, called from the session runtime as its other agents-runtime calls are), the same way opening the list does. `openMenu` and `hasAnotherAgent` use the same function.
- Not in this change: a restored subagent's row still shows no effort until it is shown or runs, since the saved effort isn't in the session's peeked state.

## Tests

- E2E: `after a resume, the agent list shows a restored subagent's own title…` now expects `main ↓` in the footer right after the resume, before the list opens. It fails on main and passes here.
- `zig build test`, `tests/e2e/tui-host-switch.test.ts` (45/45) and `tests/e2e/tui-host-instances.test.ts` (47/47) pass.

title: Name the subagents in subagent tool rows
body:
## Summary

- A subagent call's row names its subagent as soon as main has written the name, such as `Managing reviewer`, instead of `Managing`.
- A wait row names the subagents that were working when it began, such as `waiting for reviewer, builder` and then `waited for reviewer, builder`, instead of `subagents`.
- A status row that names no agent lists the open subagents, such as `checked reviewer, builder`.
- Wait and status rows keep these names after a resume.
- A subagent call written without `request` shows its subagent instead of its action, so it no longer reads `Managing message`.
- Wait results, and status results that name no agent, give the model the names in a `subagents` list.

title: Show why an MCP server rejected a call's arguments
body:
## Summary

- When an MCP server refuses a call's parameters with JSON-RPC `-32602`, the TUI row now names the fields it rejected and the types it wanted, such as `Failed mcp_datadog_get_datadog_metric: arguments rejected: limit is a string, the schema wants a number`, instead of the first characters of the protocol error.
- fx reads the fields and types from the Go MCP SDK's validator messages and from the TypeScript SDK's zod issues. Any other `-32602` reads `the server rejected the call's parameters (-32602)`, and other failures keep their current text.
- The fx trace adds the same text as `cause="..."` to each failed tool call in its Problems and Tool Calls sections.
- The model still gets the server's full error, including the tool's schema.

title: Keep the toolbox menu across compaction
body:
## Summary

- The first request after an automatic or overflow compaction sends the toolbox menu, not a block of NUL bytes.
- A conversation sends the same toolbox menu before and after a compaction.
- When a skill or MCP server changed before a compaction, the first request after it tells the model again what the toolbox holds now.
- /clear, /new and opening a saved session still start with a menu of what the toolbox holds now.

title: Use the stored sign-in for session titles and the model list
body:
## Summary

- Session titles send the stored sign-in token, so a title no longer fails after another fx process refreshes the shared login.
- A title the gateway rejects with 401 is sent once more when another fx process has already stored a newer token, and keeps the derived title otherwise.
- The model list loads with the stored token and, after a 401, tries once more with a newer stored token before it falls back to the public models.
- A title or model list request never refreshes the shared login and never uses a stored login for another account or team.
- Interrupting the first turn no longer starts a second title request, so the title comes from the first prompt.
- fx ask, ACP sessions, and Codex and Grok subscriptions read the stored sign-in for titles the same way.

title: Add a safe_git store route for workspace captures
body:
**Summary** --- - Adds a second `safe_git` route for fx's own workspace capture store. Typed `StoreCommand`s read the user's worktree with every program its repository config can name turned off, and write only into a separate bare store with alternates into the user's objects. - `repo_path.isValid` in `src/core/shared/repo_path.zig` checks each repository-relative path before git sees it: no empty, `.`, `..` or `.git` component in any case, no leading or trailing slash, and no NUL. `update-index` still exits 0 when it refuses a path, such as an HFS or NTFS spelling of `.git`, and prints `Ignoring path`. The store route then fails the command as `path_rejected` and traces git's stderr, so a capture missing a path never looks complete. - The store route admits git 2.29 or newer, which it needs for `init --object-format` and `rev-parse --show-object-format`. It bounds every run by a shared deadline and runs git in its own process group, so a timeout reaches any filter git started. Filters named by bare command, such as Homebrew's `git-lfs`, resolve on a fixed PATH. - `repositoryFacts` returns a `FactsResult`: the facts, or a `FactsFailure` that names why git could not read the repository (`spawn_failed`, `timeout`, `cancelled`, `paths_unreadable`, `unexpected_output`, `head_unreadable`, `config_unreadable`). It reports a repository as unborn only when HEAD is a symbolic ref to a branch that does not exist yet. A HEAD that names a broken ref or a non-commit, detached or not, is `head_unreadable`. A git run that times out or is cancelled during the unborn check is reported as `timeout` or `cancelled`, not as an unreadable HEAD. - Config booleans such as `index.sparse`, `core.splitIndex` and `core.ignoreCase` are read with the indexer's `parseConfigBool`, git's own rule: a key with no value is true, and any non-zero integer is true. `git_config.parseBool` becomes public and `indexer.zig`, the indexer's front door, exports it, so the rule is defined once. - `listRepository` takes an optional `skip_folder`, passed to git as a `:(top,literal,exclude)` pathspec, so git neither enters nor lists that folder. #1844 uses it to keep fx's profile folder out of a capture. - Every store command here is one a capture runs. The commands only retention and the fork ref copy need land in #1845 with their tests. - `safe_git` owns the `ls-files` parser and OID validation, with a new fuzz target, `safe_git_output`. - `GitAdmission.tla` models the capture caller. It plants one bug, a store route that reads the repository, which both `CaptureNeverFires` and `CaptureLeavesUserIndex` must catch. - fx's own capture git never fetches: the capture reads (`repositoryFacts`, `listRepository`) and every store command set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` and pass `-c protocol.allow=never`, so a repository whose own config names a promisor remote (`extensions.partialClone`, `remote..promisor`, `remote..uploadpack`) cannot make a read such as `rev-parse HEAD^{commit}` start a fetch that runs its transport programs. `protocol.allow=never` also covers git older than 2.45, which ignores the variable. The agent's own `git status`, `git diff` and `git log` keep main's behavior, so history diffs in a partial clone still fetch what they need. - Both routes turn off hooks that config defines with `hook..command` (git 2.54), which `core.hooksPath=/dev/null` does not reach, by passing `-c hook..enabled=false` for each name. The read route lists them in `prepare` with `git config -z --name-only --list` in the repository, so its own config, global and system config and their includes all count. Every store command lists them in the store's own context first, so a global `includeIf "gitdir:"` that applies only to the store is seen too. A name with `=` cannot be turned off, so `prepare` and `prepareStore` refuse (`unsupported_hook_name`) and a store command fails (`hooks_refused`); a listing that fails refuses as `hook_config_unavailable`. - `prepareWithin` builds on main's `prepareWith`: its checks run through a `CheckRunner` bounded by the caller's `Limits`, and a check the deadline or the cancel flag ends refuses with `timed_out` or `cancelled`. The version cache keeps git's own output, so the read route (2.25) and the store route (2.29) share one probe. **Design** --- A workspace capture records the user's uncommitted work as a git tree, commit, and ref. Neither existing way to run git can do that safely: - **The user's own `.git`.** Building a tree there means `git add` and `write-tree` against the user's index. That writes the index and takes its `index.lock`, so a capture can race the user's own git and change what they stage next. It also writes objects and refs into a repository fx does not own, and plain git runs whatever the repository's config names: hooks, fsmonitor, filter drivers. - **The agent's read-only route** (`git status`, `git diff`, `git log`). It already turns those programs off, but it cannot write a tree, a commit, or a ref. Giving it that ability would widen the route every agent command goes through. Captures therefore get their own route: - **A separate handle type.** `StoreReady` is a different type from the agent's `Ready`, so a store handle cannot reach a route that must blank the repository's filters. - **Explicit paths.** Every store run sets `GIT_DIR` to the fx-owned bare store, `GIT_INDEX_FILE` to a capture index inside fx's folder, and `GIT_WORK_TREE` to the user's worktree. It turns off fsmonitor and hooks and uses a fixed identity. git never reads the user's repository config or index on this route. - **Alternates.** The store borrows the user's objects through alternates, so unchanged files cost nothing. - **A closed set of commands.** Commands are a union with typed arguments, not argv, so a caller cannot pass an option. Paths and refs are checked before git starts. The capture still reads facts and listings from the user's repository, such as HEAD, the object format, and `ls-files`, through the existing read-only route. Before: one route, read-only. ```mermaid flowchart LR agent["Agent: git status, diff, log"] --> ro["safe_git read-only route
repository programs off"] ro -->|reads| repo[("User repository
.git, index, worktree")] ``` After: the agent route is unchanged, and captures add a store route that writes only into fx's store. ```mermaid flowchart LR agent["Agent: git status, diff, log"] --> ro["safe_git read-only route
repository programs off"] capture["Workspace capture"] -->|"HEAD, format, ls-files"| ro ro -->|reads| repo[("User repository
.git, index, worktree")] capture --> store["safe_git store route
typed StoreCommand"] store -->|"reads worktree files only"| repo store -->|"writes objects, capture index, refs"| fxstore[("fx store: ~/.fx/captures/.../store.git
bare, no hooks")] fxstore -.->|"alternates, read only"| objects[("User .git/objects")] ``` First of a stack that adds per-turn workspace capture behind `experimental.workspace_capture`. Nothing calls this route yet.

title: Add the workspace capture selection policy and store
body:
**Summary** --- - `workspace_capture.zig` decides which files a capture holds: tracked files as they are on disk, and untracked files git does not ignore. It leaves out untracked paths that are sensitive, larger than 2 MiB, past the first 1,000, missing, or a nested repository, and records each with its reason. - `capture_store.capture` records a folder's repository in an fx-owned bare store at `~/.fx/captures//store.git`. Captures are chained per session and worktree under `refs/fx/sessions//`, and each ref moves only by compare-and-swap. The capture never writes content into the user's `.git`, and the tree matches the one the user's own git would record. - Before its ref moves, a capture copies into the store every object its tree reaches that it borrowed through `objects/info/alternates` (`list_objects`, then `pack_objects`, both new store commands). Pruning the user's repository therefore never breaks a capture. Git still freshens the modification time of a borrowed object in the user's objects folder; it never writes content there. If the copy cannot finish, the ref stays put and the capture reports no tree: `timeout` at the deadline, `io_error` otherwise. A capture with a parent leaves out what the parent's tree holds; the first capture of a session leaves out the trees of the store's 16 newest capture refs, which `list_refs` lists. The copy writes packs of at most 20,000 objects and skips objects the store already holds, loose or in its own packs, so a copy cut off by the deadline keeps its progress. A repository keeps the first-capture budget (10 s) until one capture lands. Only a missing file counts as missing: a check that fails or is cancelled fails the capture and never sets the store aside. - fx's own profile folder (`~/.fx` or `$FX_HOME`) is never listed, even when the captured work tree holds it. The untracked listing hands it to git as an exclude pathspec (#1843), and tracked files under it are dropped from the tracked listing. Untracked files there record nothing, so the capture stays `complete` and comparable. If the user's git tracks files there, the folder is recorded once as a `sensitive` exclusion, however many files it holds. A work tree that is the profile folder itself is `unavailable` with `private_root`. - `foreign_git_dir` refuses a folder that git would hand to another checkout: a `.git` symlink, a `gitdir:` file into another checkout's `.git` folder, or one into a linked worktree's git directory that records a different `.git` file. A `gitdir:` file into a separate git directory, such as one `git init --separate-git-dir` makes, is captured as git sees it, on its own chain: its worktree key is the git directory plus the work tree, so two folders that point at it never share a capture index or a ref. - fx reads only regular files of bounded size from the user's git directory. A user index that is not a regular file of at most 1 GiB, such as a FIFO, is rebuilt from HEAD instead of copied, and a linked worktree's `gitdir` record that is not a regular file is not opened. - Every refusal is an outcome with a reason, not an error. Each reason pairs with one status: `budget`, `untracked_timeout`, `foreign_git_dir`, `capture_locked`, `index_sparse`, `not_git`, `git_refused`, `timeout`, and `cancelled` are `unavailable` only. `unavailable` covers `private_root` too, which this PR produces for a work tree that is the profile folder, or whose root is `/`, `HOME`, the host's home folder, or a folder above one of them. - `encodeRecord` turns an outcome into the session item, with exclusions counted by reason and a bounded sample of at most 32 paths. It rejects an outcome whose status, reason, and object IDs disagree. - Tests run real repositories with the user's git as the oracle. - Sensitive names also cover `.ssh/`, `.gnupg/`, `.aws/` and `.config/gcloud/` folders, `.kube/config`, `*.tfvars`, `.htpasswd`, `credentials.json`, `service-account*.json`, `secrets.{yaml,yml,json,toml,env}` and dot-file shell histories. - An untracked regular file whose first 4096 bytes hold `PRIVATE KEY-----` is left out as `sensitive`, whatever its name. - A file with a sensitive name that the index holds but HEAD's tree does not, such as a staged new `.env`, is left out and removed from the capture index. `ls-tree --literal-pathspecs` checks these names in batches that keep each command line under 64 KiB. Committed files are still captured; when git cannot answer, every such file is left out and a trace line says so. - `capture()` itself refuses a worktree root that is the filesystem root, `HOME`, the host's home (`Request.home`), or a folder above either (`private_root`). - The cancel flag reaches the native untracked scan, so a cancel during the listing reports `cancelled`, not `untracked_timeout`. **Design** --- **What a capture selects.** A capture holds what `git add -A` would stage: tracked files as they are on disk, plus untracked files git does not ignore. Ignored files are left out because they are usually build output, caches, or local secrets that the repository has already marked as not belonging. This keeps the tree comparable with the user's own commits (`comparable` in the record). Tracked files are captured as they are, since they are already in the user's history. An untracked file is new to fx, so it gets the stricter checks. An untracked or newly staged `.env` never reaches fx's store; a committed one is captured, as git already holds it. Sensitive names are matched without case, because a case-insensitive disk opens `.ENV` as `.env`: - **Exact names:** `.env`, `.envrc`, `.netrc`, `.npmrc`, `.pgpass`, `.pypirc`, `.git-credentials`, `credentials`, `auth.json`, `hosts.yml`. - **Prefixes:** `.env.`, `id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `id_ecdsa`, `id_dsa`. - **Suffixes:** `.pem`, `.key`, `.p12`, `.keystore`, `.jks`. - **Docker:** `.docker/config.json`. fx's profile folder is skipped whatever its contents, because it holds sessions, credentials, and the capture store itself. It is skipped in the listing itself, not filtered afterwards: otherwise every capture of a work tree holding the profile would list the objects earlier captures wrote, and the listing would grow with each capture. The indexer skips folders only outside a repository, so when the work tree holds the profile, git lists the untracked files instead of the native indexer. When anything of the user's is left out, the capture is `partial`, and the record names the most serious reason. A capture never looks complete when it is not. **Why an fx-owned store.** Writing into the user's repository would touch their index, objects, and refs (see #1843). Instead, each repository gets a bare store keyed by its common git directory, so linked worktrees of one repository share a store. The store has alternates into the user's objects, so unchanged files are never copied. Each worktree gets its own capture index, `flock` lock, scratch folder, and ref. The first capture of a worktree copies the user's index and keeps its timestamp. git then trusts the stat data it already has and re-hashes only files that changed. git's racy-entry check still catches files changed in the same second as the index. A split index keeps entries in a shared file the copy would miss, so the capture rebuilds it from HEAD instead. Later captures reuse the persisted capture index. **Which checkout a folder belongs to.** git follows a `.git` symlink or a `gitdir:` file and reports that checkout's HEAD. If fx trusted that, a capture would chain onto another checkout's ref with the wrong files. fx checks that the git directory's own record of its work tree, where it keeps one, names this folder's `.git`. A separate git directory keeps no such record, so git's view stands, and the work tree joins the worktree key to keep the two folders apart. **Time bounds.** The caller passes one deadline (#1847 uses 2 s). Every git run, every lock wait, and the untracked listing stop at it. - **Linux.** The store's private folder is opened with `iterate`, since a plain directory open on Linux is `O_PATH` and cannot change permissions. - **Untracked listing.** The native indexer takes the deadline as a stop time its workers check themselves, while walking and while assembling the tree, so it stops on time however busy the machine is; this PR adds that option to `src/core/indexer/scan.zig`. Sorting a very large listing cannot be interrupted, so a capture can overrun by that sort. The git fallback stops at the deadline itself. A listing cut short ends the capture as `unavailable` with `untracked_timeout`, and nothing is written. - **First capture.** The capture that creates a repository's store or a worktree's capture index also writes every object the new store lacks, which in a large repository takes longer than a turn's budget. From its setup on, that whole capture runs on a one-time budget, `first_capture_budget_ms`: 10 s after setup begins, or the caller's deadline if that is later. Steps before setup keep the caller's deadline, so a first capture can take up to about 12 s, once per worktree. - **Stale locks.** A git that died, for example when fx was killed, can leave the capture index's `index.lock` or this session's `.lock` behind. Only a capture holding the worktree lock runs git on them, apart from one short ref command at most, and fx's git stops at its deadline. A lock older than 2 minutes is therefore removed; a newer one reports `capture_locked`. The worktree lock is a `flock`, which the kernel releases if fx dies. ```mermaid flowchart TD resolve["resolve repository
read-only route"] lock["lock worktree (flock)"] resolve -->|"no repository"| notgit["unavailable: not_git"] resolve -->|"git missing or older than 2.29"| refused["unavailable: git_refused"] resolve -->|".git hands the folder to another checkout"| foreign["unavailable: foreign_git_dir"] resolve -->|"sparse index"| sparse["unavailable: index_sparse"] resolve --> profile["find profile folder in the work tree"] resolve -->|"root is /, a home folder, or above one"| private["unavailable: private_root"] profile -->|"work tree is the profile folder"| private profile --> lock lock -->|"still held at deadline"| locked["unavailable: capture_locked"] lock --> stale["clear stale index.lock and ref lock"] stale -->|"lock younger than 2 min"| locked stale --> setup["set up store and capture index
first capture: 10 s budget from here"] setup --> select["select: tracked files plus untracked not ignored
profile folder never listed, apply policy"] select -->|"listing cut off at deadline"| untracked["unavailable: untracked_timeout"] select -->|"past deadline"| timeout["unavailable: timeout"] select --> apply["apply selection to capture index"] apply --> commit["write-tree, commit-tree
update-ref with compare-and-swap"] commit -->|"nothing left out"| complete["complete"] commit -->|"paths left out"| partial["partial: most serious reason"] ``` A git failure at any step after `resolve` ends the capture as `failed` or `unavailable`, depending on the failure. Stacked on #1843.

title: Keep workspace captures within a 5 GiB budget
body:
**Summary** --- - Before a capture writes, `capture_retention.check` measures the space `~/.fx/captures` takes against one budget per profile: 5 GiB. It never maintains. `capture_retention.admit` measures and then runs maintenance; #1847 runs it only as a background task. - The space is cached per store in `captures/usage`, in a new `v2` format. An admit measures a store again only when its object folders changed, it is new, or its measure is 10 minutes old. A fingerprint of the object folders' modification times detects the change. The capture indexes, refs and scratch files are outside that fingerprint, so their part of a store's size can be up to 10 minutes stale; they are small next to the objects. `usage` is read only as a regular file of at most 1 MiB, never through a symlink. A negative time, a time more than a day ahead of the clock, any other content, and the earlier one-line format all count as no cache. - Over the budget, one maintenance per profile runs (`captures/maintenance.lock`), at most once per 10 minutes. The interval is checked again under the lock, and no write of `usage` brings back an older maintenance time. - Maintenance runs in three steps, each re-measuring only the stores it touched: - **Finish prunes.** It prunes stores a stopped maintenance left marked `prune.pending`, within half the time left. A store still locked keeps its marker, and maintenance goes on. - **Pack.** While still over 4 GiB, it packs every store with at least 1,024 loose objects, within half the time then left, using the new `repack` store command (`git repack -a -d -k`, without `-l`, so it keeps every object, the copies captures took from the user's repository included, and prunes nothing). - **Evict.** While still over 4 GiB, it evicts whole inactive sessions: sessions no longer in the catalog first, then the longest unused. The current session and sessions another process has open stay. - Before a session's refs are deleted, each store they are in is marked `prune.pending` unless it already is. Only those stores are pruned afterwards, which removes the marker. A store that kept every ref deletes the marker only if this eviction created it; a marker a stopped maintenance left stays until that store's prune finishes. - Each eviction is journaled in `captures/evictions.jsonl` as two synced lines. An `intent` line lists the refs found before any ref is deleted. A `done` line lists the refs deleted and those `kept` because a capture moved them meanwhile. - Eviction stops when a marker or journal line cannot be written, a store it deleted refs from cannot be pruned, or the space cannot be measured, including the measure right after finishing prunes or packing. - `Admission.refusal` says why a capture was refused: `over_budget`, `measure_failed`, `busy`, `git_refused`, or `maintenance_failed`. - The store commands retention needs land here with tests: `delete_ref` deletes a capture ref only while it still names the expected commit, `gc` runs `repack -a -d` without `-l` and then `prune --expire=now` (not `git gc`, whose repack always passes `-l` and would drop the objects captures copied). Maintenance uses `gc_locked`, whose prune expires only objects older than the second it took the store's locks, so a prune left running after fx dies cannot delete a new capture's objects. And `repack` packs loose objects without pruning anything. - New fuzz target `capture_retention_parse` covers the ref listing and `usage` parsers. - A store whose prune keeps failing loses no more sessions: eviction skips every candidate with a ref in a store that still carries `prune.pending`. - A session another process has open is never evicted, even when this process's catalog does not list it. - A store with at least 1,024 loose objects is packed off the turn even under the budget: `check` reports it as `due` and `admit` packs it, so `check` stays quick as captures add objects. - The cancel flag also ends maintenance's lock waits, and a maintenance it stops counts as cancelled. - A store whose worktrees folder cannot be listed in full is neither packed nor pruned, since a capture in an unlisted worktree could be running. - The journal's done line records `kept` (refs a capture moved) apart from `failed` (deletes that could not finish, such as at a deadline). - A capture of an existing store waits at most 250 ms while maintenance holds the store, on `init.lock` and on its worktree lock alike, and then reports `capture_locked`. A worktree lock that another capture holds, such as a parallel subagent's, is still waited for until the capture's deadline. - `evictions.jsonl` and `prune.pending` are never opened through a symlink, and the journal rotates to `evictions.jsonl.1` past 1 MiB. - Stale `usage.tmp-*` files are removed under the maintenance lock; dropped capture indexes and stores whose refs cannot be listed are traced. **Design** --- **One budget per profile.** All sessions in a profile share one store per repository, so a per-session limit cannot predict the space on disk. The space is measured where it is used, across `~/.fx/captures`. **Whole sessions, not single captures.** A session's captures in a worktree form a commit chain under one ref. Dropping a capture from the middle would mean rewriting the chain, and the session log would then name commits that no longer exist. The unit of eviction is therefore a whole session, and its refs go in every store. **Space, not age.** An old session is still one the user can resume or convert, so its captures stay while the session exists and the space allows. Age only orders the candidates, after sessions that no longer exist in the catalog. **Cheap to check on every capture.** Walking every store before each capture would cost more as the folder grows. The `v2` usage file keeps one line per store, with its size and a fingerprint of its object folders. A new loose object changes its fan-out folder's time, and a new pack changes the pack folder's time. A fingerprint taken within 2 s of a folder's time is written as zero and never matches, because a later write in the same clock tick would leave the time unchanged. 2 s covers the coarsest file clock in use, FAT's. A full maintenance runs at most once per 10 minutes, so a profile that stays over the budget refuses captures without retrying eviction on every turn, and eviction stops at 4 GiB rather than 5 GiB so the next maintenance is not due at once. Two processes can both read an old `usage` before one takes the lock, so the interval is checked again under it. **Pack before evicting.** Captures run git with `gc.auto=0`, so nothing else packs a store that loses no refs, and loose objects take many times the space of a pack. Packing frees space without losing a capture, so it comes before any eviction. `repack -a -d -k` writes every object the store holds, loose or packed, reachable or not, into one new pack and deletes the loose objects and packs it replaced. Without `-l` it keeps the copies captures took of the user's objects, and it prunes nothing, so an object a capture has written but not yet named stays. A pack that fails or finds a store locked leaves the store as measured, and eviction goes on from that measure. **Prune only what changed.** Packing and pruning every store before evicting could spend the whole deadline before anything is evicted. Each step therefore gets a share of the time, and eviction prunes only the stores a session's refs left. The `prune.pending` marker is written before the journal's `intent` line, so a crash after it leaves at most a prune the next maintenance does first. A store that ends up keeping every ref has nothing of this session to prune, so the marker goes again only when this eviction wrote it. A marker an earlier, stopped maintenance left still records an unfinished prune, so it stays. **A record before every deletion.** An eviction is never silent. The `intent` line is synced before any ref goes, and refs are deleted with compare-and-swap, so a capture that just moved a ref keeps it. An `intent` with no matching `done` line is an eviction that a crash stopped. If the marker or journal cannot be written, maintenance stops before deleting anything else. **Immediate prune under all locks.** Deleting refs frees nothing until git prunes. A grace period does not work here: git loosens objects from the pack the first prune wrote with that pack's time, so an evicted session's objects would stay for an hour and the space would not drop. Maintenance therefore prunes at once, with `gc_locked`: its prune expires every unreachable object older than the second maintenance took the store's locks (`--expire=@`), so a prune left running after fx dies cannot delete a newer capture's objects. Packing and pruning both hold the store's `init.lock`, which a capture passes before writing any object, and then each worktree's lock. No capture of that store is running, so no capture has objects it has not named yet. A store still locked at the deadline is left unpacked or unpruned this time, and stays marked when it awaits a prune. Maintenance also deletes each worktree's capture index before pruning, because git trusts the index for unchanged files and a pruned blob could otherwise end up in a later tree. The next capture starts the index again from the user's. **Stop instead of over-evicting.** After each eviction, maintenance prunes and re-measures only the stores the refs left. If that prune or measure fails, eviction stops. Without a fresh measure the space would not be seen to drop, and continuing would remove sessions the budget does not need gone. The caller bounds measuring and maintenance with a deadline. #1847 gives the quick check the capture's own 2 s and maintenance 30 s in the background. ```mermaid flowchart TD admit["admit"] --> refresh["refresh usage
measure only stores that changed"] refresh -->|"cannot measure"| measurefail["refuse: measure_failed"] refresh --> under{"total under 5 GiB?"} under -->|yes| ok["admit capture"] under -->|no| recent{"maintained in the last 10 min?"} recent -->|yes| over["refuse: over_budget"] recent -->|no| lockfree{"maintenance.lock free?"} lockfree -->|no| busy["refuse: busy"] lockfree -->|yes| recheck{"maintained meanwhile?
checked under the lock"} recheck -->|yes| final{"total under 5 GiB?"} recheck -->|no| finish["prune stores still marked prune.pending
within half the time left"] finish --> packq{"total over 4 GiB?"} packq -->|no| final packq -->|yes| pack["repack stores with 1,024 or more loose objects
within half the time then left"] pack --> target{"total over 4 GiB?"} target -->|no| final target -->|yes| pick["next session: orphans first, then least recent
skip current and open sessions"] pick --> mark["mark its stores prune.pending
unless already marked"] mark --> intent["journal intent, synced"] intent --> del["delete refs with compare-and-swap"] del --> done["journal done, synced"] done --> prune["prune stores that lost refs, under all locks
measure them again"] prune --> target finish -->|"measure failed"| final pack -->|"measure failed"| final mark -->|"marker failed"| final intent -->|"journal failed"| final done -->|"journal failed"| final prune -->|"prune or measure failed"| final final -->|yes| ok final -->|no| stopped["refuse: over_budget, or measure_failed
or maintenance_failed when eviction stopped"] ``` Stacked on #1844.

title: Store workspace captures as session items
body:
**Summary**
---
- A turn's workspace captures become `workspace_capture` items in its session log (D98). They are written outside the streamed pieces, so they never supersede the turn or reach the model's messages.
- `Session.beginCaptureTurn` returns a token for the turn. `saveWorkspaceCapture(token, payload, .start or .end)` and `commitTurnWithCaptures(turn, language, token)` take it. Each held capture carries its token, and a commit writes only its own token's captures. A save with a token the session no longer holds fails with `WorkspaceCaptureTurnClosed` and keeps nothing.
- `beginCaptureTurnKeeping(ended)` begins the next turn while keeping a turn that ended before its commit landed. Its captures stay held beside the next turn's until its own late commit. At most one ended turn waits: keeping another drops the earlier one's captures as superseded. `beginCaptureTurn` is `beginCaptureTurnKeeping(null)` and drops every earlier token's captures. When the ended turn is kept and its prepared turn is already open with no token, that open turn takes the ended token, not the new one, since it is the late commit's own turn.
