title: Flag the history rows a recovered frame never wrote
body:
## Summary

- A recovering receipt can commit stable without having written rows it owed, and the anchor it leaves has history behind the viewport and no catch-up flag. The store reconciles a source rewrite into a recovering receipt before the next frame is sealed, and that zeroes the rows the receipt owed. A frame whose source no longer extends the receipt's flow also drops them in its plan. When only compatible growth frames follow and the finality floor sits at the target, a frame releases just the rows leaving the screen top, so the rows between history and the viewport are never replayed and those lines stay missing from native scrollback. This is the follow-up to #1877, which holds rows a frame cannot replay; this change does not depend on #1877 or #1831.
- The receipt now keeps the rows a rewrite dropped in `dropped_semantic_rows`, and a recovering frame that is itself a partial write carries them to the next receipt. The recovering branch of `resolveTransitionTarget` sets `history_catchup_pending` on the stable anchor when the rows still owed plus the dropped rows exceed the rows the frame accepts, history stays below the viewport, and the geometry is unchanged. It logs `transcript_history_debt_flagged`, and the next frame replays the rows from history. The rule sits next to the other catch-up decisions, where the receipt, the accepted rows and the target are already in hand.
- The count is in rows at the receipt's width, so a resize frame does not carry it. A recovering commit keeps the count only when the frame has the receipt's width and no resize history delta is pending; otherwise it drops the count and logs `transcript_history_debt_dropped`. Without that, a resize to a width where rows wrap kept the old-width count, the settled frame flagged the anchor, and the next frame replayed rows the old width had already put in scrollback, writing them twice. After a terminal reset the resize frame could also move the owed rows into the count by itself.
- Left alone: a resize recovery (its history offsets count rows at another width and it has its own reflow debt), an invalid origin (it owes nothing, so a rewrite over it drops nothing), a recovery that writes every owed row, and a receipt invalidated while it holds a publication (it keeps its rows owed, and the anchor it commits carries the restore and catch-up flags).
- Also covered by the same comparison: a frame that accepts fewer rows than the receipt still owes. That is how rows refused by the rebase gate of #1831 would be flagged once both land. It is not unit-tested on this base; the Linux runs below include #1831.
- Tests: eleven runtime tests in `runtime_tests.zig` build the debt from a real sequence (a base frame, a partial commit of growth that leaves a receipt owing four rows, then a rewrite). Three pass the rewrite through the store's `reconcileTranscriptCommitSourceWithRewriteMode`: in both `.strict` and `.preserve_same_epoch`, after a second rewrite over the zeroed receipt, and with a rewritten frame that is itself a partial write. They fail on the first version of this PR (the anchor carries no flag and history stays 8 behind a viewport at 12). Two resize tests, one through a rewrite and one through a terminal reset with no rewrite, resize rows of 19 characters from 20 to 12 columns, to 20 columns with a pending delta, and to an unmeasured 12 columns; each settles without a flag and without writing row 4 again, and each fails if either half of the width and delta check is removed. A retry that writes two of the four owed rows before a rewrite replays from row 10. Two tests cover a rewrite that reaches the plan without the store, and three controls pass either way: a recovery that writes its owed rows, a receipt that owed nothing, and a receipt invalidated while it holds a publication.
- Linux, in a Vercel Sandbox (x86_64, the Ctrl-O history repro of `tui-full-transcript-brutal.test.ts` on three pinned CPUs plus 10 busy loops, 200 runs per arm interleaved in four rounds, both arms on top of #1831 and #1877): 0 failures in either arm, no missing chat or tool line, no duplicate chat line, and no run that ended with history behind the viewport. The store dropped owed rows in 183 runs of the base arm and 199 of the fix arm. The flag fired 453 times in the fix arm, 85 of them for rows a store rewrite dropped, and every time the following frames replayed the rows (a `document_append_plan` from the flagged history up to at least the viewport).
- Not shown live: the base arm did not end with a gap either, and the resize drop never fired in these runs. The Linux runs show the flag breaks and duplicates nothing; the stuck gap and the resize duplicate are shown by the unit tests above.

## Review

The full reviews ran on 6d0eaaa55 and 67d4019e4. The later commit 5f1bd5047 fixes the resize case the second review found, and was checked on its own.

title: Refresh a shared fx login once when several fx get a 401 together
body:
## Summary

- When several fx processes get a 401 at the same time, they now refresh their shared fx login once. Before, each of them read the rejected token from the store, forced a refresh, and rotated the login again once it got the lock, so every rotation made the token the other processes held fail.
- The forced refresh after a 401 now carries the rejected token. Under the login's lock, fx rotates the login only when the saved login still holds that token or is past its refresh deadline, and otherwise replays the request with the saved login.
- This builds on the stored-login replay from #1855, which covers a process whose token another process already replaced.
- When the saved login is rejected too, the request takes the existing refused path and does not refresh again.
- Codex and Grok subscription logins keep their current refresh behavior.

## Testing

CI does not run the TLA+ model for this or its driver yet, so I ran both by hand:

- `sh tests/tla/auth/check.sh`: every config gives its expected verdict.
- `zig build && bun test ./tests/tla/drivers/auth/`: real fx runs are behaviors of `SharedLoginRefreshTrace`.

title: Size the agent list's state column to the states shown
body:
## Summary

- The agent list's state column always kept room for its longest state, "needs approval", so with every agent idle the model sat ten columns past `idle`. The column is now as wide as the widest state the list shows, as the name, title, model, and profile columns already are.

## Tests

- New `agents_menu_presentation` test: with every agent idle, the model follows the state after the usual two-column gap.
- The nested-branch test's profile moves left with the narrower column.
- Unit tests for agents_menu_presentation, app_agents_runtime, and "the agent list": all pass (the run's other failures are the read-only folder tests that fail only as root in the sandbox).
- E2E `the agent list puts subagents that wait for the user first`, `the agent list shows each agent's title, state, and model in columns`, and `a subagent's approval can be answered on its own screen`: pass.

- `tui-host-switch.test.ts` 50/50 and `tui-host-instances.test.ts` 47/47.

title: Name the reason on tool rows that fx never ran
body:
## Summary

- A tool row that fx never ran says "Reply failed before <tool> ran" when the model's reply ended with a provider error, such as Gemini's `MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL`. Before, it said "Connection interrupted" even when the connection was fine.
- A tool call that a resend started and fx then stopped for review says "Stopped before <tool> ran".
- A dropped connection, or a reply that ended early, still says "Connection interrupted before <tool> ran".
- When one turn fails more than once, each row names the reason of the attempt that started it.

title: Read toolbox run arguments written as JSON text
body:
## Summary

- A toolbox run whose `arguments` the model wrote as JSON text, such as `"arguments":"{\"limit\":40}"`, now runs the tool with the object that text holds. Before, it failed with "toolbox arguments must be an object".
- The run is carried as the tool's own call, so permission rules, reviews, and `fx ask --json` see and report the decoded arguments, the same as for an object.
- Text that isn't exactly one JSON object, including an array, a number, or an object encoded twice, is still refused with the same message.
- JSON text nested deeper than the 64 levels fx takes for tool input is refused before fx reads it, in toolbox, shell's `shell` field, and ask_user_question's `questions`, so it can't crash fx.
- With `FX_TRACE_LOG` and the `toolbox` trace scope, fx logs each run whose arguments it read from text, with the call ID and tool name.

## Module move

`json_depth.zig` moves from `src/gateway/` to `src/core/shared/`, so the tool argument helper in `src/core/tooling/` uses the same 64-level limit as the gateway without importing it. The gateway's checks are unchanged.

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  client["src/gateway/client.zig"] --> depth["src/gateway/json_depth.zig"]
  chat["src/gateway/chat_completions_protocol.zig"] --> depth
  responses["src/gateway/responses_protocol.zig"] --> depth
  anthropic["src/gateway/anthropic_messages_protocol.zig"] --> depth
  functions["src/gateway/function_tools.zig"] --> depth
  args["src/core/tooling/tool_args.zig (no depth check)"]
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  client["src/gateway/client.zig"] --> depth["src/core/shared/json_depth.zig"]
  chat["src/gateway/chat_completions_protocol.zig"] --> depth
  responses["src/gateway/responses_protocol.zig"] --> depth
  anthropic["src/gateway/anthropic_messages_protocol.zig"] --> depth
  functions["src/gateway/function_tools.zig"] --> depth
  args["src/core/tooling/tool_args.zig"] --> depth
```

title: Report a test server's lost connection instead of hanging
body:
## Summary

- A unit test server whose poll reports a connection that `accept` then does not find goes back to waiting for its stop, so `zig build test` no longer hangs on the join of that server's thread.
- That case also fails the running test with the port, the poll result and the accept error, so its cause shows in the test output.
- The unpooled-open gateway fixture counts a connection that is gone before its accept as closed.

title: Show what fx logout waits for on a terminal
body:
## Summary

- On a terminal, `fx logout codex` prints `revoking the Codex login at OpenAI (up to 15 s)...` before it waits for OpenAI to end the login.
- On a terminal, `fx logout grok` prints `revoking the Grok login at xAI (up to 15 s)...` before it waits for xAI.
- On a terminal, `fx logout` prints `revoking the fx login at Vercel (up to 45 s)...` before it waits for Vercel.
- The line goes only to a terminal's stderr, so pipes and scripts get the same output as before.
- A logout with no saved login, or with one fx can't read, sends no revocation and prints no line.

title: Cover a turn 401 in ACP when the store still holds the rejected login
body:
## Summary

- Adds an ACP test for a turn the gateway rejects with 401 while the store still holds the rejected fx login: fx forces one refresh, saves the new login, and replays the prompt with it.
- This is the path where a rejected turn once compared the stored login against a key ACP had already freed (#1855). Until now only the Codex and Grok provider change tests reached it.

This change adds a test only.

title: Never cut off a sign-in refresh, and keep /usage and /compact working when another fx renews the login
body:
## Summary

- A cancel could stop a sign-in refresh after the issuer had already rotated the refresh token, and every fx process sharing the sign-in then had to sign in again. The fx login, ChatGPT and Grok refreshes now mark their requests from the token request until the new tokens are saved, and `Cancellable` leaves those requests running. A cancel still stops a refresh that has not sent its token request. The rule lives in the sign-in code, so it covers the prompt's sign-in check, the provider switch, `/credits`, and any new caller.
- A prompt that stops waiting for its sign-in refresh no longer waits for it either: the auth runtime keeps the refresh until it ends and saves the new login, and a full shutdown waits for it.
- Quitting never waits. A prompt refresh, provider switch, or `/credits` lookup that is still running when fx exits is left to end with the process, as a refresh in flight at exit always has.
- When the provider refuses `/usage`'s token because another fx process renewed the shared login, `/usage` reads the newer stored login and fetches once more, and later refreshes send it. It never refreshes the login itself.
- A `/compact` summary request the gateway rejects with 401 is sent once more: with the stored login when another fx process renewed it, or after one forced refresh while the store still holds the rejected token, as an agent turn does. The turn and compaction share that rule.
- A compaction request that failed with a provider error freed its error detail twice when the detail needed no masking. It now frees it once.

Automatic compaction inside a turn does not renew a rejected login yet.

This replaces #1913, whose commit is now in this branch.

title: Model-check fx's TCP connect and trace its outcome
body:
## Summary

- Adds `tests/tla/mcp_host/Connect.tla`, a TLA+ model of the connect in `src/core/shared/net_connect.zig` (#1687): one `connect` call per socket, a 20 ms `poll` slice, the kernel's answer read from `SO_ERROR`, a cancel check between slices, and a blocking socket returned. A pass of the wait is two steps, as in `awaitConnected`: `poll`, then the cancel check. Its properties are `NoFalseFailure`, `NoFalseSuccess`, `CancelWins`, `NoReissue`, `CanceledNeedsCancel`, `ReturnsBlocking` and `KernelAnswerWins` (a poll that returned ready is answered with the kernel's answer, never with a cancel that arrives in the same slice: `awaitConnected` reads poll's result before `io.checkCancel`). Smoke and stress each reach 25 distinct states (15 before this round). Two findings configs run std's own retry through the same model and fail `NoFalseFailure` and `NoReissue` (exit 12). That retry is the bug #1687 removes.
- Adds `tests/tla/drivers/mcp_host/connect.test.ts`. It runs the real `fx ask` with 10, 25 and 50 HTTP MCP servers started by one search, and with 10 healthy servers beside 2 closed ports. It reads the trace lines of each socket and has TLC check every socket against the model. It needs nothing macOS-specific, so it runs on Linux CI too. A refused connect shows `start` then `done`: macOS reports the refusal through `SO_ERROR` after `EINPROGRESS`, Linux may report it from `connect`, and the model accepts the kernel's answer at any point after `start`. CI runs it on the one ReleaseSafe `fx` that the job downloads (`fx-linux-x86_64`); setting `FX_BIN_RELEASE` runs a second binary too, which CI does not do.
- Adds one `net` trace line per connect event: `connect fd=<n> event=start|intr|done [result=ok|refused|canceled|other]`. It carries no address. `start` is written where `connect(2)` is called, so a second call on a socket that has not finished shows as a second `start` before its `done`; the driver reads that as a `reissue`, and then both its count and its TLC check fail. With tracing off, each event costs the `debug_trace` scope check and the two thread-local cancel-protection swaps around it; this body gives no time for it, because none was measured.
- `fx help` and `fx --version` leave no connect line with the `net` scope on. Those two driver tests pass on any binary, one without the trace line included, so they show that the startup commands do not connect, and nothing about the line itself.
- Adds tests for what a failed or waiting connect leaves behind: its socket is closed on a refused connect, on a connect that fails at once, and on a cancel while it waits (the cancel ends within 100 ms), and a held wait uses under 150 ms of its own thread's CPU time in 1.5 s. Two tests count the kernel's connect for a call that reports `EINTR` and one that reports `EINPROGRESS`: one call, one `start` line. The tests do not count process-wide descriptors. Each keeps the descriptor its connect was given and checks that it is closed, so other threads cannot make them flaky.
- A trace line no longer takes the cancel that its connect is waiting for (see below).
- A change to `net_connect.zig` selects both MCP jobs, `TLA+ MCP engine models and driver` and `TLA+ MCP host models and drivers`, in `scripts/detect-ci-need.sh`. Its test and the `AGENTS.md` paragraph list the file.
- The connect behaves as before. `connect` keeps its signature. Its body moves into a private `connectWith`, so a test can replace the call that starts the kernel's connect, and nothing new is `pub`. The socket is made non-blocking when it is opened, and not just before the connect, so that every failure after the `start` line ends in a `done` line.

## Where the model lives

`tests/AGENTS.md` names a model's folder after the module it describes, which would be `src/core/shared/`. Only listed folders run in CI. `tests/tla/mcp_host/` runs through the MCP jobs (`detect-ci-need.sh`) and holds the driver that tests the connects of the MCP host, so the model gets CI coverage there, next to its driver. The reason is written in the header of `Connect.tla`, in `tests/tla/mcp_host/check.sh` and in the row of `tests/tla/README.md`.

## A cancel that a trace line took

The first driver runs failed on a run where one connect had a `done` line but no `start` line, 5 s after the others, at the servers' startup timeout. `debug_trace` writes its file with an `Io` call that is a cancelation point, and it drops the line on `error.Canceled`. That took the cancel meant for the connect, so the connect went on instead of ending canceled. This happens only while tracing is on. `traceConnect` now blocks cancelation around its own write, so the cancel stays for the next `io.checkCancel`. A test makes a cancel pending, writes a trace line, and checks that the cancel is still there. It failed on the first version of the change.

`debug_trace` is not changed here: its write catches `error.Canceled` for every caller, so other `logf` calls on a cancelable task keep this behavior while tracing is on. The follow-up is to block cancelation around that write once, in `debug_trace`, and then drop the block from `traceConnect`. There is no issue for it yet.

The `done` line is also written before the socket is closed. A descriptor number can go to another thread's connect as soon as it is closed, and the two connects' lines would mix.

## Tests that were fragile

- The test of the trace line started its 100 ms gate timer before the task was waiting. A task that took more than 100 ms to start would find the gate open before the cancel was asked for, and end without one. The timer now starts once the task is ready. This fix is defensive: the race did not show by itself. Under 24 busy loops on 8 CPUs, 150 runs of the old test and 150 of the new one all passed. It fails only when the task is made slow on purpose (a plant that makes it wait 150 ms before it is ready): the old order fails then, and the new one passes.
- The held-connect test did not reset the descriptor it checks. A cancel that landed before the connect started checked a stale descriptor and passed without testing the close. It now resets the descriptor first, then waits up to 5 s for the connect to start before it cancels. With a plant that starts the task 150 ms late, the old test cancels before the connect starts, checks the stale descriptor, and passes without testing the close; the new one waits for the connect, cancels it, and passes with the close checked. A connect that never starts makes the new test fail with `ConnectNeverStarted` after 5 s, so it cannot hang.
- The held-connect test ordered its cancel by a 100 ms sleep. It now waits until `holdStart` has recorded the descriptor, for at most 5 s, and fails with its own message if the connect never starts. The two `catch {}` in the trace-line test each have a comment that says why the error is safe to ignore.
- The CPU test read process-wide CPU time. It reads its own thread's.

## Mutation check

18 planted bugs, each in a copy of `net_connect.zig`, each run with `zig test -lc -OReleaseSafe src/core/shared/net_connect.zig` on Linux x86_64, four at a time. 18 of 18 are caught, and the copy without a plant passes (79 tests, 14 skipped).

| Planted bug | Caught by |
|---|---|
| The retry is back: `connect` is called again after the wait | `a connect that is in progress is not started again, and writes one start line` |
| The retry is back, on an interrupted call | `an interrupted connect is not started again, and writes one start line` |
| `SO_ERROR` is not read | `connect reports a port nobody listens on as refused`, `a refused connect closes its socket`, the trace test |
| The wait never checks for a cancel | no test: the held wait hangs, and the run that plants the bug ends it after 100 s. No test has a timeout of its own. |
| A non-blocking socket is returned | `connect reaches a local listener and returns a blocking socket` |
| A signal that ends the wait fails the connect | `a connect that SIGIO interrupts while it waits still connects` |
| No socket is closed when the connect fails | the refused, fails-at-once and cancel tests |
| A refused connect keeps its socket | `a refused connect closes its socket` |
| A connect that fails at once keeps its socket | `a connect that fails at once closes its socket` |
| A canceled connect keeps its socket | `a cancel while a connect waits closes its socket and ends within 100 ms` |
| No `start` line | the trace test and the two start-once tests |
| No `done` line on failure | `a connect writes one start and one done line to the net trace, and no address` |
| A refused connect is named `other` | the same test |
| The line carries the address | the same test |
| The trace write allows cancelation | `a trace line does not swallow the cancel that a connect is waiting for` |
| The wait slice is 3 s | `waiting for a connect ends promptly when its task is canceled`, and the 100 ms cancel test |
| The wait slice is 0 ms (a loop that spins) | `waiting for a connect uses no CPU while it waits` |
| The `start` line is not at the call | the trace test and the two start-once tests |

The five model bugs in `Connect.mutants.json` are also caught by TLC, each by its own property; the new one, a cancel checked before poll's result, by `KernelAnswerWins`.

## Rules followed

Of `RULES.md`:

- **R2.4** (cancel stops a request fast): the cancel test ends within 100 ms and closes the socket.
- **R3.1** (a new `catch {}` says why): the two in the trace-line test have a comment each.
- **R3.9** (one owner frees each connection on success, error and cancel): the tests for a refused connect, a connect that fails at once and a cancel check the socket is closed, and the CPU test checks a held wait uses little.
- **R6.4** (a comment says why a `catch {}` is safe): the same two comments.
- **R7.2** (a model with a planted bug that the checker catches): `Connect.tla`, its five planted bugs, and the 18 planted bugs in `net_connect.zig`.
- **R7.3** (wait on a signal, never on a sleep): the held-connect test waits on `started_fd`. The trace-line test waits on `gate_ready` before it cancels, but its gate still opens after a 100 ms sleep in `openGateSoon`, so that test still uses a sleep to put the cancel before the trace line.

## Where the checks ran

On Linux x86_64, as root, with the model keys unset and `FX_SOUND=0`. The model, the drivers, the plants and the timing runs below ran on the head before the last two commits, which change only comments in `Connect.tla` and the test code in `net_connect.zig` described in the next bullets; the Zig runs of the last commit are the first two bullets:

- **Last commit, held-connect test:** under 24 busy loops on 8 CPUs, 40 of 40 runs of the held-connect cancel test pass on a ReleaseSafe build and 20 of 20 on a Debug build. A plant in which `holdStart` records no descriptor ends the test after its 5 s bound with `the connect did not start within 5000 ms of the test asking for it` and `ConnectNeverStarted`.
- **Connect unit tests:** `zig test -lc -OReleaseSafe src/core/shared/net_connect.zig`: the 13 connect tests pass (79 tests pass in the binary, 14 skip, 0 fail).
- **Planted bugs:** 18 of 18 caught, as in the table; the copy without a plant passes. The first version of this check counted a plant that survived as caught, because a Linux run ends with `78 passed; 14 skipped; 0 failed` and not with `All ... passed`. It found that the plant that calls `connect` again after the wait survived on Linux, since a loopback connect there returns at once and never reaches that path. The test with a call that reports `EINPROGRESS` was added for it.
- **Model:** `sh tests/tla/mcp_host/check.sh` exits 0 (28 pass, 101 planted bugs caught, 16 findings). For `Connect`: smoke and stress 25 distinct states each, 5 of 5 planted bugs caught, 2 of 2 findings fail as they must.
- **Host drivers,** with `fx` built in the same run (ReleaseSafe): `bun test ./tests/tla/drivers/mcp_host/`: 82 pass, 13 skip, 1 fail. All the connect tests pass: 10, 25 and 50 servers, the refused ports, the trace reader, and `help` and `--version`. The one failure is the `config-edit` test of a read-only folder, which this change does not touch: the test user is root and holds every capability (`CapEff 000001ffffffffff`), so a folder's mode does not stop its write.
- **Connect driver under load:** 24 busy loops on 8 CPUs, 3 runs: 7 of 7 tests pass each time.
- **Driver plant:** on an `fx` that calls `connect(2)` a second time on every socket and writes a `start` line for it (the answer of the second call ignored), the 3 server-count tests fail with the trace `start,reissue,doneok`. The same build without the plant passes. A plant in the path that Linux does not take (the in-progress arm) was not seen by the driver: nothing runs it there.
- **ThreadSanitizer:** the connect driver on an `fx` built with `-Dsanitize-thread=true`: 7 pass, no ThreadSanitizer report.
- **Test timing,** old against new, built from this round's patch taken out of a copy: the slow-task plant (old fails, new passes), the late-start plant (old passes, new fails; this ran before the held test waited for the connect to start, and with that wait the new test passes, as described above), and 150 runs of the gate test and 40 of the CPU test under 24 busy loops: 0 failed for old and for new. A stream that died cut the first run of the last part off, so the CPU test as it is now ran again alone: 0 of 40 failed.
- `zig fmt --check src/` and `scripts/check-public-surface.sh` exit 0.

CI runs the connect driver once, on the ReleaseSafe `fx` of the host job, with the rest of `bun test ./tests/tla/drivers/mcp_host/`. It has no Debug run of it.

On macOS arm64, on 2026-11-12 between 05:01 and 05:18 UTC, on this branch before this round, and not repeated since. The scripts are in the working folder of the run, not in the repository:

- Stress: base (`origin/main`) and this branch interleaved, one run each in turn, searching 50 and 100 servers on a Debug `fx` and 100 and 200 on a ReleaseSafe `fx`. This branch had 0 aborts, 0 hangs and 0 lost servers in every cell. Runs over 3 s: Debug 0 and 0, ReleaseSafe 100: 2 (base 0), ReleaseSafe 200: 2 (base 2). The p90 stayed within the margin in every cell, for example 389 ms against 312 ms at 200 servers. The margin was 10 points of runs over 3 s and 25% plus 300 ms of p90.
- Golden: 8 cases (a healthy search, a host with one refused address, refused on v4 and v6, closed at accept, a server that never answers, a 500 after 1.5 s, a 500 for every request) gave the same words and exit codes on the base and on this branch.
- Fault injection: the 7 fault cases gave the same words on both.
- `zig build test` on macOS: 10775 of 10777 passed, 2 skipped.

## Docs

None.

title: Match skill metadata keys only at the top level
body:
## Summary

- Match `name` and `description` only at the top level of a skill's frontmatter. A key nested under another map, such as `metadata.description` or `metadata.name`, no longer counts as a duplicate and no longer hides the skill.

Found while reviewing #1883. This branch is based on `main` and does not depend on it.

title: Add copy target completion
body:
## Summary

- Show named copy targets from the three latest nonempty assistant replies.
- Keep `/copy` and `/copy all` copying the latest reply.
- Extract commands, code, tables, quotes, lists, headings, paragraphs, definitions, footnotes, and thematic breaks.
- Reject stale picker selections when the reply history changes.

## Checks

- Zig 0.17 build and 110 focused tests with `--test-filter copy` passed.
- `FX_SOUND=0 bun test tui-slash-extra.test.ts --test-name-pattern '/copy'` passed: 4 tests.\n- `zig fmt --check` for changed Zig files, `git diff --check`, and `python3 -m scripts.check_cli_shape` passed.\n- Drove the built binary in tmux; `/copy` showed `all` and reported an empty history without stderr.\n\n## Docs\n\n- https://fx.sh/docs/using-fx/slash-commands: change the `/copy` entry to `/copy [all|target]`; describe the picker, content-derived names, the three-reply scope, and that `all` copies only the latest reply. Note that shell-labeled blocks use `cmd` names and other code uses `code` names.\n

title: Refresh a shared Codex or Grok login once after a 401
body:
## Summary

- After a 401 on a Codex or Grok subscription, fx retries with the subscription login another fx process already saved instead of refreshing it again.
- fx refreshes a saved Codex or Grok login after a 401 only when it still holds the rejected token or is past its refresh deadline.
- Several fx processes on one Codex or Grok login that get a 401 at the same time refresh it once, so OpenAI or xAI no longer sees a run of refreshes that ends with a reused refresh token and every session signed out.
- A Codex refresh that keeps the old refresh token still lets the other processes use the saved login.

## Testing

- Five `fx ask` processes on one subscription login that all got a 401 at once: on main, the Codex login was refreshed twice, and the Grok login four times with one process exiting 1. With this change, each login was refreshed once and every process exited 0.
- `cd tests/e2e && FX_AUTH_REFRESH_STRESS=5 bun test --rerun-each 60 ./auth-refresh.test.ts -t "(two fx processes|many fx processes) on one (codex|grok) login"`: 18 of 240 runs fail on main with a second refresh request, and all 240 pass with this change. Since a rejected turn reloads the stored login first (#1855), the race is narrow, so a single run of these tests rarely shows it.
- The unit tests in `src/core/auth/credentials.zig` and the `subscription_replace_rejected` fuzz target check the rotate-or-reuse decision itself, and each planted mutation of it fails them.
- CI doesn't run `sh tests/tla/auth/check.sh` or `bun test ./tests/tla/drivers/auth/` yet. Both pass.

title: Tell a parent when its subagent's command goes quiet
body:
## Summary

- When a subagent's shell command prints nothing up to the quiet limit (2 minutes) during a wait, fx posts a note from that subagent to its parent, such as ``fx: my command `node verify.mjs --mock` has had no output for 2m5s. It may still be working, or it may be hung. Message me to check on it, or stop me.`` The note wakes the parent's `subagent wait`.
- One note per quiet spell. A later wait in the same quiet spell sends no second note, and new output followed by a new quiet spell sends another.
- No note for a command that ends before the limit, for a subagent that is closing or closed, or for main's own commands.
- `subagent status` names each working subagent's current tool call and how long it has run. Before: `worker: working, reports final`. After: `worker: working, in Waiting for node verify.mjs --mock for 2m5s, reports final`.
- The agent list shows a working subagent's current call in place of its title, and that call's time with its state, such as `└ worker  Waiting for npm test  working 4m12s`.
- Secrets in a command line, such as `MY_API_TOKEN=sk_live_...`, are masked in the note, in status, and in the agent list, as they are in tool-call arguments.

title: Open web_fetch sockets close-on-exec from the start

title: Keep fx's crash reports from the macOS PGSO jobs
body:
## Summary

- The macOS PGSO training and behavior jobs now upload the crash reports macOS wrote for fx, in `crash-reports/` inside their evidence artifacts.
- The instrumented link writes `logs/instrumented-link.map`, so a training crash's offsets can be named the way the candidate's `logs/candidate-link.map` already names a behavior crash's.

## Why

fx sometimes panics with `reached unreachable code` when its window closes, and so far only in these jobs: training-19 on `fazxes/doctor-live-checks`, behavior-05 on `fazxes/load-public-roots-in-sandbox` (twice in one job), and training-20 on `fazxes/custom-connection-options`. It did not happen in about 200 local runs of the same tests on Debug and ReleaseSafe builds, or with the CI candidate binary on a Mac. These builds are stripped, so the panic prints only `Cannot print stack trace: stack tracing is disabled`.

A Zig panic ends in `abort()`, and macOS then writes a report that lists every thread's frames as offsets into the binary. With the report and the link map, the next crash shows where it happens.

## Testing

- `python3 -m unittest scripts.pgso.tests.test_distributed scripts.pgso.tests.test_pipeline`: 90 tests pass, including a new workflow contract test and a test of the copy script.
- `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/pgso/tests`: 303 of 307 pass. The 4 errors are `test_build_step` tests that read `zig build` output, which this machine builds in a remote sandbox; the PGSO workflow runs the suite on its own runner.
- `actionlint` and `shellcheck` pass.
- A stripped ReleaseSafe Zig program that panics exits with SIGABRT, and macOS writes its report to `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/<name>-<date>.ips`, with the panicking thread's frames as image offsets.

title: Read worker and skill state under their locks
body:
## Summary

- `WorkerRuntime.requestCancel` read `worker_processing` for its trace line before it took the worker lock, while the worker writes that field under the lock as it takes and ends turns. It now takes the lock first and reads it there, as `requestInteractiveCancel` already does.
- The skill runtime's `menuItemCount`, `selectedMenuSkill`, and `menuVisible` took the runtime by value, so every call from the input loop copied the whole struct, its catalog mutex included, while the worker could hold that mutex in `acquireCatalog`. They take a `*const Runtime` now.

## How they were found

A ThreadSanitizer build (`zig build -Dsanitize-thread=true`) running the TUI's reopened-recovery tests, `tests/e2e/tui-gateway-stream-lifecycle.test.ts -t 'reopened recovery shows progress' --rerun-each 20`, reported both races. Neither changed what a user sees: the first only fed a trace line, and the second copied a mutex nobody used from the copy. Both are still undefined behavior.

## Testing

- The same 40 runs under ThreadSanitizer: 22 data race reports on `main` (a4104d49b), none with this change.
- `zig build test`: the worker and skill runtime tests pass. In the remote sandbox this machine builds in, the file-permission tests fail on `main` too, because the sandbox ignores file modes; CI runs the suite on its own runner.
- Both runs also showed `fx: terminal sync recovery failed` on stderr in 2 or 3 of 40 runs, when the test closes the window mid-frame. That happens on `main` at the same rate and is not part of this change.

title: Print input diagnostics when the /effort menu does not open

The test then fails with the same error as before.

title: Print fx sessions and fx sessions --live as aligned tables
body:
## Summary

- `fx sessions` and `fx sessions --live` print one row per session in fixed columns: title, status or turns, how long ago it changed, and the session id, under a header row.
- `fx sessions --live` lists working sessions first, then any whose state is unknown, then idle ones, newest first in each, with a blank line between the groups and a count of each at the top.

title: State the rule the symlinked FX_HOME skills test checks
Never cut off a sign-in refresh once it is sent
body:
## Summary

- A cancel could stop a refresh's token request after the issuer had already rotated the refresh token, and every fx process sharing the sign-in then had to sign in again. The fx login, ChatGPT and Grok refreshes now mark their requests from the token request until the new tokens are saved, and `Cancellable` leaves those requests running. A cancel still stops a refresh that has not sent its token request yet.
- The rule lives in the sign-in code, so it covers every caller: the provider switch, `/credits`, the prompt's sign-in check, and any new one.
- Quitting still never waits. A provider switch or `/credits` lookup that is still running when fx exits is left to end with the process, as a refresh in flight at exit always has.

Stacked on #1897.

title: Accept elicitation answers to forms that a server writes with JSON escapes
body:
## Summary

- A form that an MCP server writes with JSON escapes in a field name or a choice (`\u00e9`, `\/`, `\u0041`, a surrogate pair) now takes the person's answer. Before, fx refused the answer, showed nothing but a trace line (`MCP answer not sent ... err=InvalidInputResponses`, or `err=InvalidAnswer` for a 2025 server), and the tool call never ended. It happened on both the 2026 input round and the 2025 `elicitation/create` request.
- One behavior change for such a form: a form that holds `"A"` and `"\u0041"` has the same name twice once decoded, so it is now unreadable, as a name written twice alike already was. Before, the engine read them as two fields. In the ACP e2e test the client is shown no form in either case, and fx's trace now reads the same as for a repeated name.

## Cause and fix

The host reads the person's answer with `std.json` and writes it back, which spells `café` and `a/b` without the escapes the server used. The engine kept the form's names and choices as raw JSON tokens and compared them byte for byte with the answer's, in `validContent` (an answer's key), `isOption` (a choice), and `readSchema` (duplicate keys and `required` names).

`src/mcp/protocol/elicitation.zig` now compares them with `wire.sameString`, which compares the strings the two tokens spell. It decodes both as it goes and allocates nothing. A surrogate pair and the character in UTF-8 are one string. A lone surrogate, an invalid escape, and invalid UTF-8 are still refused with today's words, because the shared scanner refuses them before any comparison, so the engine and the host agree. How the host writes the answer, the core policy, and the ACP projection are unchanged.

**One decoder.** The change that reads escaped protocol member names (#1953) added `wire.sameString` and landed first. This PR first had a private copy of the same decoder in `elicitation.zig`. As #1953 said, whichever of the two landed second removes the private copy and uses `wire.sameString`, so this PR does that. The private `sameString`, its `Decoder` and its duplicate table test are deleted, and `wire.zig` keeps the one decoder, the one table test and `std.json`'s equality as its law. The length of a string in code points (`minLength`, `maxLength`) used a second walk of the escapes. It now uses `wire.codePointCount(token)`, which counts with the same decoder. That is the only new `pub` name. A token that is not a string, or holds a bad escape or a lone surrogate, has no count, and the answer is refused.

## What it adds

- **Engine tests:** 13 in `elicitation.zig` (the 14 first written, minus the table test that `wire.zig` already has), and 1 in `wire.zig` for `codePointCount`. They cover a form at its 32-field limit with every name escaped, a form and an answer cut at every byte, an empty name and a NUL name, and the duplicate-after-decoding case. The engine test checks that the form is `error.Unreadable`; the words the person sees for it are checked by the driver and by the ACP e2e test.
- **Model:** `tests/tla/mcp/Elicitation.tla` gains `Compare` (decoded or raw), a per-request `spell`, and the rule `FitAccepted`: an answer that fits the form is never refused. `Elicitation.findings.cfg` is the byte comparison, which must violate `FitAccepted`, and `tests/tla/mcp/check.sh` requires that verdict through `tlc_verdicts`, in the one block with the other findings. Two planted bugs were added to the 15 already there. I extended the 2025 client-side model instead of adding a new one. The 2026 path is covered by driver scenarios and the e2e tests, because `Mrtr.tla` has no refused-answer outcome.
- **Driver:** 27 `u12-escape-*` scenarios, for the 2025 and 2026 paths, and the planted control, with `beforeRaw` in the fake stdio server so a server request keeps its escapes. Each trace is checked through TLC.
- **Fuzz:** `mcp_elicitation_escapes` checks, through `mcp.elicitation.check` and `parse`, that the engine's equality matches `std.json`'s decoded equality for an answer's key and a choice, and that two names that decode alike make a form unreadable and a required name finds the property it spells. It has 16 saved inputs. It is in `src/core/mcp_host/wire_tests.zig` because the engine module imports only `std` and has no `fuzz_corpus` module. The generic `mcp_elicitation` target (parsers stay bounded under fuzzed bytes) has no saved inputs and is not changed.
- **e2e:** 56 ACP cases in `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts` (2 transports, 4 places, 7 spellings), and two duplicate-name cases. `FX_MCP_RAW_FORM_SCHEMA` in both MCP fixtures sends a schema as raw JSON text, after the fixture escapes the keys it writes.

Before the fix, 6 of the 9 spellings were refused in each engine test, 32 of the 56 e2e cases failed (the 24 guards passed), and 22 of the 27 driver scenarios failed.

## Mutation check

A wrong compare was planted in `elicitation.zig`, one at a time, in a scratch copy, and run against the engine tests, the saved inputs of `mcp_elicitation_escapes` and those of `mcp_elicitation`. Every plant is caught, and each one is caught by the engine tests.

| # | Wrong compare planted | Engine tests that fail | `mcp_elicitation_escapes` replay |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A repeated name is found by its bytes | 1: `two names that are one name once decoded make the form unreadable` | fails |
| 2 | A `required` name is found by its bytes | 1: `a required name written with an escape names the key it spells` | fails |
| 3 | An answer's key is found by its bytes | 5, among them `a key the server wrote with an escape is accepted as the host writes it` and `the check is the same when the answer escapes and the form does not` | fails |
| 4 | A choice is found by its bytes | 5, among them the `enum`, `oneOf` and multi-select escape tests | fails |
| 5 | All four compares are byte compares | 9 | fails |
| 6 | A string's length counts bytes, not code points | 1: `checks form content against the schema` | passes (its law does not check lengths) |

The fuzz law first caught only plants 3, 4 and 5. A byte compare in the duplicate-name or the required-name check passed it, so on the same generated strings it now also reads a form with both as property names (unreadable exactly when `std.json` decodes them alike) and a form whose required name is one and whose property is the other (readable exactly then). A saved input decodes as before.

The generic target `mcp_elicitation` catches none of them: its law is that the parsers stay bounded, not that they agree with `std.json`. `mcp_elicitation_escapes` is the fuzz target that does.

The 13 bugs that this PR first planted inside its own decoder (the surrogate shift, hex case, a lone surrogate, an unknown escape, and so on) were measured on code that is no longer here. The decoder is now `wire.sameString`, with its table test, and those bugs are not planted again here.

## Where the checks ran

All of these ran on Linux x86_64, with the model keys unset and `FX_SOUND=0`, on the head below.

- `zig fmt --check src/` and `scripts/check-public-surface.sh`: exit 0.
- `zig test src/mcp/mcp.zig -lc`, in ReleaseSafe and in Debug: 302 tests pass. The escape tests written for the private decoder pass against `wire.sameString`.
- The Zig groups `core.mcp.` and `core.mcp_host.`: 310 tests, 0 failed, with the fuzz test of `wire_tests.zig` among them.
- Fuzz replays of the saved inputs, exit 0: `mcp_elicitation_escapes` (16 inputs), `mcp_elicitation` (none) and `mcp_object_fields` (24). Then `scripts.fuzz_nightly` for 180 s on `mcp_elicitation` and on `mcp_elicitation_escapes`: one round each, no failure.
- `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts -t "elicitation|form|MCP input|escape"`: 69 pass, 13 skip, 0 fail. `tests/e2e/mcp-stdio.test.ts`, whole: 149 pass, 0 fail. Both against a ReleaseSafe build made in the same run.
- `sh tests/tla/mcp/check.sh`: exit 0, 17 models pass, all 17 `Elicitation` mutants caught, and `Elicitation.findings` violates `FitAccepted` as required.
- `bun tests/tla/drivers/mcp/driver.ts`, with fx built first in the same run: exit 0, 149 scenarios pass. The first run's output was cut after `check.sh`, so the driver step was run again alone.

I did not run anything on macOS arm64 for this head, and no check here needs it.

## Not fixed, found while searching

Nothing is left from the search. The two places it found, `wire.objectFields` skipping a member name with an escape and the input-request keys in `mrtr.zig` compared as raw tokens, were fixed by #1953, which landed first. `mrtr.zig` now calls `wire.sameString`.

## Docs

None. fx-web #288 (questions over ACP forms) says nothing about escapes or repeated names.

title: Wait for fx's exit status in the custom connection startup tests
body:
## Summary

Where fx refuses to start and exits by itself, these tests now wait for the exit status that the pane's wrapper records, and expect it, in place of waiting for tmux to mark the pane dead or end the session:

- `tests/e2e/tui-custom-connection-errors.test.ts`: the startup case with a refused setting, and the resume cases whose connection changed its protocol or was removed.
- `tests/e2e/tui-startup.test.ts`: "TERM=dumb refuses the interactive session and points to fx ask" and "an error that stops startup is shown in plain words, with its name only in the trace".
- `tests/e2e/sessions.test.ts`: `appExit`, the fault grid's app entry (its startup race and its wait after `/quit`), and the app step of "a flipped byte in a turn the newest compaction kept stops resume and ACP load as damage, and recover still salvages it".
- `tests/e2e/tui-resume.test.ts`: "contended startup resume stays non-interactive and recovers after release", and the missing, busy and unreadable bookmark cases of "remembered continuation restores the selected conversation without discovery".

Waits for a pane to end after `/quit` stay as they are, and so does the `tui-resize.test.ts` check that tmux keeps an immediate nonzero exit, which tests tmux itself.

## Why

The custom connection tests failed often in CI: 9 of the last 40 CI runs had an E2E job fail or retry on them, on `main` and on pull requests. fx printed its message, but the pane never showed "Pane is dead" within 15 seconds.

fx was not the cause. Scratch CI runs on an `ubuntu-24.04` runner showed:

- [43288549756](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/actions/runs/43288549756): the old file failed in 7 of 15 runs, and fx's debug trace ended its shutdown and reported the error within 1 ms.
- [43290601264](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/actions/runs/43290601264): the old file failed in 2 of 15 runs this way, with the trace within 2 ms. A third failure was a different race, in "resume: /resume names a session's changed connection". In both late-reap failures, the pane's shell had exited and was a zombie whose parent was the tmux server. The server blocked no signals, caught `SIGCHLD`, and had none pending, but did not reap the shell, so it never marked the pane dead.
- [43292776142](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/actions/runs/43292776142): with this change, the file passed 15 of 15 runs.

The wrapper writes fx's exit status before the shell exits, so the status is there even when tmux reaps late. To check each changed test directly, a local harness copy made the wrapper of every pane kept after exit wait 45 seconds after it wrote the status:

- These passed on this branch and failed on `main`: the two `tui-startup` tests, the three custom connection exit tests, "the app and ACP refuse a session whose blob went missing as damaged, not missing", and "contended startup resume stays non-interactive and recovers after release".
- "remembered continuation restores the selected conversation without discovery" failed on `main` at its first refusal. On this branch it passed through all three refusals once the copy's `/quit` waits also read the recorded status, since the copy delays those panes too.
- The flipped byte test's app pane is not kept after exit, so the copy does not delay it.

title: Start a new Vercel sign-in on the team the login used
body:
## Summary

- A new Vercel sign-in starts on the team you used before, so pressing Enter in the team picker keeps it.
- This holds in every fx session and after a restart: when fx removes a login whose refresh the issuer refused, it keeps that login's team id and slug, never a token, in `~/.fx/vercel-team.json`.
- Closing the team picker after a sign-in keeps that team, instead of saving the new login with no team.
- `fx login` starts on the team of the saved login, or on the kept team when no saved login has a team.
- When the account no longer has that team, the sign-in starts on the first team, as before.
- `fx logout vercel` and `/logout vercel` forget the kept team.
- fx ignores a kept-team file that is not valid, is readable by other users, or is too large.
- The `fx login` and `fx teams` pickers mark a team `(current)` only when the login uses it, instead of marking the first team when the login has none.
- `fx login`, `fx logout` and `fx teams` write a trace with `FX_TRACE_LOG` or `FX_TRACE`. It says why a sign-in starts on the first team, and when fx keeps or forgets a removed login's team, without naming the team.
