title: Stop subagents before ACP tears down the executions they run commands through
body:
## Summary

- `fx acp` exits when the client closes stdin while a subagent is running a shell command. Before, it did not exit: it was still running after 30 s on Linux and after 90 s on macOS.
- The subagent's work is recorded as interrupted, its command is stopped, and the process exits with 0 and nothing on stderr, with one working subagent and with two.
- A session with no working subagent shuts down as before. `fx ask` already stops its subagents first, and the terminal app is unchanged.

## How

`ServerState.deinit` in `src/acp/server.zig` ran `closeOwnedTerminals`, `reapActivePrompt`, `managed_executions.deinit()`, `terminal_client.deinit()` and then `closeActiveSession`. Only `closeActiveSession` stopped the subagents, through `disableSubagentHost`, which joins each subagent's thread.

`managed_execution.Runtime.deinit` stops and joins the commands, unlocks its mutex and ends with `self.* = undefined`. A subagent that was inside a shell command had not stopped by then. Its thread was in `shell`, `startCaptured`, `prepareSnapshot` and `acquireEntry`, which locks `Runtime.mutex` of the runtime that `deinit` had finished with, and it waited there. At the same time `closeActiveSession` waited in `Thread.join` for that subagent's thread, so neither went on.

On `main` the stack of the stuck process (Linux, a Debug build from plain `zig build`, read with gdb) shows exactly that: the main thread is in `Thread.join` under `disableSubagentHost`, called from `closeActiveSession`, and the subagent's thread is in `Io.Mutex.lockUncancelable` under `Runtime.acquireEntry`. In that Debug build the runtime's mutex reads `contended`, and the four bytes after it read `0xaaaaaaaa`, the fill a Debug build writes for `undefined`.

`deinit` now calls `disableSubagentHost` right after `reapActivePrompt` and before `managed_executions.deinit()`, so the subagent's thread is joined while the runtime is still alive. The call in `closeActiveSession` then finds nothing to stop, because `disableSubagentHost` clears the host. `fx ask` already has this order: `AskContext.deinit` closes the terminals, stops the subagent host and then calls `managed_executions.deinit()`.

## Contains

- #2014 (head `73d554c1c`), which fixes `Owner.deinit` in `src/core/subagent/managed_owner.zig`: it joins every slot's thread first, with a new `joinSlot`, and only then frees the slots, so no slot is freed while another slot's thread can still walk `self.slots`. This branch merges it, and its three switch tests come with the merge.

With the order this PR gives `ServerState.deinit`, closing stdin reaches `Owner.deinit` while subagents still work, and `Owner.deinit` had a fault that this exposes. It marks every slot shut down, then calls `destroySlot` for each slot in `self.slots.items`. `destroySlot` joins the slot's thread, then frees the slot and its `child_id`, and the freed slot stays in `self.slots.items`. The thread of the next slot, when its work ends, runs `markEnding`, which walks `self.slots.items` under the owner's mutex and reads each slot's `child_id`, so it can read a slot that was freed. On Linux Debug, with two subagents inside shell commands and stdin closed soon after both commands started, `fx acp` was killed by SIGSEGV. On `main`, where that close hung earlier, it did not reach this code.

## Testing

This PR adds three E2E tests in `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts`, under `acp: model-independent`:

- `ACP closing stdin while the prompt runs stops a subagent that runs a shell command, and the server exits`
- `ACP closing stdin after session/cancel stops a subagent that runs a shell command, and the server exits`
- `ACP closing stdin with two subagents inside shell commands stops both, and the server exits`

The first two start `fx acp` in `full-access` mode against a fake gateway. The parent's reply starts the subagent `sheller`, and the subagent's first reply is a `shell` call that runs `touch <file>; sleep 30`. The test waits for `<file>`, so the command is running. The second test then sends `session/cancel`, waits for the prompt's `cancelled` response and checks that the session's log has no finished subagent yet. Each then closes stdin and waits up to 30 s for the process to exit. It expects exit code 0, empty stderr, and the subagent's `child_finished` record in the session's log to read `interrupted`.

The two-subagent test starts the subagents `first` and `second` in two separate model turns. `first` runs `touch <file>; sleep 30`. `second` runs `trap '' TERM; touch <file>; sleep 30`, a command that ignores SIGTERM. The test waits for both files, closes stdin at once, and waits up to 30 s for the process to exit. It expects exit code 0, empty stderr and two `interrupted` records in the session's log. `Owner.start` appends each slot to `slots`, so without the fix of `Owner.deinit` `first`'s slot is freed first, while `second`'s command is still ending, and that opens the window on every Linux Debug run. Without the `trap`, the same test passed in 6 of 20 runs.

Linux x86_64, in the `fx-cloud` sandbox with a Debug build from plain `zig build`, from `tests/e2e`: `FX_SOUND=0 bun test acp.test.ts -t "ACP closing stdin"`. Counts are per test.

| Tree | Result |
|---|---|
| `main` `0b85cd446` plus the two tests, without the fix | fails 3 of 3, `error: ACP process exit timeout` (the 30 s wait) |
| the tree that became `ff3339c5c`, the fix and the tests, run before it was committed | passes 20 of 20 |
| `3161e69fb`, the tests moved | passes 20 of 20 |
| `2d315574f`, the two-subagent test added, without the fix of `Owner.deinit` | the two-subagent test fails 20 of 20: the process is killed by SIGSEGV with empty stderr, where the test expects exit code 0 (the signal read from the process's `close` event in a copy of the test) |
| `2d315574f`, the same test with the `trap` removed | fails 14 of 20 |
| `6fdc60fdc`, this head: `main` `6ddd5790a` and #2014 merged | each of the three tests passes 20 of 20 |

macOS arm64: the binaries are built with `fx-cloud macos-build` and run on a Mac, with the E2E file and with a local script that is not in the repository. macOS CI skipped its jobs for this head (`macOS arm64 build`, `unit tests` and `platform E2E` show skipping, and the `macOS arm64` check passes without a macOS runner), so these counts come from the macOS binary run on a Mac. `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts` is not listed in `tests/e2e/macos-platform-tests.json`.

- The two-subagent test cannot fail on the macOS binary: on the binary built from the tree that became `2d315574f`, without the fix of `Owner.deinit`, it passes 20 of 20, so it proves nothing there and the Linux Debug runs are its proof. On the binary built from `6fdc60fdc`, with #2014 merged, each of the three tests passes 20 of 20, with `FXC_LOCAL=1 FX_SOUND=0 bun test acp.test.ts -t "ACP closing stdin"` from `tests/e2e`.
- E2E file, `FXC_LOCAL=1 FX_SOUND=0 bun test acp.test.ts -t "ACP closing stdin"` from `tests/e2e`, with the worktree's `./zig-out/bin/fx`. The `main` `0b85cd446` binary fails both tests in 2 of 2 runs, with `ACP process exit timeout`. The binary built from `3161e69fb` passes both tests in 20 of 20 runs.
- The script drives `fx acp` over JSON-RPC as the E2E does. The subagent runs `touch <file>; sleep 3; echo shell-done`, the script waits for `<file>`, optionally sends `session/cancel` and reads both responses, waits 200 ms, closes stdin, and waits 8 s before it kills the process. Per case, 4 workers of 13 runs each, so 52 runs:
  - `main` `0b85cd446` binary: stdin closed while the prompt runs, 52 of 52 still running after 8 s. After `session/cancel`, 52 of 52 still running after 8 s. With stdin closed while the prompt runs and a 90 s wait, 2 of 2 runs were still running at 90 s, though the command ends after 3 s. No run had a `child_finished` record.
  - `0b85cd446` plus the five lines of this change, built the same way: both cases, 52 of 52 runs exit in under 2 s, with exit code 0, no signal, empty stderr and an `interrupted` record.
  - The same binary with the command `sleep 97`, 3 runs: the process exits in about 50 ms with code 0 and an `interrupted` record, and no `sleep 97` process is left afterwards.

Other runs:

- The Linux sandbox, on `6fdc60fdc`: no process named `sleep` was running before the runs, and none was left after any of 3 runs of each of the three tests.
- #2014's three switch tests, which this branch carries, pass 5 of 5 each in the Linux sandbox: `FX_SOUND=0 bun test acp.test.ts -t "away from two subagents inside shell commands"` from `tests/e2e`.
- The full `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts` on `6fdc60fdc`, in the sandbox: 186 pass, 13 skip, 1 fail. The failing test, `an attached folder whose rule file cannot be read is reported in the note, not in the instructions`, failed the same way on unmodified `main` `0b85cd446` there, because the sandbox user can read a file the test makes unreadable.
- A Linux ThreadSanitizer build (`zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe -Dsanitize-thread=true`) of `6fdc60fdc`, one run of the three stdin close tests: with `TSAN_OPTIONS=report_thread_leaks=0` all three pass with no warning. With the default options each of the three runs reports one `thread leak` warning and no other, and the test fails on it. Where that thread is created was not read in these runs.

## Not in this change

- `fx acp` on `main` still ends with SIGSEGV when a shell command that its turn left running writes output after the turn has ended. This needs no subagent and no stdin close, and it happens on Linux and on macOS. It is a separate fault, and this change neither removes it nor makes it more likely. A command `sleep 1; echo late-output; sleep 1`, run with `yield_time_ms: 200` so that the turn ends first, killed a Debug build about 0.8 s after the turn in 6 of 6 runs on Linux and in 6 of 6 runs of the macOS binary, on `main` `3fd4905af` and on this head alike; with `tty: true` the same command ended cleanly in 6 of 6 runs on each. Earlier, a subagent's quiet shell session followed by `session/new` and stdin close ended with SIGSEGV on the macOS binary in 52 of 52 runs on `main` `0b85cd446` and in 52 of 52 runs on `0b85cd446` plus the five lines of this change.
- The Linux ThreadSanitizer build reports the shell snapshot capture thread, started at `src/core/terminal/shell_snapshot.zig:686`, as a thread that finished and was never joined, at exit. `main` has it.

title: Fix flaky subagent empty-reply E2E test
body:
## Summary

- The empty-reply E2E test releases the parent's held reply only once the worker has taken the subagent's report into the open turn, so the report always continues the turn instead of a nudge.
- Before, about 1 run in 100 failed with `Expected length: 3, Received length: 4`, because the test released the reply on a trace line that comes one main-loop tick before the worker has the report. It passes in repeated runs now.
- fx itself does not change. Only the test changed.

title: Raise the macOS arm64 and Linux arm64 PGSO size ceilings
body:
The macOS arm64 PGSO candidate in the v0.0.17 release run measures 6.287 MiB. It meets the 6.500 MiB ceiling but not the 0.250 MiB preferred headroom, so qualification fails and the release cannot package macOS arm64. Linux arm64 had 0.306 MiB under its ceiling at the previous release attempt, so the same growth leaves it short as well.

- macOS arm64 ceiling: 6.500 MiB to 6.750 MiB
- Linux arm64 ceiling: 6.750 MiB to 7.000 MiB
- Linux x86_64 stays at 8.750 MiB

`python3 -m unittest scripts.pgso.tests.test_linux` passes.

title: Stop tracking compiled Python caches
body:
## Summary

- Removes 29 compiled Python files under `scripts/**/__pycache__/` from the repository. Each one holds an absolute path from the machine that compiled it, and `scripts/check-public-surface.sh` rejects them.
- Ignores `__pycache__/` at the repository root, so running the Python scripts leaves no untracked files.

## How

- Runs `git rm --cached` on the 29 files that `git ls-files` lists. Nothing else is removed.
- Adds `__pycache__/` to the root `.gitignore`, in the same form as `tests/tla/.gitignore`.

## Testing

- On Linux (`LANG=C.UTF-8`), `bash scripts/check-public-surface.sh` exits 1 on `main` with 29 `Binary file ... matches` lines, and exits 0 on this branch.
- On macOS in a UTF-8 locale the check already passes on `main`, because `git grep` reports no match in the binary files there. With `LC_ALL=C` it exits 1 on `main` and 0 on this branch.
- `python3 -m scripts.check_cli_shape` prints `CLI shape: ok`, and `python3 -m unittest scripts.pgso.tests.test_corpus` runs 38 tests and passes. Both started with no `.pyc` file present, and `git status` stayed clean after each.
- `git ls-files | grep -c pyc` prints 0.

title: Hold the joined report test's child reply until main's wait starts
body:
- The joined-report TUI test opened the child's gate as main received its wait call. On a fast build the child finished before main's wait began, so both waits read `waited for subagents` instead of `waited for helper`. The macOS arm64 PGSO candidate of the v0.0.17 release failed its behavior corpus on this test twice in a row.
- The fake gateway now sends the child's reply only once main's row shows `waiting for helper`, so the wait always begins while the child works.
- fx itself does not change. Only the test changed.

`FX_SOUND=0 bun test tui-gateway-stream-lifecycle.test.ts -t "a report that joins a running turn"` passes three runs in a row.

title: End an MCP call whose server sends a reply fx can't read
body:
## Summary

When an MCP server wrote a line fx could not read, a call waiting for it could wait for its whole operation timeout (5 minutes by default), and the model was then told that the server did not answer, though it had. fx now gives each such call 30 seconds, then ends it with the words "the server's answer was malformed" and tells the server it was cancelled. A valid reply, or progress for the call, inside the 30 seconds keeps the call alive.

Which calls get the 30 seconds depends on the transport. Stdio has one stream for every call, so a line that names no request is about all of them. HTTP gives each call its own SSE stream, so an event that names no request is about the call on that stream alone, and calls on other streams keep their normal timers.

## What was wrong

I measured it with the built ReleaseSafe fx through `fx ask`, a fake gateway and fake servers. The operation timeout was 3 s unless I say "default".

| Server | Before |
|---|---|
| stdio: bytes that are not UTF-8, or JSON nested past the engine's limit, with the id first or last; a cut line; an object id; `id: null` | The call waited its whole timeout (300.9 s at the default). The model was told the server "did not answer within its operation timeout". |
| stdio: id readable but `jsonrpc` wrong | Ended in 0.9 s with `invalid reply (its jsonrpc isn't "2.0")`. This path already worked. |
| HTTP, a JSON body that cannot be read | Ended in 0.5 s, but said "the connection failed". The server had connected. |
| HTTP SSE, an event that cannot be read, stream held open | The event was dropped without a trace. The call waited (300.7 s at the default). Even a readable id with a wrong `jsonrpc` waited, where stdio ends it at once. |
| `tools/list` with such a reply | 900 s at the default, three timer periods, before the model heard "unavailable". |

Both causes are server mistakes (MCP says messages are UTF-8 and a stdio server must not write anything else to stdout). JSON-RPC says nothing about what a client does with a reply it cannot read, and a reply with no id cannot be tied to a call, so fx does not guess. The MCP lifecycle says clients should time requests out and send a cancellation, which is what this does.

## What fx does now

After a refused line that names no request, the calls it is about get 30 seconds each (`request.Timeouts.refused_ms`, an engine option that the host never reads from a user's settings):

- **stdio:** every `tools/call` and `tools/list` in flight, because there is one stream.
- **HTTP:** only the call on the stream that carried the event. The table's `refused_line` event names that call (the stream's key, which is the request id), and it names none for stdio, so the two cases are one event and one code path. A stream that carries no normal call in flight (`initialize`, the listen stream, a call that has ended) gives nothing.

`server/discover`, the probe fx sends first, is a normal request too, so it gets a grace as well when the line is about it (see the next list).

- A valid reply inside the 30 seconds still matches its call, and the grace does nothing.
- Progress for the call's own `progressToken` clears its grace, and its normal timers go on. Progress for another call clears nothing.
- A call sent after the line gets no grace. `initialize` keeps its start deadline, because a client must not cancel it. A listen has no timer.
- `server/discover` keeps its grace, and `initialize`'s reason does not apply to it, because a client may cancel a probe. The start budget (30 s from detection, `Timeouts.start_ms`) already cuts the probe, and the grace is 30 s from a line that came after detection began, so the budget ends the probe first. A test pins that premise (`grace: the grace is no shorter than the start budget, so the budget ends a probe first`), so a shorter grace would show up there. The host sets neither value.
- One timer covers the calls a line finds without a grace, and a second line neither extends it nor arms another. When the last call that holds a line ends or shows progress for its own token, the request table says `disarm_refused` for that line and the server drops its timer. So the timers armed for refused lines never outnumber the calls that hold a grace, however many lines and progress notifications come. Progress and a bad line in turns, a thousand times, leave one timer for one call.
- At the end the call ends with the existing `.malformed` outcome, so `model.zig` is unchanged, and a cancellation goes out (`notifications/cancelled` on stdio, the session's cancel or the closed stream on HTTP).
- HTTP: a 2xx JSON body that cannot be read now ends its call at once as malformed. An error status keeps its HTTP failure. An SSE event that cannot be read takes the same path as a stdio line, and one with a readable id and a wrong `jsonrpc` ends its call at once, as on stdio. This is the one behavior change for such an event.
- An SSE event answers the call whose stream it came on, as a valid reply does: an event on one call's stream that names another call is a stray and ends neither. Before, it ended the other call.
- An SSE event that names no request gives the grace to the call on its stream alone. Before, it gave one to every normal call on every stream, so a slow call on another stream, with no progress, ended malformed 30 seconds later because of someone else's bad event. The rule is the same one a valid reply follows.
- The debug trace gets one line for every call that ends malformed because fx could not read what the server sent, with the server, the transport, the code, the reason and a length, and no server text: `MCP call ended server=… transport=… code=malformed reason=unreadable_body bytes=N` for a 2xx body (the body's length, in bytes) and `reason=unreadable_line` for a line whose grace ran out (the length of the last line with no readable id that the server wrote before the call ended, which is not necessarily the one that gave this call its grace).

## Why `Request.tla`

`tests/tla/mcp/Request.tla` (U02) already holds the timers, progress and `cancelSent`, so the grace is a few more actions there (`RefusedLine`, `GraceExpired`, `ProgressClears`) and not a new model. The model found a bug in my first version of the progress rule: after progress had cleared a grace, a later refused line must give a fresh one, and my ghost state did not start over. Its timers were a count with one timer per request grace, which the code did not do: the code arms one timer per line, and it did not drop one when progress cleared the last grace that held it, so progress and a bad line in turns grew the server's timer list by one per round. The model now keeps the set of lines whose timer is armed, with three invariants (`TimersBounded`, `TimersAreGraces`, `GraceHasTimer`). A refused line also carries the call whose stream it came on, or none for stdio, and the model checks `ScopedGrantsOnlyItsCall`: a line scoped to one call never gives a grace to another. A property about two normal calls does not fit the smoke config's budget (a fourth id ran out of memory), so it has its own small config, `Request.scoped.cfg` (two ids, no initialize or listen, 51,516 states), which the catalog lists under `also`, so `run.py check`, the command CI runs, runs it after the smoke config and CI checks the scope rule. It takes about 7 seconds in the same 512 MB heap. A planted bug can name its own config in `Request.mutants.json` for this. The model has a findings config for the code before the grace (`SoonAfterRefusal` is violated, as required) and 22 planted bugs in all. The ones added since the first version are "a new grace appends a timer without dropping the stale one", "a grace with no timer armed" and "an SSE refusal grants a grace to every call".

## Tests

- Table tests and a stress test in `request.zig` (18 grace tests and the stress test, 1,000,000 steps over 64 slots; the stress test and the fuzz oracle send lines with and without a scope). They count the refused timers a server would hold, from the table's `arm_timer`, `disarm_refused` and fired timers, and check after every step that each timer is for a line some call still holds and that the timers never outnumber the calls. Two tests send progress and a bad line in turns a thousand times, one for a line on a stream and one for a line on the connection, and both check that the timers stay within the calls. One checks that a line on one call's stream gives a grace to that call alone, and that a line on the connection gives one to all. One checks that a line scoped to `initialize`, a listen, an id never sent or a call that has ended arms nothing. One checks that a call that ends or shows progress drops its line's timer only when it was the last to hold it, and one pins the premise of the `server/discover` decision. The model-driven observer also checks that a `disarm_refused` names a line no call holds, and that a line scoped to one call arms a timer only that call holds, over every exhaustive and random sequence it walks. The exhaustive walk now carries the line counter from step to step; it started each step with a fresh one, so two lines could share a number in the test but never in the table.
- Server tests in `server.zig`: the same thousand rounds against a real `Server`, counting its timer list, and a test that sends a bad line through `onRefusedLine` with a stream and without one and checks which calls hold a grace.
- Two Zig tests in `http.zig` for the new endings (a 200 body, a refused SSE event, and a 500 body that stays an HTTP failure).
- Fuzz target `mcp_request_grace`, 48 saved inputs, registered at 1,000,000 iterations.
- E2E: in `mcp-stdio.test.ts`, one test runs the three silent variants, the progress case and the call-sent-later case at once, and a second holds the guards. In `mcp-legacy-remote.test.ts`, four tests: one runs two `fx mcp call` commands in one shell command, so two calls are in flight on two streams. The server writes an unreadable event with no id on one stream and answers the other after 36 seconds. The call on the first stream ends at about 30 seconds as malformed, with one cancellation, and the other returns its result. The other three: the JSON body words (it now also checks the trace line, to the byte, and that nothing the body held is in the trace), the readable-id SSE event, and an SSE event with no usable id on an open stream. The stdio test checks that none of four marker strings from the server's line is in the trace.
- Ten u12 scenarios for refused lines and seven trace-wrapper controls in `bridge.test.ts`. Three are about the scope: a slow call, and a second call whose SSE stream names ids 1 to 12 (the slow call must return its result); a slow call beside a call whose stream carries an unreadable event with no id (the slow call must return its result, and only the other call ends by its grace, with its stream closed); and, as a guard, two stdio calls that both end by the grace after one bad line. The two controls are a scoped line that gives a grace to its call and one that gives a grace to another call, which the model rejects.
- Planted-bug check on the code: 20 plants, each in a scratch copy of `src/mcp` and each caught by named tests. The newest are: a line on one stream gives a grace to every call (4 tests fail), and the server drops the stream a bad SSE event came on (1 test fails). Earlier ones include: progress leaves the line's timer armed (a new grace appends a timer without dropping the stale one), a request that ends leaves it, the timer goes while another call still holds the line, and the server does not drop the timer the table says is stale.
- Planted-bug check on the model: 22 planted bugs, all caught; the scope bug is caught by `ScopedGrantsOnlyItsCall`. With that bug planted in a copy of the model, the old `run.py check` passes and the new one fails on `Request.scoped` (TLC exit 12), so CI would now catch it. `run.py check` as CI runs it (one worker, 512 MB heap): 504 s and 538 s before, 536 s after, on an 8-CPU Linux x86_64 machine. The `Request` smoke run alone varied from 70 s to 81 s between rounds, so the added run, 7.3 s over 51,516 states, is inside the noise. Peak memory was 654, 666 and 675 MiB (JVM included), which is noise too.
- Shard weights: `mcp-legacy-remote.test.ts` goes from 122 to 158 for the new test, which waits 36 seconds. `ci-shards.test.ts` passes.

Each test was written first and recorded failing on the code it guards against:

- The timer tests (three Table tests, the stress test and the server test) failed because the refused timer stayed armed after progress.
- The scope tests failed with the scope ignored, which is what the code did before: four Table and server tests (the scope, the no-normal-request case, the thousand rounds on a stream and on a connection, and the server test). With only the server dropping the stream, the server test fails.
- `u12-refused-http-sse-no-id-other-stream` failed on a checkout of the previous head with the new scenario file: the slow call ended early (`h.called.1.result` not met). The stdio guard `u12-refused-grace-every-waiting-call` passes there.
- The new E2E test fails on the previous head's binary: the call that should not be touched ends as malformed at 30 seconds (`slow exit=1`, "the server's answer was malformed").
- The trace assertions failed because no `MCP call ended` line existed for an unreadable body.

## Where each check ran

- macOS arm64, API keys unset, on the merged tree: the whole `src/mcp/mcp.zig` root (272 tests, with the Table, stress, server and `http.zig` tests), the fuzz replays of `mcp_request_grace` and `mcp_challenge` (25 tests each over the saved inputs), `zig fmt --check src/`, `scripts/check-public-surface.sh` and `ci-shards.test.ts` (11 pass).
- macOS arm64, API keys unset, a ReleaseSafe build of this tree: `mcp-stdio.test.ts` (118 pass), `mcp-legacy-remote.test.ts` (34 pass, with the new two-stream test), `mcp-http.test.ts` (32 pass).
- Linux x86_64, on the merged tree: `tests/tla/mcp/check.sh` whole (exit 0: 15 runs pass, `Request` over 415,056 states and `Request.scoped` over 51,516, 180 planted bugs caught, the findings config is violated as required), `python3 tests/tla/mcp/run.py check` and `tests/tla/mcp_host/check.sh` as CI runs them, every MCP driver scenario, and the `mcp_host` drivers (52 pass, 0 fail; 12 of their 64 tests skip themselves).
- Not rerun for this change: the ThreadSanitizer run and the full `zig build test`. The earlier ThreadSanitizer run (two refused-line stdio tests on a `-Dsanitize-thread` build) was for the trace line, which this change does not touch. CI runs the full suite.

## Notes for the merge

- **`tests/tla/mcp/check.sh`:** I add a `tlc_verdicts` block with the `Request` findings. #1914, #1953 and #1989 add blocks to the same file, so whichever lands second merges them into one block.
- **Near other PRs:** #1815 edits `server.zig` at line 138 (my `called` field is at 130) and `wire_tests.zig` at 258, where #1914 and this change both append. #1753 edits `http.zig` at lines 31 and 491, near the `Ending` enum and the JSON body decode. These are text conflicts only.
- **Shared lists:** `tests/fuzz/targets.json`, `tests/tla/README.md` and `ci-shard-weights.json` are append-only lists that many open PRs touch.

## Not changed here

- **ACP:** my first measurements said ACP never ends such a call. That was wrong. ACP ends an MCP call exactly as `fx ask` does (a 3 s timeout ended it at 3.7 s in both, and a supplied server at the 300 s default ended at 300.7 s with the same words). The ACP test client lost the message that came after a timed-out read, so my probe saw no result. The fix is test-only and is its own change, #2018.
- **A bad `initialize`** still takes about 94 s. `initialize` keeps its start deadline.
- **An id that comes before the unreadable part** could end its call at once, but keeping an id read before the scan failed needs a change in `wire.zig`, where #1953 is open. It follows that PR as its own small change.
- **A stray excerpt** still reaches the model inside `invalid reply (…)`, as before.
- **A string id `"7"`** matches request 7, as before.
- **The timers** keep their defaults (300 s idle, 600 s hard).
- **A slow tool** whose server writes one unreadable line loses its call at 30 seconds unless the server replies or reports progress for that call. I do not know how common this is. Progress for the call's own token avoids it.

## Not verified

- The TUI, and Esc during a graced call.
- A grace over the 2026 era on HTTP. My fixtures speak 2025-06-18.
- The macOS ThreadSanitizer build.
- The 30 second grace through ACP. ACP ends calls at the operation timeout like `fx ask`, but I did not run the grace through it.

## Docs

The fx.sh MCP protocol page describes the timers (`operation_timeout_ms`), so vercel-labs/fx-web#324, a draft that should merge after this PR, describes the rule there: what a line with no readable request id does over stdio and over Streamable HTTP, and the words a call ends with.

title: Remove compiled Python caches from the PGSO scripts
body:
- The PGSO size ceiling change committed 29 `__pycache__` files under `scripts/` and `scripts/pgso/`.
- The compiled files hold a local home path, so `Audit public surface` fails on `main` and `Build & Test` fails with it.
- This removes them. `sh scripts/check-public-surface.sh` passes.

title: Limit how fast the doctor process-group test starts processes
body:
## Summary

- The test "stopping a check that keeps starting processes in groups of their own leaves none of them" started processes as fast as the machine allowed. A slow stop let thousands start, and their load slowed the stop and the exit of what it killed even more, so the final per-pid check (1 s each) failed. On a 16 GB sandbox the processes could also use all the memory and end the run, which the review logs show as "failed without output" or a crash.
- The forker now starts one process about every millisecond, and the check that a first process started comes after the stop, so a test that fails there does not leave the forker running.
- Each perl child ignores SIGHUP before it moves to a group of its own. Without that, the kernel hangs up a stopped process in a group that its parent's death orphans, and that did the work of the kill of what a check started outside its group. With the first version of this change (a 5 ms pause, no ignore), removing that kill from the stop path was not caught, and neither was removing the stop-first step and second listing: a process started just before the stop was still in the forker's group when the group kill came.
- fx itself does not change. Only the test in `src/core/cli/doctor_probes.zig` changed. In every failing run of the original test every stop landed and the kill reached each process; the survivor was gone by the time `ps` ran.

## Checks

All runs were in a fresh sandbox, Debug unless noted, with free memory and load logged every 0.4 s and a 60 s limit on each run. The branch is behind `main`, which the build tooling cannot record, so the runs used a worktree on a newer `main` with this file applied. `src/core/cli/doctor_probes.zig` and `src/core/execution/process_tree.zig` are the same on both. The same checks also passed on this branch's own tree before the commit.

Unchanged stop path:

- The exact `zig build test-focus` step passed 30 of 30 repeats; the test binary passed 200 of 200 runs, and 60 of 60 runs with eight busy loops beside it. A ReleaseSafe series with the same load passed 60 of 60.
- Free memory stayed above 16,000 MB and the load average stayed under 3.3. At most 28 processes started before a stop.
- `tests/e2e/doctor.test.ts` on the built binary passed (31 tests).

Planted changes to the stop path, which the test must fail on:

| Planted change | First version (5 ms, no SIGHUP ignore) | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Stop-first step and second listing removed | caught 1 of 30 runs | caught 28 of 30 runs (28 of 30 again in a second series) |
| Kill outside the group removed | caught 0 of 10 runs | caught 10 of 10 runs (10 of 10 again) |
| No stop and no kill outside the group (group kill only) | caught 10 of 10 | caught 10 of 10 |
| No group kill | hangs, ended by the limit, 4 of 4 | hangs, ended by the limit, 3 of 3 |

A short sandbox script confirms the cause: a child that was stopped in a group of its own is gone after its parent dies, and one that ignores SIGHUP is still there.

## For review

- The stop-first change is caught in most runs, not every run, and the rate depends on timing: 28 of 30 and 29 of 30 here, 7 of 10 in the ship gate's own harness, and 6 of 20 in an instrumented run of mine that added listing and printing around the stop.
- A pause of 1 ms allows more processes than 5 ms. With the group kill removed (a planted change), the forkers that nothing killed started 18,056 processes in three hung runs and free memory fell to 5,733 MB. That needs a broken group kill and a hung test, and the limit ended each run.
- The test "a check killed at the deadline takes with it what it started in a group of its own" has the same blind spot: with the kill outside the group removed, it passed 8 of 8 runs. I did not change it here.

title: Open Ctrl+O without reading the session log
body:
## Summary

- Ctrl+O opens at once after a compaction, including the first open after a resume and the first open after a turn ends. Before, each of those opens waited while fx replayed the older compaction cycle from the session log on the main thread: 0.4 to 0.8 s on a 62 MB session log whose older cycle has 1,076 entries, measured on a macOS ReleaseFast build as the time from `open_request` to `depth_transition` in the `full_transcript` trace scope. With this change the same opens take 0 to 4 ms.
- Between turns, a background thread reads the older compaction cycle that the newest Ctrl+O page joins, and the main thread replays it a few turns at a time, so typing and painting keep running while it loads.
- While Ctrl+O is closed, fx keeps only the part of that cycle the newest page shows, at most one page of 256 entries, instead of dropping it on close and reading it again on the next open.
- Scrolling above the part that was kept loads the whole cycle and lands on the same entry.
- A compaction, a resume, a clear, or the turn end that drops the previous cycle discards the kept part, and a background read that finishes after one of those is ignored.
- Each agent keeps its own older cycle, so switching agents never shows another agent's history in Ctrl+O.

title: Free a closing owner's slots only after every slot thread has ended
body:
## Summary

- `Owner.deinit` freed each subagent slot as soon as its own thread was joined, but left the freed slot in the owner's list. A slot's thread ends its work in the host's end hook, which walks that list (`Owner.markEnding` compares each slot's `child_id`). With two subagents working, the second slot's thread read the first slot's freed memory when its work ended.
- On Linux, in a Debug build of `main` at `b2bf785e0`, the process ended with `SIGSEGV` (read from its `close` event) in each run where the second subagent ended after the first slot was freed: ACP `session/close`, `session/new`, `session/load`, a reload of the active session, and `fx ask` ended with SIGINT.
- Now `deinit` joins every slot's thread first and frees the slots after that.

## How

`Owner.deinit` cancels every slot under the lock, then:

1. `joinSlot` joins each slot's thread. Every slot stays in `self.slots` and alive, with `closed`, `shutdown` and `cancel` set, so a thread that is still ending its work walks a list of live slots. Every walker takes `self.mutex`, as before.
2. `destroySlot` then frees each slot. No slot thread runs any more.

`destroySlot` joins through `joinSlot`, which joins once and clears `slot.thread` under the lock. Its other callers are unchanged: `start`, `wait` and `cancelAndJoin` take the slot out of `self.slots` under the lock before they free it, so no walker can reach it.

The slots stay listed during the joins, and are not unlinked first, because a slot's own thread must still find its slot in `markEnding` while it ends.

Other places that free or join a slot, read in the code:

| Place | Result |
|---|---|
| `Owner.start`, `Owner.wait`, `Owner.cancelAndJoin` | Safe: they remove the slot under the lock first. |
| `closeTree`, `closeChild`, `stop`, `cancel`, `closeByUser` | Safe: they set flags and free no slot. |
| `Runtime.deinit` | Calls `Owner.deinit` first, then frees its own lists. Covered. |
| ACP `session/close`, `session/new`, `session/load` of the active session, `session/load` under another cwd | Same fault on `main`. Covered. Run: the entry-point probes under Testing. |
| `session/load` of another id | Covered. Run: the E2E tests under Testing. |
| `fx ask` ended with SIGINT while two subagents work | Same fault on `main`. Covered. Run: the entry-point probes under Testing. |
| The interactive app's instance close and quit | Same `Runtime.deinit`, so covered. Run in tmux with two hosted subagents inside commands, on Linux (Debug): `/exit` on `main` at `b2bf785e0` ended with exit status 139 in 2 of 44 tries and with 0 in 42; with this change (`73d554c1c`) it ended with 0 in 44 of 44. The cause of the two failures on `main` was not traced. Instance close did not fail on either side in 14 tries. |
| The app's `stopSet` | Cancels every agent, joins them one at a time, and frees only afterwards (`dropSet`). Same order as this fix. Read, not run. |

## Testing

- `closing the owner frees no slot that another slot's thread can still reach` in `managed_owner.zig`. Two slots with threads, an allocator that notes each freed slot, and a hold: the second slot's work ends only after the first slot is freed, or after 50 ms, which is how long it waits on a fixed owner because that owner frees nothing before the second thread ends. It then counts the freed slots the owner still lists. The test calls `io_mod.getIo()` before it starts threads, so the process's `Io` is built by one thread: the lazy setup in `core.shared.net_connect.wrap` takes no lock, and ThreadSanitizer reports it when two threads make the first call.
  - On `main` at `b2bf785e0` with only this test added, it fails with `expected 0, found 1` in 20 of 20 runs on Linux x86_64, and in 100 of 100 runs of a macOS arm64 binary built from this branch with the join loop in `deinit` removed.
  - With this change (`73d554c1c`) it passes 100 of 100 on Linux and 100 of 100 on macOS arm64.
  - How it was built and run: a local `build.zig` edit, not in this PR, adds a test filter (`zig build test-one -Dtest-filter=<name>`), and the built test binary runs in a loop with a different seed each time. The macOS binaries were cross-built in the Linux sandbox with `-Dtarget=aarch64-macos` and a second local step that installs the test binary, then run on a Mac (arm64, Darwin).
  - Under ThreadSanitizer (`-Doptimize=ReleaseSafe -Dsanitize-thread=true`, same filtered build) it passes 20 of 20 runs with no report.
- `ACP session/new`, `session/load` and `session/close` away from two subagents inside shell commands, in `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts`. The subagents start in two model turns, so they are listed in that order. The first runs `touch f1; sleep 30`. The second runs `trap '' TERM; touch f2; sleep 30`, so it ends only after its command's grace period, which is after the first slot is freed. The test waits for both files, switches away, and checks that the process answers and that two `child_finished` records exist.
  - On `main` at `b2bf785e0` with only this test added, each of the three fails in 20 of 20 runs on Linux (Debug), with `signal=SIGSEGV` read from the process's `close` event. A local copy of the test that also prints the signal produced those runs; the committed test prints `code=null` when the process dies.
  - With this change (`73d554c1c`) each passes in 20 of 20 runs.
  - On the macOS binary (built with `fx-cloud macos-build`, run on a Mac with `FX_SOUND=0`) each passes in 20 of 20 runs both without and with this change. A read of freed memory does not fault there in these runs, so this test can fail on Linux only. The unit test fails on both platforms.
- Entry-point probes, run from a local script that is not in the repository, on Linux (Debug): two subagents inside commands as in the E2E, then ACP `session/close`, `session/new`, `session/load` of the active session, `session/load` of the active session under another cwd, and `fx ask` with SIGINT sent. On `main` at `b2bf785e0` the process ended with `SIGSEGV` (read from its `close` event) in 6 of 6 runs for each of the five. With this change (`73d554c1c`) the four ACP requests were answered in 6 of 6 runs each, and `fx ask` ended with `signal=SIGINT`, after its cleanup, in 6 of 6.
- `core.subagent` (169 tests) passes, and 30 runs of the built `core.subagent` test binary pass. Both use the local filtered build described above.
- `zig fmt --check src/`, `python3 -m scripts.check_cli_shape` and `scripts/check-public-surface.sh` pass on this branch merged with `main` at `6ddd5790a`.

## Not in this change

- A test for the interactive app's instance close and quit, which reach the same `Owner.deinit`.
- ACP stdin close with two working subagents. #2005 adds the host stop at stdin close, with its own test.
- `Owner.deinit` still reads `self.slots` outside the lock, and `cancelAndJoin` has no `closed` guard as `wait` has. Both rely on the caller having drained tool callers first, as before.

title: Start the next turn after the previous one is saved
body:
## Summary

- A subagent's report or message that arrives while the app still holds an agent's finished turn now starts that agent's next turn with that turn in its history. Before, with a subagent's approval or question open when main's turn ended, that one request carried only the report: the user's first prompt and the turn's tool calls were missing.
- Only that one request ran without the turn. The saved session kept it: the turn was written again right after, so later requests and `fx -c` have it. The log held two turns marked superseded, which replay drops, and the trace had `dropped=stale_turn`. Neither happens now.
- A turn that the worker starts on its own, from mail queued while the previous turn ended, no longer streams into the session before that turn is saved. The two `/fork forks without the subagents` tests in `tests/e2e/sessions.test.ts` failed on this in 12 of 100 runs on Linux.
- The screen is unchanged with the prompt open: the finished turn once, the prompt, and the report turn's answer after the prompt closes.
- A report that waits for its agent's finished turn is posted on a later loop pass than before, and shows up then. If the session closes or switches while it waits (`/new`, `/clear`, `/fork`, `/resume`, closing an instance), or fx quits, the report is not posted into the new session. It stays owed in the session it came from and is posted when that session is opened again. A report for a hidden agent also waits while a scrollback handoff is pending, and is posted once it ends.

## How

- `WorkerRuntime.holds_start_for_finish`, set by the app on each agent worker thread it starts (main, instances, subagents), makes a turn's finish event hold queued work. `finish_unapplied` is set under the lock that queues the event, so the worker cannot start the next turn between the two. `waitAndTakeNextPrompt`, `waitAndTakeNextWork`, `tryTakeNextPrompt` and `tryTakeNextWork` start nothing until `finishApplied`. `fx ask`, ACP and libfx never set the flag and start work as before. A slow or blocked UI thread now also delays every agent's next turn after a finish, since the loop's tick releases the hold. In practice that is one loop pass.
- `settleHeldFinish` runs after each agent's tick, in that agent's own context. It calls `finishApplied` once the finish event is applied and the pacer holds no finished turn. An open prompt pauses the pacer, so when queued work waits behind a turn the pacer holds, it flushes the pacer at the boundary that the next turn's own start flushes at.
- `settleBeforeMail` runs before `postAgentMessage` builds the prompt. It applies the target agent's pending events and settles its held turn, in the target's own context, on screen or hidden. If the finish event is still queued after that drain, the post waits for the next pass, so the prompt always takes a history that has the turn. The drain keeps its 32 ms budget, so the screen keeps answering, and nothing loops on the loop thread: a stopping agent's tick never drains, and a cancelled turn's tool closure can keep the first event back until the worker pushes the terminal.
- A post that waits is kept by `deliverReports` and offered again on each pass. While the agent's finish event is still queued, it waits, and the loop's own tick applies the events; the retry does not tick the agent again. Once the event is applied, the offer settles a finished turn that the agent's pacer keeps behind an open prompt, as a first offer does, so the post does not wait for the prompt. Posts behind it for the same agent wait with it, in order; other agents' posts go on. A message keeps its place in its agent's queue and the `started_by` that its first offer read, so it queues as an immediate message does. An agent that is stopping holds nothing: a post for it fails as it did before.
- A held post ends in one of four ways. It is delivered. Its agent is gone, and the next pass drops it. Its host closes, and `dropReportsOf` drops it after the host's threads are joined, because a post holds the host's pointer and a host made next can take the address. Or fx quits, and `closeHandoffs` drops it. Each wait and each drop writes one trace line naming the receiver, the kind of mail and the reason, and a dropped message gives back its place. A dropped report is still owed in the parent's log: a `child_report` item marks a report taken, and it is written with the turn that carries the report, not when the post is handed over. The next open of the session posts it.
- A post waits only while its agent's last turn has ended and its finish is not applied, so that agent is running no tool. No `wait` or `status` call of its own can see the report as missing or as sent. The first call in the report's turn finds it queued. The footer stops counting a subagent once its finished turn is applied, as before.
- A hidden agent is visited while its worker holds work, so the hold always ends. While a scrollback handoff is pending no hidden agent is visited, because a visit swaps its transcript onto the screen and the handoff does not allow that: the loop's tick leaves a hidden agent's events for a later pass, so its finish stays queued and its start stays held, and both go on once the handoff ends. `deliverReports` also holds mail for a hidden agent through a pending handoff (`reason=scrollback_handoff_pending` in the trace), because the offer's settle visits the agent, and offers it on the first pass after. The agent on screen is not held: its mail goes at once, and the turn it starts makes the handoff yield (`agent_busy`). The handoff reads only the agent on screen, never a hidden agent or a held post, so nothing waits on them. A held post for a subagent that its parent closed waits with the drop that the handoff defers, and goes with its host when that drop runs. Without the hold the offer reaches the assertion in `swapSlot` (`src/ui/transcript/runtime.zig:5058`) that no handoff is pending. The test `a report for a hidden agent waits while a scrollback handoff is pending, and the agent on screen's goes` pins it.
- `src/main.zig` takes two call lines, one in each place, and the tests of that wiring, with a fixture for an app whose subagents take mail, a real subagent host, and a trace reader. `app_worker_runtime.drain_budget_for_tests_ns` lets a test narrow the drain budget; a build that is not a test ignores it.
- Paths that start a turn while the app holds the previous one: a report or message after the end (history and session), mail queued before the end that the worker starts on its own (session), mail posted while the app has not applied an agent's finish event (history, the post waits), a queued prompt or a compaction (their start waits for the finish).

## Testing

- `3fd4905af` (`main`), Debug, Linux x86_64: `cd tests/e2e && FX_SOUND=0 bun test tui-host-switch.test.ts -t "a report that starts main"`. The approval and question tests fail in 5 of 5 rounds, because the report turn's request has no first prompt. The no-prompt test passes in 5 of 5. On the macOS arm64 binary of `main`, 3 rounds give the same.
- `fbbb66389`, same command: 60 of 60 pass in 20 rounds on Linux, and 30 of 30 in 10 rounds on the macOS arm64 binary (`fx-cloud macos-build`, then `FXC_LOCAL=1 FX_SOUND=0`, one run at a time). On the macOS binary of the head before it, `686b7fa55`, one of two 10-round runs gave 29 of 30. The one failure was the question test, where the test's fake gateway closed every connection: all 8 requests of the app in 30 s ended in `HttpConnectionClosing`, the first turn never got a response, and no turn, hold or report was reached. The other 10 rounds gave 30 of 30.
- Each test checks that the report turn's request has the first prompt and the turn's tool calls, that the screen shows the finished turn once while the prompt is open and every turn once at the end, that the trace has no `dropped=stale_turn`, and that the session log has no superseded turn and has the first turn committed. The tests wait for the prompt on the screen and for `processing_finished` of main's first turn in the trace, and use no sleep.
- 36 unit tests: the 23 that this change adds and the 13 that the scrollback handoff change added in `src/main.zig` and `src/ui/resize_tests.zig`. Their names select 63 tests. They run as a loop over the built unit test binary on `fbbb66389`. `build.zig` has no `test-one` step, so the binary comes from a local edit that is not part of this change: a `test-filter` option passed as the `.filters` of `exe_tests`, and a `test-one` step that runs `exe_tests`, used as `zig build test-one -Dtest-filter="<name>" ... --summary all` with the 36 names: 100 of 100 runs in sequence and 100 of 100 in 8-way parallel, in Debug and in ReleaseSafe.
- Each held-post test fails without the piece it pins. `mail posted while the finished turn waits behind the drain budget is not queued without that turn` fails against `889e6dccb` with this change's test seam and the drain budget at zero: the post succeeds and queues the report with no history, where it must wait. On `fbbb66389`, with one piece broken at a time: with a held post held again whenever its finish is unapplied, as at `33967fa53`, `a held report is offered again once the loop applied its finish, though an open prompt keeps the turn in the pacer` and `a held report released after the pacer kept the finished turn goes before the reports behind it` fail. With no hold for a hidden agent's mail during a handoff, the three tests of a pending handoff abort on the assertion in `swapSlot`. With no purge in `disableSubagentHost`, `closing an agent's session closes its host and drops the reports held for it` and `a subagent its parent closes during a pending handoff keeps its held reports until the handoff ends, then drops them` fail. With a second give-back of a message's place, `mail for an agent that is stopping is not held, and a message gives back its place once` fails.
- The tests of a held post cover each way it ends (delivered in order with another agent's post going on, its agent gone, its host closing, a subagent closed by its parent during a handoff, fx quitting, with and without a handoff pending), a stopping agent, and a message's place and `started_by`. They read the trace for one `report held` line per post and the drop lines. The paused pacer is the loop's own tick with an API key entry open.
- A throwaway probe on the Linux binary of `fbbb66389` (Debug), with main's last step a burst of 60,000 text deltas, so that the finish waits behind the drain and the report is held: `/clear` in that window, 3 of 3 runs. Each run dropped the report (`reason=host_closed held=true`), the new session got no report, and `--resume` of the old session posted it once, with the first prompt and the helper's call in its history. In 3 runs that only looked at the screen, the footer read `Generating` and the agent list showed main and the helper as idle, and the report was posted 6.7 to 7.2 s later.
- ThreadSanitizer (`zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe -Dsanitize-thread=true`) on `fbbb66389`: the unit tests, 20 runs, 0 reports; the same E2E tests, 60 rounds, 180 of 180 pass, with 3 reports. All three are one race between `enableSubagentHostV2`, which writes a new subagent's session fields on the loop (`app_session_runtime.zig:4837`), and `childRole`, which reads every subagent's host on a slot thread (`app_agent_runtime.zig:1539`). Neither function is in this change. The same E2E tests on `3fd4905af` give 7 reports in 180 flows, at the same two sites, so the race is not new and is not fixed here. No report names code this change adds.
- `bun test sessions.test.ts -t <name>` on Linux, Debug. On `main`: `forks without the subagents when the answer is n` failed 8 of 60 runs, `... is Esc` 4 of 40, `asks nothing when no subagent existed at the fork point` 0 of 40. On `fbbb66389`: 0 of 100 runs of each of the three. The two failures traced on `main` both show two superseded turns (`streamed=3 final=2`, then `streamed=3 final=4`) and two reports posted within 19 ms.
- A throwaway probe with the user on a subagent's screen, so main is hidden: 2 of 40 report requests on `main` lacked the first prompt (30 runs with the report released with main's last reply, 10 with a subagent's approval open), and 0 of 40 on `fbbb66389`.

## Not in this change

- A report or message posted between the worker's history publication and its finish event is not covered: the publication is at `finalization.zig:277`, and `finalization.finish` pushes the finish event last, after it releases the turn's terminal leases and pushes the turn-finished event. Its prompt would take the app's history before the finish event exists. No run reached it: 40 probe runs and 300 `/fork` runs on `fbbb66389`. Closing it takes a hold that begins when steering closes and a delivery that waits for it, which is a separate change.
- A queued prompt and a compaction (`/compact`) take their history when they are queued. The hold covers their start. One queued while the finish event still waits behind the drain budget takes the old history, as on `main`. No E2E test drives one while a turn is held; the unit tests `a finished turn holds queued work until the host applies it` and `a finished turn holds a queued compaction until the host applies it` pin the hold.
- A finish kept back behind a cancelled tool's closure holds the agent's next turn until the closure arrives, up to the 500 ms stop grace. No run or test drives it.
- An open prompt pauses only the pacer of the agent that shows it, so a hidden main is not held for long: no stale turn in 13 runs on `main` with a subagent's approval open. No E2E test drives a hidden main; the unit tests drive hidden subagents.
- No E2E test drives `/fork` or `/resume` with a report held: in the probe runs the screen still showed the turn as running while the report was held, and neither command opened its picker. A session closed by `/new`, `/clear`, `/fork`, `/resume` or by closing an instance ends in `closeV2Session`, which calls `disableSubagentHost` before the session closes. `/clear` ran on the binary, and the two tests named above drive that close.
- A pending handoff is not driven on the binary: it could not be kept pending there. The tests above drive it, and the hold, the yield to a busy agent and the drop at a quit are pinned by them.

title: Keep the recording fault test's profile out of Linux PGSO training
body:
- The recording fault test in `tui-startup.test.ts` runs fx under `ulimit -f 0`, which leaves an instrumented build's profile empty. It unset `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` to keep that profile out of training.
- The Linux instrumented build has a default profile path inside the training folder (`opt -profile-file=.../profiles/raw/train-%m-%p-%c.profraw`), so unsetting the variable sent the empty profile there. The `e2e-tui-startup` training scenario failed with `produced no raw profile` on Linux arm64 and Linux x86_64, which blocks the v0.0.17 release.
- The script now sets `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` to a file in the test's own folder, which overrides the default on every platform. Only the test changed.

`FX_SOUND=0 bun test tui-startup.test.ts -t "a debug recording that cannot start says why"` passes.

title: Stop test clients dropping the line that follows a timed-out read
body:
## Summary

Five test clients keep the line that follows a read that timed out; four of them lost it. Each client queued a waiter for its next line and a timer that rejects the read, but the timer never took the waiter off the list. The next line from `fx acp` went to that dead waiter and was dropped, which looks like a reply fx never sent. One shared `LineQueue` now keeps the list, and a read that times out removes itself from it. The fifth client, in `ultrafast-fake-gateway.test.ts`, already did that, and now uses the same helper. No file under `src/` changes.

This is how a probe in #2010's investigation saw "no result" for an MCP call through ACP: the call ended at its operation timeout, the prompt response came, and the client dropped it. #2010's description said ACP never ends such a call; that was wrong and is corrected there.

## What was wrong

`readLine` in `tests/e2e/acp.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/tui-command-permissions.test.ts`, `tests/e2e/web-fetch-fake-network.test.ts` and `tests/e2e/web-search-fake-gateway.test.ts` (the same code in each):

- A read with no queued line pushed a waiter and set a timer. The timer rejected the read and left the waiter in the list.
- The next line went to the first waiter, which was already rejected, so it was lost. Each further timeout left one more dead waiter, so each took one more line.
- `readResponse` and `readUntilResponses` in `acp.test.ts` retry every 3 seconds on that timeout, so after 3 seconds of quiet they could lose the reply they were waiting for. A probe that did the same with `readLine(30_000)` got no answer at 423.7 s for a call that ended at 300.7 s; one patient read got it.
- `ultrafast-fake-gateway.test.ts` already removed its waiter on a timeout. These four did not.

## What changed

- `tests/e2e/line-queue.ts` holds the queue and the waiting reads. `next(timeoutMs, onTimeout)` takes a queued line at once, or waits for one; on a timeout it takes its own read off the list before it rejects. A line that arrives at the instant of the timeout goes to the queue.
- The four clients use it, and so does the one in `ultrafast-fake-gateway.test.ts`, which had its own copy that was right. Each keeps its own errors (`AcpReadTimeoutError` in `acp.test.ts`, `Error("ACP read timeout")` in the others; the `ultrafast` one also keeps "ACP exited before a response": after its process has closed, no line is still to come, so a read takes a queued line or ends at once). I used one helper and not four inline fixes because the four classes carry the same code and `tests/e2e/` already keeps shared helpers as `.ts` files beside the tests.
- The four loops in `acp.test.ts` that catch the timeout and go on (`readResponse`, `readUntilResponses`, and the two that `break`) still mean what their tests say. The `break` loops, in the tests "session cancellation interrupts a pending MCP elicitation" and "ACP cancellation ends the wait for subagent reports, and a late report follows the next prompt", end the read after the timeout, so they never read again. The retry loops can only get more messages than before, never fewer. The whole file passes with the fix.

## Tests

- Fail first, on today's reader: a read that times out and then a line that must reach the next read, in each of the four files (the line was lost); two timeouts in a row; a retry loop on a short timeout. Edge tests that must keep passing: queued lines in order, and a read that gets its line in time leaves no timer that takes a later one. These use a stand-in process, so no fx runs.
- Guards that ACP ends MCP calls as `fx ask` does, with a profile server (the session opts in with `_meta.fx.profileMcpServers: true`) and a 3 second `operation_timeout_ms`, with a fake gateway and no model call. They pass on today's code and pin it:
  - a call the server never answers, a line fx cannot read, a `tools/list` that is never answered and an `initialize` that is never answered each end in the same words through ACP and through `fx ask`, to the byte (about 16 s, the four cases run at once). The test is named for that ("ACP gives the model the same words as fx ask, to the byte, when an MCP server never answers …"). A turn that makes fewer than three model requests now ends the ACP side with no words, like the `fx ask` side, and the test says so by what it expected; before, it threw on `gateway.requests[2]`;
  - `session/cancel` and `session/close` end a waiting call at once (the test allows 10 s) and the server's wire log holds `notifications/cancelled` for that call.
- The existing test "ACP includes profile MCP servers only when the session opts in" already pins that a profile server loads only with the opt-in.
- Two new modes in `fixtures/mcp-modern-stdio.mjs`, `stall_list` and `unreadable_operation`, which only a test that sets `FX_MCP_MODE` reaches.
- `ci-shard-weights.json`: `acp.test.ts` 128 to 144. The weights are relative run times, not seconds, and +16 is the measured cost of the new tests: the parity guard takes about 16 s, and nothing else in them is slow.

## Where the checks ran

- Linux x86_64, keys unset, `FX_SOUND=0`, against a ReleaseSafe `fx` built in the same run, on the head with the changes below, whole files:
  - `acp.test.ts`: 292 pass, 14 skip, 0 fail
  - `ultrafast-fake-gateway.test.ts`: 25 pass
  - `web-fetch-fake-network.test.ts`: 9 pass
  - `web-search-fake-gateway.test.ts`: 19 pass
  - `tui-command-permissions.test.ts`: 64 pass (including its `/sound on` test, which does not run on a Mac)
- The parity test's guard, on one test with a plant that gives the fake gateway a one-reply script, so the turn makes one model request. Before the guard, the ACP side threw `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'gateway.requests[2].body')`. After it, the test fails on its own check that the text holds the scenario's words. Without the plant the test passes (15.3 s).
- The reader tests of the four clients failed first on the old reader in every file, and pass on this one. That was shown before this round, and the review reproduced it on Linux x86_64. The whole-file runs above cover the tests again. The `ultrafast` client behaves as before in every case a test reaches, so it has no fail-first of its own. One case changes: when the process closes while a read waits, the read now ends with "ACP exited before a response", where it ended with "ACP read timeout" before.
- `ci-shards.test.ts` was not rerun: no weight changed in this round.
- CI runs the E2E shards on Linux x86_64 and the macOS arm64 E2E jobs.

## Notes for the merge

- Many open PRs touch `acp.test.ts`. Two have hunks near the lines this changes: #1722 (`:767-778` and `:786-793`, the lines of `readLine`, and a third hunk at its base line 660, `@@ -660,7 +674,15 @@`, the stdout `push` lines that this change rewrites) and #1770 (`:726-732`). The second of these PRs to land merges `main` and keeps both sides.
- `main` moved while this was open, and the merge in this branch had one conflict, in `tui-command-permissions.test.ts`: the two imports (`EventEmitter` from `node:events` here, `processAlive` there). Both are kept.
- `tui-command-permissions.test.ts`, `web-fetch-fake-network.test.ts` and `web-search-fake-gateway.test.ts` change only the field, `push` and `next` lines of the client and add one test at the end.

## Not changed here

- The TLA+ driver clients in `tests/tla/drivers/` have the same shape, but each throws on its first timeout and ends, so none reads a line after it.
- An ACP call that waits through an elicitation round has its own deadline (`src/acp/prompt.zig`). I did not run it.

## Docs

None. The ACP page says that profile servers need `_meta.fx.profileMcpServers: true` and that cancellation stops pending MCP input requests, and the MCP protocol page describes `operation_timeout_ms` for every client. I read both pages, and nothing in them changes.

title: Bug: fx ignores SSL_CERT_FILE, so it can't reach a model behind a TLS-inspecting proxy
body:
### Issue details

## Environment

- fx 0.0.16 (release, `481104fdbc24`) and a build of `main` at `b6b2835` (reports 0.0.17)
- Linux arm64, Debian trixie container
- Provider: a custom `openai-chat-completions` connection
- The container's outbound HTTPS goes through a proxy that re-signs TLS with a private CA

We hit this running fx in Spacesheep's cloud sandboxes, where model credentials are added outside the container by such a proxy.

## What happens

fx trusts only the certificates in the operating system's store. It does not read `SSL_CERT_FILE`, so a CA supplied the usual way is ignored and every model request fails the TLS handshake.

On 0.0.16 the request stops with:

```text
[notice] ⚠ Network interrupted · TlsInitializationFailed · retrying request in 1s
[notice] ⚠ Network interrupted · TlsInitializationFailed · kept failing at the same point · stopped
```

On `main` it keeps retrying (I stopped it after 40 seconds), and the message no longer names TLS:

```text
[notice] Connection lost · next try in 1s · attempt 1
[notice] Connection lost · retrying · attempt 2
[notice] Connection lost · next try in 2s · attempt 2
…
```

`curl` in the same container, with the same variable, connects.

Adding the CA to the system store (`/usr/local/share/ca-certificates` + `update-ca-certificates`) makes fx work, so the certificate itself is fine.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a private CA and a server certificate for `api.openai.com` signed by it.
2. In a Linux container, map `api.openai.com` to `127.0.0.1` and serve HTTPS on port 443 with that certificate. Any handler that answers `POST /v1/chat/completions` with a streamed completion will do.
3. Point fx at it in `~/.fx/settings.json`:

   ```json
   {
     "provider": "local",
     "providers": {
       "local": {
         "protocol": "openai-chat-completions",
         "base_url": "https://api.openai.com/v1",
         "auth": { "type": "none" },
         "model_metadata": { "m": { "context_window": 128000, "supports_tool_use": true } }
       }
     },
     "models": { "local": "m" }
   }
   ```

4. Write the system bundle plus the private CA to one file and run:

   ```sh
   cat /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt ca.crt > /root/ca.pem
   SSL_CERT_FILE=/root/ca.pem fx ask --json --no-save "say hi"
   ```

## Expected behavior

fx trusts the CAs in `SSL_CERT_FILE`, as curl, git, Node.js and Python do, and the request succeeds.

## Where it comes from

Every place that loads trust anchors calls `std.crypto.Certificate.Bundle.rescan`, which reads the system store and no environment variable:

- `src/core/shared/http_pool.zig`, `ensureTlsReady`
- `src/tools/web/http_fetch.zig`, `fetchTls`
- each `std.http.Client` created elsewhere (the gateway client, MCP, sign-in, the updater, the permission reviewer), which rescans by itself on its first request

So this affects model requests, MCP servers, sign-in, `web_fetch` and upgrades alike.

## Related

#1493 asks for a supported way to provide trusted certificates when a sandbox blocks the macOS system keychain. Reading `SSL_CERT_FILE` in place of the system store would cover that case too.

I'm glad to send a pull request. Since the bundle is loaded in several modules, tell me whether you'd want one shared loader that every client uses, and whether `SSL_CERT_FILE` should replace the system store (as OpenSSL does) or add to it.

### Trace

Not attached. The steps above reproduce it without a model account.

### Sensitive information

- [x] I reviewed the information above and removed secrets and other sensitive data.

title: Hold many sessions on one fx acp connection
body:
## Summary

- One `fx acp` connection holds many open sessions. `session/new`, `session/load` and `session/resume` leave the sessions already open as they are, instead of closing them and cancelling their turn.
- Turns in different sessions run at the same time, and a prompt in one session never waits for a turn in another.
- Each session works in its own `cwd`: file tools, project instructions, skills and project MCP servers follow that session's folder.
- Each turn's `session/update` notifications and requests to the client carry that turn's own `sessionId`.
- `session/cancel` and `session/close` stop only the session they name, and `$/cancel_request` only the prompt it names. Other sessions' turns, permission requests and MCP servers keep running.
- `session/list` answers during a turn. `session/set_config_option` and a plain `session/prompt` wait only for their own session's turn.
- Loading or resuming a session that is already open reuses it, and its turn and MCP servers keep running. A `cwd` in another workspace fails with `-32602` "Session is open in another workspace", and a changed `systemPrompt` during a turn fails with `-32600`.
- Each session keeps its own provider credential, so a provider switch or a token refresh in one session leaves the others as they were.
- The libfx kernel and the web core still hold one session.

Stacked on #1786.

title: Add a subagent failure test that needs no permissions, and guard the one that does
body:
## Summary

- The test "subagent failure retains its cause after effects and worker cleanup" made the child's blobs folder read-only to force a write failure. Root, and any user that holds `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`, writes into a read-only folder, so for them the write succeeded, the child never failed, and the test ran into its 15 s limit. That happens in a sandbox whose user holds every capability, on `main` too. CI passes it because its jobs run as the hosted runner's unprivileged user.
- Two tests now share one body and differ in how they break the child's blobs folder:
  - The read-only folder test is back as it was on `main`, with its `AccessDenied` assertions, so the check that a refused blob write while the child streams a step keeps its cause stays. It skips, with a warning that names the reason, when a write into a read-only folder succeeds for the user running the tests.
  - A new test, "subagent failure keeps its cause when the child's commit fails after effects, whatever the user's permissions", puts a file where the blobs folder must be. That fails the child's commit for every user, and the child reports `SessionCommitFailed`.
- Both check the same things: the effect is written once, the failure arrives as the child's report, the parent's log and the saved history name the cause, and the next message to the same child works. fx itself does not change.
- The skip uses `ignoresFileModes()`, the probe `tui-startup.test.ts` already had. It moves, unchanged, to `tests/e2e/file-modes.ts`, and both tests skip on it. It skips only when the write succeeds, so a write that fails for another reason, such as `ENOSPC`, `EROFS` or `EIO`, cannot hide the restored test.

## Checks

All runs were in a sandbox whose user holds every Linux capability ("kept"), and again as the same user with every capability dropped with `setpriv` ("dropped"), which enforces permissions as a CI runner does.

- On `main`, with the capabilities kept, the test timed out 5 of 5 repeats (`runFx` returned code null after 15 s). With them dropped it passed 5 of 5, so the capabilities are the whole cause.
- Kept: the read-only folder test is skipped on every repeat, with its warning, and the new test passes: 100 of 100 repeats. Dropped: both run and pass: 100 of 100 repeats each. All 30 subagent tests in the file pass when the capabilities are dropped; with them kept 29 pass and the read-only folder test is skipped.
- The `tui-startup` test that uses the probe, "a debug recording in a folder fx cannot write says permission denied", is skipped 5 of 5 with the capabilities kept and passes 5 of 5 with them dropped, as before the move.
- A `bun test` that forces the probe's write to fail shows the difference. With `ENOSPC`, `EROFS`, `EIO` or `EDQUOT` the previous probe in this pull request skipped the restored test, and the shared probe runs it; with `EACCES` or `EPERM` both run it. With a real write the shared probe answers true with the capabilities kept and false with them dropped, and leaves no folder behind.
- With the skip condition removed on the sandbox copy and the capabilities kept, the read-only folder test times out again (2 of 2), so the skip is what avoids it.
- Planted changes to the product, applied to the sandbox copy only:
  - A change that loses the cause (the adapter replacing it with a fixed word, the registry not keeping it, or the report text leaving it out) fails every test that runs: the new test with the capabilities kept (3 of 3), and both tests with them dropped (3 of 3 each).
  - A change that makes `storage.ioFault` report a refused write as `Io` fails the read-only folder test (5 of 5 with the capabilities dropped) and not the new test (5 of 5 pass). Before this change nothing caught it.

## For review

- The new test reaches the failure through the commit, not through the streaming write, so only the read-only folder test covers the streaming-write `AccessDenied` path. For a user that file modes do not hold back, that path has no E2E check; the warning says so.
- The same pattern is in 10 other files (`chmodSync` to 0 or a read-only mode), for example the session-recovery "committed-history corruption (unreadable)" test and `tests/tla/drivers/session_manager/prompt-images.test.ts`. I did not change them here.
- On the hosted macOS runner, `sessions.test.ts` "/fork forks without the subagents when the answer is n" and "... Esc" sometimes fail on the first attempt, with a `superseded` item in a session log (`saved-sessions.ts:61`), and pass on the file's retry. The same failure shows in macOS runs of other branches and in this branch's earlier commits, `main` passed in the one run I looked at, and neither test failed in 10 runs on a Mac. This pull request changes no product code and does not touch `sessions.test.ts`.

title: Retry MCP sign-outs that the server did not confirm
body:
## Summary

- `fx mcp logout` and the TUI's MCP logout keep a login's tokens when its server refuses the revocation, doesn't answer in time, or can't be reached, and say that fx will try again later.
- A sign-out that its server confirms leaves nothing kept.
- The next `fx mcp login` that signs in and every `fx mcp logout` send the kept revocations again, and forget each one the server confirms.
- Each TUI start sends them again on a worker. With nothing kept, the start only checks for the record.
- A server that refuses a retry holds back only its own kept sign-outs. The other servers' still go.
- Kept sign-outs live next to the MCP credential store: in the macOS Keychain when the store is there, otherwise in `~/.fx/mcp-revocations.json` with mode 0600. They are dropped after 30 days.
- A retry sends a revocation only to an endpoint the MCP server's own sign-in could use.

The unconfirmed logout line changes from:

```
Signed out of NAME here, but its server didn't confirm the revocation, so its tokens may stay valid until they expire.
```

to:

```
Signed out of NAME here, but its server didn't confirm the revocation, so its tokens may stay valid for now. fx will try again later.
```

## Design

- MCP sign-outs use `pending_revocation.zig`, which already keeps the Codex, Grok, and fx login sign-outs. The lock, the lease that stops two fx processes from sending the same one, the 30-day expiry, the size limits, and the handling of a damaged record stay in one place. A separate MCP store would copy all of it.
- One MCP record holds the sign-outs of every server, so a failed retry skips only the later sign-outs of the same server (`server_url`). Codex, Grok, and the fx login keep no server URL, so their first failure still ends the retry, as before.
- A kept MCP sign-out has five more fields than the others, so the record's size limit rises from 128 KiB to 256 KiB for every source, the fx login's Keychain item included. One sign-out still always fits.
- A retry sends the request from core through the OAuth transport, not through the engine. Giving the engine an old credential would replace the login the server holds now. The request uses the engine's own OAuth helpers, and its endpoint is checked with the engine's rule (`discovery.fetchable`).
